cantar.c: CANTAR I ICK POLE, is the Southern Pole, or End of the Earth ’ s Axis; ’ tisfo called because op - polite to the Ar icl ( of North - Pole.

cutbastion.c: CUT BASTION, is. that which makes a Re - entring Angle at the Point; and is sometimes called,,

caballinealices.c: CABALLINE Alices, is a coixrfer fore, which being generally used by Farriers to purge Hories, is called by this Name of Caballine Alices.

cable.c: CABLE of a Ship, is ( as is well known ) a great Rope of Strands, which being fastened to the Anchor holdeth the Ship fast when ( lie rides. The Sea Terms about it are, x. T he Cable is well laid, that is, is well wrought or made. z. Serve the Cable, or Plat the Cable, that is, bind it about with Ropes, Clouts, &c to keep it from galling ' in the Hawse.. To splice a Cable, is to make two Pieces fall: together, by working the several Strands of the Rope one into another;. To Quoile the Cable, is to roll it up round in a Ring, of which the several Rolls one upon another are called Cable Tire.. They fay. Pay more Cable, that is, let it more out from the Ship, that the Boat which carries the Anchor may the more east - Iy drop it into the Sea; and sometimes they fay Pay cheap the Cable ( f e. ) put or hand it out apace. In the fame Sense, as Pay more Cable, they fay also Veer more Cable, that is, hand or let more out. When two Cables are spliced together, ’ tis called A Shottof a Cable.

cabosed.c: CABOSED ( Spanijh ) the Term in Heraldry for the Head of any Beasts, being cut off just behind the Ears by a Section parallel to the Face, or by a perpendicular Section; whereas Couping is usually expressed by an Horizontal one, and is never so dofeto the Ears as Cabofing.

caburns.c: CABURNS fin a Ship ) are Lines uled to bind Cables withal; they are usually made of Pope Tarn or Spun Yarn.

cacatoriafebris.c: CACATORIA Febris, is an intermittent Fever, ( so called by the famous Sylvius ) accompanied with a violent Purging, which is Sometimes griping and very painful, extreamly afflufting and weaning to the Patient.

cachecticus.c: CACHECTICUS, is one that has an ill Habit of Body. "

cachexy.c: CACHEXY, is an ill Habit of Body, proceed - ing from a bad Disposition of the Fluids and Hu - hours; whence lingering Fevers, Confumptions and Dropfies are contracted: In this Disease the Face is often Pale and Difcoloured, and the Body big and swoln. Cachexia, taken also in a large Sense, is opposite to and as a good Habit of Body is common to all lound Parts, so an ill one is propagated by all the ill Parts. Stricftly, Cachexy is only taken for an ill Disposition of the Habit of the Body; and Euexia, on the contrary, for a good Disposition of the Humours, or Blood, and Body. Blanchard.

cacochymy.c: CACOCHYMY, is the abundance of ill Hu - hours in the Blood; and it is either Ulcerous, Bilious, Pituitous, Melancholick, Acid, Salt or Sharp. Blanchard.

cacoetheschironiumview.c: CACOETHES, Chironium View, or Telephium; is a Disease or Ulcer beyond Cure, which is called a Malignant Vlcer; this happens when an Ulcer is Callous or Sinuous, under which there some - times lie little purified Bones that have fallen down. Blanchard,

cadenceorclose.c: CADENCE, or Close, in Musick, is a kind of Conclusion of the Tune, which is made of all the Parts together in divers Places of any Key, C A L

caducusmorbus.c: CADUCUS Morbus, or the Epilepjy, is a Con - vulfive Motion of all the Parts of the Body, more especially in the Hands and Feet, accompanied with a Deprivation of the Inward and Outward Senses.

cjecumintestinum.c: CJECUM Intestinum, the Blind Gur, so called because one End of it is shut up, insomuch that the Faces and Chyle both come in and go out at the fame Orifice. Its Use in Man is obscure, as be - ing very small and commonly empty. CiESAREAN SeBion, the cutting open of a Woman ’ s Belly or Womb, to make way for the Child to be taken out. CiESURA, in Grammar, is when in a Latin ’ or Greek Verie there remains a Syllable after a Foot, and that Syllable ends the Word. Of this they reckon four forts, Triemimeris, Penthemimeriss Hepihemimeris and Enneemimeris: Which fee. If it were not for this C recur a, few Verses could be made to run well; as is plain in these two, where there is no C recur a at all, Aursa Carmina, full, feribis, maxims datum Vrbemfortem ccepit nuper for tit or Heft is..

caissonorsuperficialfour.c: CAISSON, or Superficial Four neats, is a Wood - en Case or Chest, into which,, or Bombs, according to the Execution they are to do, or as the Ground is simmer or looser ( sometimes the Chest is only filled with Powder ) when the Be - figed dispute every Foot of Ground, this Caisson is buried under some Work the Enemy intends to possess himself of, and when he is Master of it, they fire it by a Train conveyed in a Pipe, and so blow them up. Thus they fay after the Mine had destroyed the Bonnet, A Caisson was buried under the Ground thrown up, and the Enemy advancing to make a Lodgement on the ftuins of the Bonnet, the Caisson was fired, and blew up the Post thefecond time. ! '.

caisson.c: CAISSON, is also a covered Waggon to carry Bread or Ammunition.

calamusscriptorius.c: CALAMUS Scriptorius, is a certain Dilatation in or about the th Ventricle of the Brain, whole lower Part is inserted into the Medulla Oblongata, making there a Cavity in Shape of a Pen; whence it was anciently called Calamus Scriptorius.

calcaneusoroscalcis.c: CALCANEUS, or Os Calcis, the Heel Bone, is a Bone of the Tarsus; it lies under the Aftragalius, to which it is articulated by the Ginglymus. Behind it has a large Protuberance which makes the Heel, and into which the Tendo Achillis is inserted; and Before it has a Cavity which receives a Part of the Os Cubiforme.

calchoidea.c: CALCHOIDEA, are three little Bones in the Foor, which, with others, make up that Part of the Eoot succeeding the Ancle; and Fallopius calls them Cuneiformia, because they are made like Wedges.

calcination.c: CALCINATION, is the Solution of a mix ’ d Body into Powder by Fire, or any corroding things, as Mercury, Aquafortis, &c. and when Horns, Bones, Hoofs, &c. are hanged over boiling Water ( or other Liquor ) rill they have loft their Mucilage and will easily be powdered, this, by some Chy - miffs, is called Calcination Philosophical, CAL - A CALCINATION of Copper: See JEs VJlum.

calcinationofflints.c: CALCINATION of Flints, of of Ghryjlal, Peb - bles, is made by heating them red hot, and then halting them, whilst so, into cold Water or Vine - gar; for after this is done p or times, they will be very friable, and easily powdered, for which end they are calcined.

calcinationofleaf.c: CALCINATION of Leaf, melt the Mettle in an Earthen Pan unglazed, keep it stirred over the Fire with a Spatula, till it be reduced into a Pow - der. This is what they call Calx of Lead, and by this M ns the Metal is made more open and fit to be wrought upon by Acids. Lead, as well as Tin, sensibly encreases its Weight in Calcination.

calcinationoftin.c: CALCINATION of Tin. Put Engiijh Tin into a large Earthen Pan unglazed in a great Fire, and then the Tin will melt; continue the Fire very strong for Hours, stirring the Matter with an Iron Spatula from time to time; then take it off the Fire and letitcool, and you will have the Calx of Tin. The Tin will encrease its Weight in this Operation, for Ounces of Metal will yield Ounces of Calx.

calcinationofvitriol.c: CALCINATION of Vitriol, is usually of the Green fort ' tis put over the Fire in an Earthen tjnglazed Pan; the Vitriol will dissolve into a kind of Water; then ’ tis boiled till the Moisture be consumed, or till it return into a grayish Mass. This is called Vitriol Calcined to Whiteness. Then if it were kept long over a strong Fire -, it Would turn Red, and is then called Col cot bar.

calculationofclock.c: CALCULATION of Clock, and Watchwork ' - See Clock and Watch - work.

calculusdifferentiate.c: CALCULUS Differentiate, is the Arithmetick of the infinitely small Differences between variable Quantities: This, in England, we call the Arith - rnetick. of Fluxions: See Fluxions.

calculusintegrate.c: CALCULUS Integrate, is the Method of find - ing the proper flowing Quantity of any given Flux - ion; and is the Reverse of the Calculus Different - ate, which finds the Fluxion from the flowing Quantity.

calendaroralmanack.c: CALENDAR, or Almanack, is a Political Du ftribution of Time accommodated to Use, and taken from the Motions of the Heavenly Bodies: Of this kind are those Annual Books wherein the Days of the Month, the Feftivals, the Sign the Sun is in, the Suns Riling and Setting, the Chan - ges of the Moon, &c. are exhibited; which we also call Almanacks. But the Word Calender seems to come from the Calendar, which, amongst the - Romans, were the first Days of every Month. There have been many Corrections and Refor - motions of the Calendar: The first was made by Numa Pompilius; and this afterwards was much improved by Julius Cafar, and was by him called the Julian Account, which, in our Nation, and some other Places, is still retained, and is called Old Style. Pope Gregory the XHIth pretended to reform it again, and ordered his Account to be currant, as it still is in all the Roman Catholick Countries, where ’ tis called the Gregorian Calendar; ‘ and with us New Style: It now begins eleven Days before ours. A particular Account of the Nature of the Juli - an and Gregorian Account, see in a Book called The Julian and Gregorian Tear: And how both are pretended to be reform ’ d, lee in a stitch Pamphlet called The Reformed Calendar; Printed scr Sam. Man Up ' at the Ship near the Royal Exchange Cornhill,.

calends.c: CALENDS; so the Romans call ’ d the first Days of very Month, from the Greek Word Kafiv, vo - co, to call j because anciently counting their Months by the Motion of the Moon, there was a Priest ap - pointed to observe the Times of the New Moon - who having seen it, gave Notice to the Prefidenr over the Sacrifices, and he called the People toge - ther, and declared unto them how they must reck - on the Days until the Nones, pronouncing times the Word v. ate, if the Nones happened on the th Day, or times if they happened on the th Day of the Month. f

calibreorcaliper.c: CALIBRE, or Caliper, is the Bigness, or rather Diameter of a Piece of Cannon, or any Fire Arms, at the Mouth.

calipers.c: CALIPERS, is an Instrument made like a Sli - ding - Rule, to einbrace the two Heads of any Cask, to find the Length. There is also the Gunners Calipers or Compasses for finding the Diameter of the Ball, and Bore of the Gun.

calipercompasses.c: CALIPER Compasses, are Compasses used by Gunners, with crooked or bowing Legs, to mea - sure the Diameters of Bullets and Cylinders of Guns.

calkingorcauking.c: CALKING or Cauking of a Ship, is driving in Oakam, of fomethingof that kind, into the Seams of the Planks, to prevent the Ship ’ s Leaking.

callippickperiod.c: CALLIPPICK Period, was an Improvement of the Cycle of Meton of Years, which Callipus, a famous Grecian Aftronomor, finding in reality to contain of Nabondjfor's Years, Days and he, to avoid Fradions, quadrupled the Golden Number, and by that Means made a new Cycle or Period of Years; which time being expired, he supposed the Lunations or Changes of the Moon would all happen on the fame Day of the Months " and Hour of the Day, that they were on Years before.

callous.c: CALLOUS: A Swelling is said to grow Callous, when ’ tis hardened, as sometimes the Lips of a Wound. This is derived from

callus.c: CALLUS, which is a kind of Swelling without Pain, like Skin contraded by too much Labour. - Blanchard.

calthrops.c: CALTHROPS: See Cause - trapes or Cows - feet.

calvathehairyscalp.c: CALVA, the Hairy Scalp, or upper Part of the Head, which either by Disease or Old Age grows Bald first.

calxinchymistry.c: CALX, in Chymistry, is that which is produced by Burning or Calcination ( " which fee ) of any Metal or Mineral in a Crucible, &c.

calx.c: CALX, is the second Bone in that Part of the Foot which succeeds the Ancle, bigger and strong - er than the reft; oblong and grows backward, that a Man may stand more strongly upon it, and not fall fp easily backward.
CALX also is that which by Calcining is either turned into Alcoal, as Calx Saturni, or at least is made friable, as jars s - Horn burnt.

calxofantimony.c: CALX of Antimony: See Antimonium Diapho - reticum.

calxofgold.c: CALX of Gold. Though it hath been look'd upon as a thing of great Difficuly, yet the Noble Mr. Boyle tells us, that if you grind well together a thick Amalgama of Gold and Mercury, with at x least; C A Ifeaft an equal Weight of finely powdered Sulphur, and then put the Mixture to sublime in a proper Glass, there will rife, by Degrees of Fire, a In - nabar; and this will leave behind it a finer Calx of Gold than is to be had by some far more diff - cut Processes. See the Meehan, Product of Vola - vility.

calyxinbotany.c: CALYX, in Botany, signifies the Cup which contains or encloses the Flower in any Plant; and sometimes ' tis used for the Flower it self when its Figure is like that of a Rose, and not yet having its Leaves Expanded.

camberng.c: CAMBER NG, the Sea - man fay a Deck lies Cam - bring when it doth not lie Level, but higher in the Middle than at either End. Also if her Reel is bent in the Middle upwards f which may happen from her lying a - ground on a place where neither her Aft nor Fore - part do touch it, and from many other Reasons taken from her make ) they fay file is Chamber - steel ’ d..

campaign.c: CAMPAIGN, is a Military Term, signifying the Space of Time during which Armies are main rain ’ d every Year in the Field. So a Man is said to have made twenty Campaigns, when he hath spent so many Years in War - like Service in the Field. T,,

campflying.c: CAMP Flying, is a strong Body of Horse and Foot commanded usually by a Lieutenant Gene - ral, which is always in Motion, both to cover our own Garrifons, and to keep the Adverse Army in continual Alarm.

canal.c: CANAL, is a Word frequently used by Anato - mical Writers, to signify a Channel or Passage, through which any Juices or Fluids of the Body do flow.

canaliculusarteriosus.c: CANALICULUS Arteriosus, is a Vessel betwixt the Arterious Vein in the Lungs, and the great Ar - tery in the Foetus; for its obliterated in Adult Per - sons: It ’ s Use in Foetus ' s is, that the Blood may be discharged by this DuSlus out of the Arterious Vein, into the great Artery, because that the Blood is not accended in the Lungs, for want of Respiration in the Womb..

cancer.c: CANCER, one of the iz Signs of the Zpdiack, drawn on the Globe in the form of a Crab, and thus marked g. Through the beginning of this Sign passes a Circle parallel to the Equinoctial, cal - led the Tropic of Cancer, or the Northern Tropic to which Circle, when the Sun comes, it makes the Summer Soljlice, and is turning his Course back a - gain towards the Equinoctial.

caninafames.c: CANINA Fames, or Dogs - Appetite, is an inordi - name Hunger attended with a Vomiting and a Loose - ness which proceeds from a depraved ACtion of the Stomach, craving Food in a greater Measure than Nature requires.

canini.c: CANINI are two Teeth m each Jaw, one on each side of ’ the Incisivi; they are pretty thick and round, and they end in a sharp Point; they have each one Root which is longer than the Roots of the Incisivi; their proper use is to pierce the hard - er kinds of Meat.. C ANINUS, a Muscle of the Lip, lerving to put the Lips upwards. - '

canismajor.c: CANIS Major & Minor, the greater and lesser Dog, are two Confte Uations of Stars drawn upon the Globe in Figure of this Animal; and the great - ter of them hath in his Mouth that vast Star called

caniculus.c: CANICULUS, or the Dog - star, which rising and letting with the Sun from about the th of July to the th of August, gives occasion to that time which is usually very Hoc and Sultry, to be called the Canicular or Dog - days;

cannonifioyal.c: CANNON Ifioyal, is a Piece of Ordnance In - neo Diameter in the Bore, Foot long, weighs / A its Charge lb. of, Powder; its Bail of / A weight, and Inches i in Diameter, shoots point blank Paces. This is the lame with & Cannon of Eight.

cannonapieceofordnance.c: CANNON, a Piece of Ordnance j See Ord - ance.

canoninmathematicks.c: CANON, in Mathematicks, is a Rule to solve all things of the lame Nature with the present En - quire: Thus every lass step of an Equation in Al - zebra is such a Canon, and if turned into Words is a Rule to solve all Questions of the fame Nature with that proposed. Canon also is the Word for the Tables of Logarithms, ’ Artificial Sines, Tan - gents, and Secants, which are of admirable use in Trigonometry. ’ Tis also the Name of a Surgeon s Instrument, which they make use of when they few up Wounds.

canonicalequations.c: CANONICAL Equations: See Quadratic A E - equations.

canon.c: CANON - LAW, is a Colle & ion of EcclefiafK - cal Rules, Definitions and Constitutions taken from ' the Ancient, General and Provincial Councils, the Writings and Refolutions of the Fathers of the Church, and the Refcrips of Popes. This Law is modeled according to the Form of the Civil, and is reduced into Volumes. The First is called the Decrees of Gratian, and is composed of the Ancient Canons, and Colle & ed from the Ancient Councils and Writings of the Fathers. The Second Volume is called the Decretals; and doth contain th decretal Epiftles or Refcripts of Popes, and chiefly from Alexander III. to Gregory IX. by whose Authority it was compiled. The Third Volume is called Sextum; and con - tains the Refcripts of the Popes from Gregory IX. to Boniface the VIII. by whose Authority it was Collected. To the End of this Volume are added the Clementina, which are the Constitutions of Cle - ment V. enabled in the Council of Vienna, as also the Extravagant s, which are some Refcripts of Pope John XXII. and some other Popes. They were called Extravagants, because not contained in the Body of the Canon Law; which is compo - fed of the three lately mentioned Volumes.

CANON, in the Ecclefialtical Law, was original - ly a Book wherein the Religious of every Convent had a fair Transcript of the Rules of their Order: These were often read over to them as their Local Statutes, and therefrom were called fecula and Canon, Their Rule.

canthusorhircw.c: CANTHUS or Hircw, is the Angle or Corner, of the Eye; which is either the greater or the In - ternal, or the less or External.

cantonanordinaryinheraldry.c: CANTON, an Ordinary in Heraldry, framed ? of two strait Lines, one drawn perpendicularly ! from the Chief and the other so from the Side of the Escutcheon. This is always ' ( less than a Quarter of the Field; and if drawn from the Left Corner of the Escutcheon, is called a Can - ton Sinister. Its Form is thus; He beareth Ermin, a Canton Argent charged with a Cheveron Gules, by the Name of Middleton.

canvas.c: CANVAS - BAGS, or Earth - Bags, Sacs a Terre l as the French call them, are Bags holding about a Cubicle; ark A A A A'AAAA t TT CAP CAP Cubick Foot of Earth, and are used to raise a Pa - tapet in haft, or to repair one that is beaten down: They are chiefly used when the Ground is Rocky and affords no Earth to carry on the Approaches, then are these Bags of Earth very necessary, which can be filled at another place and rertloved at plea - sure: These Bags are sometimes upon occasion filled with Powder, of which they hold about pound.. -

cap.c: CAP in a Ship, is a Square Piece of Timber put over the Head or upper End of any Mast, hav - ing a round Hole to receive a Mast. By. these Caps the Top - Masts and Top - Gallant - Masts are kept steady and firm in the Trejfel - Trees, where their Feet stand, as those of the lower Mails do in the Steps. They call also that Piece of Lead which is put over the Touch - hole of a great Gun to keep the Prime from being wafted or spilt, the Cap of the Gun.

CAP - SQUARES, are broad Pieces of Iron on each Side of the Carriage of, a great Gun, and lock ’ d over the Trunnions of the Piece with an I - ron Pin: Their use is to keep the Piece from fly - ing out of the Carriage, when ’ tis shot off with its Mouth lying very low, or as they call it under Me - tal.,

capacity.c: CAPACITY ( In Law ) signifies the Ability of a Man, or Body Politick, to give or take Lands or other things, or lue A & ions.

capacityingeometry.c: CAPACITY, in Geometry, is the solid Con - tents of any Body: Also our Hollow Measures for Wine, Bear, Corn, Salt &c. are called Measures tf Capacity.

cape.c: CAPE, is a Writ Judicial, touching Plea of Lands or Tenements; and divided into Grand - Cape and Petit - Cape, both which takes hold of things immoveable, and seem to differ in this, that the Grand - Cape lieth before Appearafice, and Pe - tit - Cape afterwards.,.,

capeorpromontory.c: CAPE, or Promontory, is any high Land run - ning out with a Point into the Sea, as Cape Very, Cape Horn, the Cape of Good Hope, &c.

capeparvum.c: CAPE Parvum, is a Writ that lieth in case where the Tenant is summoned in Plea of Land, and cometh at the Summons, and his Appearance s of Record; and after he maketh Default at the Day that is given to him, then this Writ shall go for the King.

capeadvalentiam.c: CAPE ad Valentiam, is a Writ of Execution er a Species of Grand Gape, so called of the End whereunto it fendeth p In the Old Nit. Brev. it is thus described; This Writ lieth, where any im - pleaded of certain Lands, and he vouches to war - rant another, against whom the Summons ad War - anti andmn hath been awarded, and the Vouchee comes not at the Day given; then if the Deman - dant recover against the Tenant; he shall have this Writ against the Vouchee, and shall recover so much in Value of the Vouchee ’ s Land, if he have so much; and if fie have not so much, then the Tenant shall have Execution, by this Writ, offuch Lands and Tenements as descend to him in Fee - simple; or if he purchase, afterwards, the Tenant shall have against him a Re - summons, and if he can fay nothing, he shall recover the VaHie. Note, This Writ lies before appearand.

capella.c: CAPELLA, a bright fixed Star in the Left Shoulder of Auriga, whose Longitude is. Deg Min. Latitude ll Deg. Min. Plight Ascension c. V

capias.c: CAPIAS, is a Writ of two forts, one before Judgment, called Capias ad fiefpondendum, in an Adlion Personal, where the Sheriff upon the first Writ of Distress, returns nihil habet in halliva no - fra; and the other is a Writ of Execution after Judgment, which are of divers kinds, as these following.

CAPIAS conduces adprofcifcendum, is a Wyc for taking up such as having received Prest Money to serve the King, slink away, and come not in at the time: This is an Original Writ directed to the Serjeant at Arms, to arrest and bring them in, having included a Clause of Afllftance.

CAPIAS pro fine, is, where one being by Judge - ment fined unto the King, upon the fame Offence committed against a Statute, doth not discharge it according to the Judgment, for by this is his Bo - dy taken and committed to Frifon, until he con - tent the King for his Fine.

CAPIAS utlegatum, is a Writ of Execution which lieth against him that is out - law ’ d upon any Suit, by which the Sheriff, upon the Receipt there - of, apprehendeth the Party out - lawed for not appearing upon the Exigent, and keepeth him in fare Custody till the return of the Writ, then bringeth him into Court, there further to be order - ed for his Contempt,

CAPIAS utlegatum & Inquiras de bonis catafi lis, is a Writ all one with the former, but it gives a farther Power to the Sheriff, besides the Appre - pension of his Body, to enquire of his Goods aud Chattels.,

CAPIAS ConduLlos ad Proftcifcendum is a Writ that lies for taking up such Men as having receive ’ d Press - money to serve the King, slink away and come not in Time. Tis an original Writ dire & ed to the Serjeant at Arms, having included a Clause of Assistance.

capiasadsatisfaciendum.c: CAPIAS ad Satisfaciendum, is a Writ of Eye - cution aster. Judgment, lying where a Man rec - vers, in an Aiftion Personal, as Debts, or Damages, or Detinue in the King ’ s Court; and he against whom the Debt is recovered, and hath no, Lands nor Tenements, nor fufficientGoods, whereof the Debt may be levy ’ d: For in this Case he that re - covereth shall have this Writ to the Sheriff, com - minding him, that he take the Body of him against whom the Debt is recovered, and he shall be put in Prison until Satisfaction made.,

capiasinwithernamium.c: CAPIAS in Withernamium de homine, is a Writ that lieth for a Servant in Withernam.

capiasinwithernamdeaveriis.c: CAPIAS in Withernam de Averiis, is a Writ that lieth for Cattle in Withernam.

capillamentscapiliamenta.c: CAPILLAMENTS, Capiliamenta, are those small Threads or Hairs ( whence the Word ) which grow up in the Middle of a Flower, and are a - dorned with little Knops at the Top: Those Knops are called the Apices of a Flower; and these C - pill aments are called the Stamina.

capillaryplants.c: CAPILLARY Plants, are such as have no main Stalk or Stem, but grow to the Ground as Hairs to one ’ s Head, and, which beartheir Seeds in little Tuffs, Bunches or Protuberances on the Back - side of their Leaves, whence by some they are called ! Dorfiparte and Ter gi feet a. And these are either with an.. Undivided Leaf, as the Hasmionitis and the Phyfi litis; or with a Singly divided Leaf; and these have the Leaf ei - ther cut or jagged in, but not divided into Pinna clear home to the main Rib; as Poly podium, Lon - chit is Scolopendria, Adianthum, Acroftichon That , Or else divided quite home to the Rib, and. hanging like Pinna - as the Chamafelix Marins and the. Trichomanes. Others have the Leaf Doubly divided, or at least once subdivided; the first Division being into Branches, md the d into Pinna Pinna, as the Hcmionites Multifida, the Filix mas, the Filix P & luftris, Filix Saxatilis, the Adiantum Album, and Nigrum. And others have the Leaf Trebly divided, or twice subdivided, vig. first into Branches, then into little Twigs, and after this into Pinna - and these are the Filix Scandens of Urn file, the. Filix Florida or Ofmunda Regain, the Filix mas Ramofa, the Filix Femina Vulgaris, the Adiantum album Floridum, and the Dry opt er is Ni - gra. Ray ’ j Hiftoria Plant arum. - CAPILLARY Vessels, small Veins and Arteries, like Thread or Hairs.

capillation.c: CAPILLATION, according to some Writers, is a Frudinre in the Skull so small that it can scarce be found, which yet often proves mortal.

capitatepi.c: CAPITATE Pi ant a, in Botany, are such Plants whose Flowers are composed of many edged and hollow little Flowers; and Mr. Ray calls them by this Name, because their Scaly Calyx ( or Cup of the Flower ) most usually swells out into a large and round Belly, containing within it the Pappous Seed as Carduus, Centaury, Knapweed, Cinara, Cirfium, Lappa maj. Cyantts, ( c.

capital.c: CAPITAL of a Bastion, in Fortification, is a Line drawn from the Angle of the Polygon to the Point of the Bastion, or from the Point of the Ba - stion to the Middle of the Gorge. These Capitals are from to Fathom long, that is to fay, from the Point of the Bastion to the Place where the two Demigorges meet.

capitalorchapitel.c: CAPITAL, or Chapitel, of Chapiter, fignifiesin Architecture the Top of a Pillar and this is dise - rent, according to the different Orders.

capite.c: CAPITE, is a Tenure that holds immediately of the King, as of his Crown, be it by Knight - service or Soccage, and not of any Honour, Castle or Mannor.

capituluminbotanicks.c: CAPITULUM, in Botanicks, is the Head or Flowing Top of any Plant, being composed of many Flowers and Threads ( or Stamina ) closely connected in a Globous, Circular or Discous Fi gure as the Flowers of Bltw - bottles, Scabiius, Carduus, ( c.

caponniereinfortification.c: CAPONNIERE, in Fortification, is a covered Lodgment of about or Foot broad, encom - passed with a little Parapet of above two Foot high, which serves to support the diverse Planks laden with Earth. This Lodgment is large enough to Contain or Soldiers, and is usually placed upon the Ex - tremity, of Jhe Counterscarp, having sometimes fe - veral little Embrasures made therein, commonly called Mardrejfes. They are generally on the Glacis, or in dry Moats. CAPRiE Saltantes, is the Term for a fiery Me - teor or Exhalation which sometimes appears in the Atmosphere, and is not fired in a strait Line, but With Inflexions or Windings in and out.

capreolariavasa.c: CAPREOLARIA Vasa, in an Animal Body, are such as twine about like the Capreoli or Tendrils of Vines.

capreolusinbotany.c: CAPREOLUS, in Botany, is the Clasp or Ten - dril, by which the Vines and such like creeping Plants fasten themselves to those things Which are designed to support them. CAPREOLATAi Plant at, are such Plants as turn, wind and climb along the Surface of the Ground, by Means of their Capreoli or Tendrils as Gourds, Melons, Cucumbers ( c v

capricornthegoar.c: CAPRICORN, the Goar, one of the Zodiacal Signs marked thus, v: Through the first Degree of it, the Southern Tropick, or the Tropick of Capricorn passes at. '. Distance from the E quator.

capstan.c: CAPSTAN, or as the French write ir C abaft an,. others Capstan, of a Ship, is of two kinds, the Main Capstan, and the Jeer Capstan The Main Capstan is that Piece of Timber which is placed next behind the Main Mast, its Foot or lower End standeth in a Step, on the lower Deck j and its Head is between the two upper Decks. Its several Parts are thus called the smallest Part of ir the Spindle the Brackets fee unto the Body of the Capstan dole under the Barrs, they call the Whelps. The main Substance orPoftof the whole Piece is the Barrel, through which the Barrs go. The Pawl is a. Piece of Iron bolted to one End of the Beams of the Deck, close to the Body of the Capstan, to stop the Capstan from turning back and this Stoppage they call Pawling the Capstan. The Use of the Capstan is to weigh the Anchors, to hoise up, or ( Iris ? down Top - Masts, to heave any weighty thing, or to strain a - ny Rope that requireth a main force. The Jeer Capstan is placed in the fame manner as the Main Capstan, between the Main - Mast and the Fore - Malt, and its Use is chiefly to heave upon the Jeer Rope ( which fee ) or to heave upon the Viol, and to hold off by when the An - s chor is weighing. The Terms belonging to the Use of the Capftam are, Come up Capstan, that is, slack the Cable which you heave by; in which Sense also they fay. Launch out the Capstan Pawl the Capstan, is stop ’ d it from going back, as was above hinted.

capsulacommunis.c: CAPSULA Communis, of GUJfon, is a Mem - brane proceeding from the Peritoneum, and includ - ing both the Porus Bilarius and the Vena Porta in the Liver.

capsulaseminal.c: CAPSULA Seminal is, in Botany, is the Case or Husk, that holds the Seed of any Plant.

capsuleatrabilaria.c: CAPSULE Atrabilaria, the fame with the Red nes Succentuariati: Which fee.

capsuleseminales.c: CAPSULE Seminales, in Anatomy, are the extreme Cavities of the Vessels which convey the Semen in an Animal Body they are dilated like little Coffers, which by two small Holes emit the Semen received from the Testicles into the little Seminary Bladders, thatic may either be preserve - ed there against the time of Coition, or be re - duced into Blood by the Lymphetick Vessels. Blanchard: See Testes and Testicle.

caption.c: CAPTION, when a Commission is executed,, ' and the Commissioners Names subscribed and re - turned, that is called the Caption,
CAPTION, when a Commission is executed, the Commissioners Names subscribed and return ’ d, that is called a Caption.

caputmortuum.c: CAPUT Mortuum, is that thick dry Matter thac remains after Distillation of anything, but of Mi - nerals especially and very commonly ir denotes only that which remains of Vitriol in its Distil - lation, which they call Golcothar Vitriols: See Earth and Terra Damnata. This Caput Mortuum though in some Cafes there be but little, if any Adtive Principle left in it, yet is never pure, and the Colcothar Vitrioli, if exposed to the Air, will turn into Vitriol again.

carat.c: CARAT: A Carat of Gold is properly the Weight of Grains or one Scruple so that Carats make an Ounce U If an Ounce of Gold be so pure, that in its Pu - rification ( ' with Antimony, or otherwise ) it loles nothing at all; ' tis then said to be Gold of Ca - rats: If it lose one Carat, ’ tis then Gold of Ca - rats and if it lose two Carats in Purification, ’ tis called Gold of Carats, ( c. But perhaps there is no such thing as Gold of Carats, for it will retain some stall Portion of Silver or Copper, pu - rify it as long as you will. A CARAT of Diamonds, Pearls, or Precious Stones, is the Weight of four Grains only.

CARAT is nor any certainWeight orQuantity, but the Part of any Quantity or Weight. And the Minters and Gold - smith divide it into Parts, which they call Grains of a CaraB and one of these they subdivide in Halves and Quarters.

carbunculation.c: CARBUNCULATION, is theblafting of the new spouted Buds of Trees or Plants, either by excefllve Heat, whereby the Texture of the Fibres of the Vegetable are so dissolved, that its Pores become wholly changed; or else by excessive Cold, which compresses its Fibres so, that the Pores thereby are shut up, and leave no Passage for the Alimentary Juice.

carcass.c: CARCASS, is an Iron Case or hollow Capacity about the Bigness of a Bomb, sometimes made all of Iron ( except two or three Holes through which the Fire is to bla ? e ) and sometimes made only of Iron Bars or Hoops, and then covered over with Pitched Cloth, Hemp, ( c. and filled with several kinds of Materials for firing of Houses: They are thrown out of Mortar - Pieces, like Bombs, iritoBe - siege Places, ( c.
CARCASS of a House, in Architecture, are the Partitions, Floors, Rafters, &c. made by the Carpenter.

carcinodesatumour.c: CARCINODES, a Tumour resembling a Can - ter. Blanchard.

carcinomacarcinus.c: CARCINOMA, Carcinus, or Cancer, is a Tu - mour that arises round, hard, livid, painful; at the Beginning as big as a Pea, but afterwards its surrounded with great ( swelling Veins, which re - sperable the Feet of a Crab ( though not always, ) whence the Name. Blanchard.

cardiac.c: CARDIAC, is a Suffocation of the Heart from a Polypus or coagulated Blood. Blanchard.

cardiadicumacordial.c: CARDIADICUM, a Cordial, is a Medicine which ( as they formerly thought, ) corroborates the Heart; but it rather only puts the Blood into a fine. ' gentle Fermentation, whereby the Spirits formerly decayed are repaired and invigorated, so that the Blood, by consequence, circulates more easily and briskly.

cardiacusplexus.c: CARDIACUS Plexus, is a Branch of the eighth Pair of Nerves or the Par Vagum, which about the first or second Rib, is sent from its descending Trunks, and is bestowed upon the Heart and its Appendage.

cardialgia.c: CARDIALGIA, is a gnawing Pain sometimes felt in the Scrobiculut Cordis; or, as Blanchard faith, CARDIALGIAand Cardiogmos, the Heart - burn - ing, is a Gnawing or Contraction of the Nerve called Par Vagum, and the Intercostal implanted in the Stomach,, proceeding from a pungent vellicate - ing Matter in the Ventricle -; so that the Heart be - ing ftraitened and contracted by Consent with the Stomach, occasions sometimes a swooning away.

cardinalwindsorpoints.c: CARDINAL Winds or Points, are the South, Weft, North and End Points of the Compass; and also the EquinoCtial and Solstitial Points of the E - ecliptick, are called the Cardinal Points;

cardinalsigns.c: CARDINAL Signs, are those Signs of the qV diacli called Aries, Libra, Cancer and Capricorn.

careen.c: CAREEN: A Ship is said to be brought to a Careen, when the most Part of her Lading, ( c. being taken out, there k laid by her Side another Ship or Vessel lower than her, unto which ’ she is haled down as low as Occasion requires, as. to the th or th Strake, and there kept by the Weight of Ballast, Ordinance, ( c. as well as by Ropes, left it should strain her Malts too much. ' Tis done with a Design to trim her Sides or Bottom, to caulk her Seams, or to mend any thing that is at fault under Water: And from hence if a Ship lie on one Side much when she fails, they fay She fails on the Careen:

caryatides.c: CARYATIDES; an Order of Pillars in Archi - texture in the Form of the Bodies of Women with their Arms cut off, and cloathed in a Garment down to their Feet: Thele Figures do support the Entablature. There are some Columns of this Or - der in the famous Building at Bourdeaux, called the Tutellcs, and in the great Hall of the Smfs Guards at the Louvre in Paris; where four Carya - tides support a Gallery enriched with Ornaments very well cut. The rife of this Order of Pillars was this; The Inhabitants of Cary a in Pelopmnefus did once trea - cheroufly join with the Persians against their own Country; but the Grecians got the Battle, and put CA'S put all the Male Inhabitants of Cary a to the Sword, reducing the City to Allies. The Women they took Captives, and carried in Triumph: And the more to perpetuate the Memory of this base Acti - on, they would not permit these Women ever to put off their Triumphal Veftments; but ordered the ArchitCts of those times to express them in that dress, as supporting the heavy Weight of their Edifices, instead of usual Columns. The Perfidy Order of Pillars had much the fame Original: Which fee. Vitruv. lib. z. c. I.

caries.c: CARIES, is the Corruption of a Bone from the continual Afflux of vicious Humours, or from their Acrimony and Malignity, or from a Bruise that some way assess the Bones, or from sharp Medicines, ( c. Blanchard.

carlingvfnees.c: CARLING Vfnees, are those Timbers which g athwart the Ship from her Sides to the Hatch - way, and which bear up the Deck on both Sides, )

carlings.c: CARLINGS, are Timbers in a Ship lying Fort and Aft along from one Beam to another on these the Ledges reft, on which the Planks of the Deck are made fast. All the Carlings have their Ends let into the Beams, which is called Culvert ail.

carminativemedicines.c: CARMINATIVE Medicines, are Remedies that dispel or discuss Wind, either by appealing the Fermentations that occasion it, or by making it thin and opening the Pores that it may be ex - pelled. Blanchard.

carnation.c: CARNATION, is a Term in Painting, figni lying such Parts of an Human Body as are drawn naked, without any Drapery, or which express th bare Flesh; and when this is done Natural, Bold and Strong, and is well coloured, they lay of the Painter, that his Carnation is very good.

carnelthebuildingofships.c: CARNEL, The Building of Ships first with their Timbers and Beams, and after bringing on their. Planks is called Carnel - Worf, to distinguish it from Clinch - Work. Those Vessels also which go with Missen - Sails instead of Main - Sails, are by some called Cartels.

carnivorousanimals.c: CARNIVOROUS Animals, are such as feed on Flesh wholly or chiefly.

carnosity.c: CARNOSITY, is a more than ordinary Flefhf ness in any Part of theBody.

carnousfleshy.c: CARNOUS, Fleshy; whence the Membrane Carnosa or Panniculus Carnosus takes its Name, which is a Fleshy Membrane covering the whole Body.

carotheflesh.c: CARO, the Flesh of an Animal Body, is by Ana - tomifts defined to be a Similar and Fibrous Parr, soft and thick: They account it Five - fold; Muf - cular, Fistular or Fibrous, as is the Substance of the Heart and other Muscles.. Parenchymous, as the Lungs, Liver and Spleen were thought to be by the Ancients: But since the use of Glasses, ’ tis plainly discovered, that there is no such thing as a, Parenchyma, properly ( peaking,. but that all the Vi - seer, as well as other Parts of the Body, are Vafcu - Ur, and nothing but a Plexus or Net - work of ( mail Vessels and Canals. They call the Flefn of the Stomach and Guts,. Vifcerous; and the reckon a Fourth fort, whi h they call Glandulom as i F that that of the Pancreas, the Tonsils, the Breasts, &c. And,. They call the Fiefti of the Lips, Gums, of the Gians of the Penis, &c. Spurious, as being of a different Constitution from all the reft.

caroabotanickword.c: CARO, a Botanick Word for the Pulp, Flesh Or soft Substance contained within any Plant or its Fruit; such as the Pulp of Coffin, Tamarinds, Prunes, &c.

carotide.c: CAROTIDE, are Arteries in an Animal Body so called; they spring from the ascending Trunk of the Aorta or great Artery at the fame Place hearly where the Subclavian Arteries arise; here the Trunk begins to be divided into two Branches, which are these Carotides; they ascend diredlly upwards ( though the Right sometimes ariles from the right Subclavian ) and at their rife are sustained by the Thymus; then having bellowed Twigs on the Larynx, Tongue, the Muscles of the Os By - aides, and the adjacent Glands, they pass up on each Side by the Sides of the Wind - Pipe to the Say - cet, together with the Internal Jugular Vein, and there are subdivided into the External and Internal Branches. The External is smaller, and is dispersed into all the Muscles of the Cheeks, Forehead, Temples, Lips, and in general, through all the outer Parts of the Head and Face. The Internal, which is larger, fends first some more Twigs to rhe Larynx, Tongue, and so ai - so to the Glands behind the Ears, and the Ipongy Parts of rhe Palate and Nose: Then it entreth the zipper Jaw, and bellows a small flip on the Root of each Tooth ( as the External did on the Roots of the Teeth of the lower Jaw ) whereby fliarp Humours flowing in upon them, sometimes cause a very painful Tooth ach. The remainder of it climbs upon the Skull, being about its Basts divi - ded into two Branches; the less and hinder where - of having sent one flip to the inner Muscles of the Neck, and another through the Hole of the up - permoft Vertebra into the Membrane that inverts the Spinal Marrow, amending further enters the Skull at the Hole by which the sixth Pair of Nerves ( commonly so called ) comes out, and creeping a long the Dura Mater, ends near its Sinus ( which yet some fay Centers. ) The larger Branch, tend - ing upwards, is carried through the bony Channel in the Wedge - like Bone, with a winding Dudl to the Sella Equina -, at whose Basis, after it hath sent out a Twig on each Side into the Dura Mater, it opens it self into many small Slips, which being interwoven with those of the Cervical Artery ( a - abovementioned ) make the Bpte Mirabile, which is more observable in Beads than in Men, yet it is not all spent on the said Slips, but perforating the Dura Mater, it enters the Pia Mater with two notable Branches, which being divided into very small Twigs, are mingled with those of the Cer - vical Artery, with which they pass out of the Skull and accompany the Spinal Marrow even to the Loins. Afterwards i t fends a small Branch thro ' the second Hole of the Wedge - like Bone with the Optick Nerve, out of the Skull to the Eye: And yet still supplying more Twigs to the Substance of the Brain and Pia Mater, and being united with some other Twigs of the Cervical Artery, it makes the Plexus Choroides.

carpia.c: CARPIA. is a Tent that is put into a Wound or Ulcer to cleanse it.

carpus.c: CARPUS, commonly Brachiale, the first Part of the Palm of the Hand: Hefchyus calls it that Part of the Arm which is betwixt the lowermost Part bl the Cubit and the Hand, or the Wrist; it consists of eight small Bones, with which the Cu - bit is joined to the Hand. Blanchard.

carriage.c: CARRIAGE of a great Gun, is the Frame of Timber on which a Piece of Ordnance is laid fixed, and mounted. The common Proportion is i ' - of the Length of the Gun for the Carriage, the Wheels p of the Length of the Piece in Height, and times the Diameter of the Bore of the Gun, gives the Depth of the Planks at the Fore - end, in the Middle

cartilage.c: CARTILAGE, is a white Part, drier and har - der than a Ligament, and softer than a Bone; it is by some said to be a Similar and Spermatick Part, but sally; for it ’ s no more made of Seed, than any other Parts j it renders Articulation more easy, and defends several Parts from the Injuries from abroad. In aged Persons the Cartilages com - monly grow Bony. They have a Membrane just like the PerioJleumt and ’ tis indeed but a Continuation of it.

cartridgesorcarthrages.c: CARTRIDGES, or Carthrages, are Cafes of Paper, ' or as now they are usually made for the King ’ s Ships, to prevent Danger from Fire in, a Gun not well spunged, of Parchment; fitted ex - actly to the Bore of a Piece of Ordnance, and containing its due Charge of Powder. There are also Tin Cartridges, in which the Paper or Parch - ment ones are both formed and carried.

carunculjemyrtiformes.c: CARUNCULJE Myrtiformes, are the Wrink - lings of rhe Orifice of the Vagina, or Membranous Inequalities, not to be reckoned in any certain Number, which in Women with, Child, and af - ter Child - birth are so obliterated, that they are altogether imperceptible; there are for the molt part four of them. Blanchard. C RUN CULiE Oculi, are Glandules placed at each great Corner of the Bye, which separate Moisture for moistening the Eyes, the fame with Tears, which afterwards by the PunEt a Lachryma - ls a, placed in the Bone of the Nose, are difeharg - ed into the Nostrils. These are called Caruncula Lachrymales by some.

caruncuijepapihares.c: CARUNCUIJE Papi Hares, are Ten little Bo - dies that are in the Reins and Kidneys; they are properly little Bundles, which arise from the cen - thing together of a great many small Channels, which the Reins are in a great measure made up of; and those receive the Serum from the little DuBufs, and convey it into the Plevk. Blanchard.

carus.c: CARUS, is a Sleep, wherein the Person afleefted being pulled, pinched and called, scarce shews any sign of either hearing or feeling; it is without a Fever, greater than a Lethargy, and less than are Apoplexy. Blanchard.

cascabel.c: CASCABEL, is the hindermost round Knob or the utmost part of the Breech of a Piece of Ord - ance.

cascadeanitalianword.c: CASCADE, an Italian Word, fignifyingafall of Water, whether Natural or Artificial.

cascaninfortification.c: CASCAN, in Fortification, is a certain Hole or hollow Place in Form of a Well, from whence a Gallery dug in like manner under Ground is con - vey'd, to give Air to the Enemy ’ s Mine. Some of these Cafcans are more hollow than others, be - ng usually made in the Retrenchment of the Plat - form near the Wall.

casemateinfortification.c: CASEMATE, in Fortification, sometimes is the Well with its several Subteraneous Branches or Passages dug in the Passage of the Bastion till the Miner is heat'd at work, and Air given to the Mine. Also a certain Vault made of Mason ’ s Work, in that Part of the Flank of a Bastion which is next the Curtain, on purpose to fire upon the Ene - my, and to defend the Face of the opposite Ba - stion of the Moar. Sometimes it confiftsof Plat - forms one above another, the Terreplan of the Bastion being the highest. Behind the Parapet, which fronts along the Line of the Flank, there are Guns placed la - den with Cartridges of small Shot to scour along the Ditch; and these are covered from the Ene - my ’ s Batteries by Earth - works Faced or Lined with Wall, and are called Or i lions or Epaulments. This is the best Defence a Place can have.

caserninfortification.c: CASERN, in Fortification, is a little Room, or Lodgment, or Building, ereCted between the Rain part and the Houles of Fortified Towns, to serve as Appartments or Lodgings for the Soldiers of the Garrison, to ease the Garrison: There are usually a Beds in each Casern for fix Soldiers to lie and j but the d part being always on the Guard, there are but left in the Casern, z in a Bed.

case.c: CASE - SHOT, is when Musket Bullets, Stones, old Pieces of Iron, &c, are put up into Cafes and so shot out of great Guns. ’ Tis chiefly used at Sea to clear the Enemy ’ s Decks when they are full of Men.

CASE - HARDENING, is a way of making the Outside. of Iron hard. And ’ tis used sometimes by file Cutters when they make course Files for C ’ heapneis; and formerly most Ifajps were Case - hardened. Gunlmiths alio ule it to harden the Barrels of Guns; and for Tobacco Boxes, Cane Heads, Buttons, &c. ’ Tis done thus: They take Hoofs or Horns of Kine, dry them in an Oven, and powder them; then they put an equal Quanti - ty of Bay Salt to it, and mingle both together with stale Urine or White Wine Vinegar. Some of this Mixture they lay upon Loam, and wrap it about the Iron, putting also more Loam over all. Then lay it upon the Hearth of the Forge to dry and harden; and when ' tis dry and hard they put it into the Fire, and blow till they give the whole Lump a blood - red Heat, but no greater. Then ’ tis taken out and quenched, and at last the Case har - dened Iron is taken out of the Case.

caskets.c: CASKETS ( in a Ship ) are small Strings made of Sinnet, and fattened to the upper Sart of the Yards in little Rings ( which they call Grommets. ) Their use is to fasten the Sail to its Yard when ' tis to be furl ’ d up. The biggest and longest of these is in the middle of the Yard, just between yes, and is called the Breajl Casket.

cassiopeiaorcajfiopceia.c: CASSIOPEIA, or Cajfiopceia, the Name of one of the Constellations of the fix ’ d Stars in the Northern Hemisphere, consisting of a Stars, and - is placed opposite to the Great Bear on the other side the Pole Star.

castapoint.c: CAST a Point ofTraverfe, in Navigation, figni - fies to prick down on a Chart the Point of the Com - pass any Land bears from you, or to find on what Point the Ship bears at any instant or what Way the Ship has made.

But perhaps Ink. - horn is corrupted front Inkern or Inner.

catagma.c: CATAGMA, is a breaking of Bones, or a Se - pacation of the Continuum in the hard parts of the Body i which is afledred with some hard Instru ment forcibly impressed upon the part; whole Dis - ferences are taken from the Form, the Part, and several Accidents. Blanchard

cataphora.c: CATAPHORA, is the fame with Coma; they, only differ in this, that Cataphora is taken as the Genus to all forts of Stupors that are not attended with a Fever. Blanchard.

cataplasm.c: CATAPLASM, is a topical Medicine of the confidence of a Pultife; it is usually preferib ’ d two ways, either boiled, or without it; the former is mote frequent, the latter of more efficacy: In the former, they are to take such Vegetables as are proper, as Roots, Herbs, Seeds, Flowers, Fruits, &c. adding proper Meals, or omitting them; all which are boiled up in a convenient quantity of Liquor, v. g. Water, Beer, Milk, Honey, &c. to the confidence of a Pultife: The latter is prepared commonly of Vegetables shred final ! with theinfu - sion of lo much Liquor only as may make it of the former Confidence. You may add here Meal, Crums of Bread, Oyls, Ointments, as in the for - mer fort of Cataplafms. Blanchard.

cataptosis.c: CATAPTOSIS, is one Symptome of an Epi - lepfie, when Men fall suddenly to the Ground. Blanchard.

Blanchard.

catenaria.c: CATENARIA, is the Curve Line which a Rope hanging freely between two Points of Suspension forms it self into. What the Nature of this Curve is, was enquired amongst the Geometers in Gali - laus's time, but I don ’ t find any thing was done to - wards a Discovery till in the Year, James Bernoulli published it as a Problem; which, about two Months after, Leibnit declared he had found out, and would communicate within the Year: In December,, John the Brother of James Bernoulli communicated an Investigation of it to the Editors of the ABa Eruditorum, Which was pub - lich ’ d afterwards June. This Catenary or Funicular he faith he found not to be truly Geometrical, but of the Mechanical Kind, because its Nature cannot be expressed by a determinate Alge - brick Equation; but Leibnit z gives its Conftrudi - on Geometrically, In the Year, the Month of August, Dr. Gregory published a Method of In - veftigation of the former and some other new Pro - parties of this C curve which you will find there, from whence this Method of finding the general Property of the Catenaria is taken. x. catharpings.c: CATHARPINGS, are ( mail Ropes in a Ship running in little Blocks from one Side of the Shrouds to the other near the Deck, they belong only to the Main - Shrouds and Fore - Shr uds; Their use is to force the Shrouds taught, for the ease and safety of the Masts when the Ship rowls they are alio at the setting on of the Puttocks of the Shrouds, but there they do not run in Blocks but are made fast. CA ARTICK, is a purging Medicine which cleanse the Stomach, the Guts, and whatsoever is vitious and heterogeneous in the Blood, and throws it into the Common - Shore of the Guts, Blanchard, See Purgatio & Vomitorium.

catheter.c: CATHETER, is a Fistulous Instrument which is thrust up the Yard into the Bladder, to provoke Urine when its suppressed by the Stone; or into whose Cavity an Instrument called Itinerarium is thrust to find out the Stone in the Bladder, that then the SphinBer of the Bladder may be Crown and an Incision be made in the Perinxum.

cattorcatt.c: CATT or Catt - Field, a large Piece of Timber so called in a Ship; tis fattened aloft over the Hatofe, having at one End two Shivers, in which is reeved a Rope with a Block, and at the End of the Rope a large Hook, which is called the Catt - Hool: its use is to arise up the Anchor from the Hawse to the Top of the Fore - Caflle, where there is fattened a Stopper ( i. e. a Piece of Rope spliced in - to it ) at the Anchor, which serves to hitch the Hook of this Catt - Rope into the Ring of the An - chor.

catt.c: CATT - HOLES, in a Ship, are Holes in her Stern above the Gun - Room Port, and through them, by Means of a Stem - fast ( that is, some Fa - ttening behind the Stern ) to which a Cable or Haxtfer is brought, a Ship ( upon Occasion ) is heav - ed a - stern.

cavalierinfortification.c: CAVALIER, in Fortification is aHeaporMafs of Earth railed in a Fortress, to lodge the Cannon for scouring the Field, or oppofing a Commanding Work. These Cavaliers are fometimesof a Round, I sometimes of a Square Figure, the Top being bordered with a Parapet to cover the Cannon therein mounted. There must be Foot between Cannon and Cannon; and if they are raised on the Enclosure of any Place, whether in the Mid - dle of the Curtain, or in the Gorge or Bastion, are generally or Foot high above the Terre - plan of the Rampart. A Cavalier is forhetimes called a Doubly Bastion, and is designed to overlook the Enemy ’ s Batteries; and to scour their Trenches.

cavavena.c: CAVA VENA; the greatest Vein in the Body descends from the Heart; so called from its great Cavity, and into it, as into a common Channel, do all the letter Veins, except the Fulmonaris, em - pty themselves. Its Root may very properly be said to be in the Liver; for by its Capillaries it receives the Blood that is transcolate through the Glandulous Parenchyma of the Liver, from the Capillaries of the Porta, and by its attending Trunk conveys it to the Heart. These Capilla - ries emptying all the Blood exhausted out of the Liver into the Cava, it is prettntly divided into the Ascending and Descending Trunk.. The Amen - ding enters the Diaphragm and goes up the Thorax. The Descending Trunk, is somewhat narrower than the Ascending, and passes down along with the great Artery, continuing undivided till the fourth Vertebra of the Loins. But in the mean time fends forth divers Branches from its Trunk, as the Ve - nx Adipose, Emulgents, Spermatickj, Lumbares; All thele Veins being sent forth of the Trunk, by the time it is come to the fourth Vertebra of the Loins, where it turns to behind the Arteria Mag - na, above or before which it had thus far dettend - ed, and is then divided into equal Branches, called Iliad, because they pass over the Os Ilion, &c. as they go down to the Thighs. This Vein carries nothing to the Liver, but re - chives the Blood from thence, carrying it, and what it receives from its other Branches into the Right Ventricle of the Heart, that it may be there anew improved and inspirited.

If it be with - in Musket - foot, ’ tis a Place of Arms ready made to Hand; and a Convenience for opening the Trenches out of Fear of the Enemy's Shot. C AULEDON, is the breaking of Bones across, when the Parts of the Bones are so separate that they will not lie diredb.

causalpropositions.c: CAUSAL Propositions, are those that contain two Propositions joined together by Conjunction of the Cause ( because, or to the end that ) as. We to the Rich, because they have their Felicity in this World. The Wicked are advanced, to the end, that falling from on high, t. heir fall may be the greater.

causticsstonesorcauteries.c: CAUSTICS Stones or Cauteries, ard thus shade of Lime and Gravelled Afoes: Put into a large Earthen Pane one Part of Quick - lime, and two of Gravelled Afoes, of of Calcined Tartar, both pow - dered and mix'd; on these pour good store of hot Water, and then leave the Matter to kifule or Hours, then boil it a little r Then filtrate through Cap - Paper, and evaporating the Liquor that parted the Filtre, a Salt will remain at the Bottom. Put this Salt into a Crucible, and melt and boil it till all the Humidity which came from the Water is exhausted. The Matter will still remain fluid; and when by trying some of it on the End of a Spatula, you find it of a due Consistence, and that it looks like Oil in the Bottom of the Cruci - ble, cast it into a Balon, and cut it, and form it into Pieces while it is warm; put them quickly ih - to a strong Glass Bottle, with a ground Stopple of the some Metal, for they will dissolve and be poll - ed if the Air come to them. These are the strong - eft Cauteries that can be made, and are soon and easily prepared.

celerrimidescensusline.c: CELERRIMI Descensus Line a, the Curve of the swiftest Descent of any Body; or that in which an heavy Body descending by its own Gra - city should move from one given Point to another in the shortest Time. This was proposed as a Problem by that excellent Mathematician M. For if any heavy Body descend from any given Point, and describe a Curve, and hath its Velocity in a Subduplicate Ratio of the Altitude And if a Particle of Light coming from a given Point, and pass through a Medium whose Rarity increases in a Subduplicate Ratio of the Altitude or Depth, then will the Ve - locity of the Particle or Ray of Light, be in a Sub - duplicate Ratio of such Height or Depth; and consequently, since the Velocity becomes the fame, whether produced by the uniform Action of Gra - city, or by the Rarity of the Medium, the Line of Descent or Motion, or the Curve described will be in both Cafes the fame. centre.c: CENTRE of a Circle, or of a Sphere, is that Point from whence all Right Lines drawn to the Circumference or Surface are equal. To find the Centre of a Circle, fee Chord.

CENTRE of a Dyal, is that Point where the Axis of the World inter feds the Plane of the Dyal; and from thence, in those Dyals that have Centres, all the Hour Lines are drawn. If the Plane of the Dyal be parallel to the Axis of the World, it can have no Centre at all, but all the Hour - Lines will be parallel to the Style, and to one ano - ther.

CENTRE ( common ) of the Gravity of two Bo - dies, is a Point in a Right - line connecting their Centres; and lo posited in that Line, that their distances from it shall be reciprocally as the weight of these Bodies: And if another Body be placed in the fame Right - line, lo that its distance from any Point in it be reciprocally as the weight of both the former Bodies taken together, that Point shal ! be the common Centre of Gravity of all, &, c.
CENTRE of heavy Bodies, is in our Globe the fame as the Centre of the Earth, towards which all heavy Bodies do as it were naturally tend.

CENTRE of Gravity. The Consideration of the Centre of Gravity is one of theNobleft Specu - lations in Geometry; and line the New Methods have been in use, such Advancements in it have been made, that hardly much more is to be ex - peated: For the whole Business of the Invefiiga - tion of Centres of Gravity is now reduced to one General Proposition, which depends on a few simple Mechanical Principles, such as these: . If several Bodies be suspended on each Side the Point C, then multiply every Weight by its respective Distance from the Center of Suspension C. - And then if the Sum of all the Rectangles on one Side be equal to the Sum of all those on the other, the Weights or Bodies will be in Alquili - brio; if they are not equal, that Side will pre - ponderate, whose Sum is the greater. Thus, v: gr. the Sum of all the Rectangles on the Right Hand of C is B D. - I fay, BD ( supposing - f - to signify towards the Right Hand, and to - wards the Left j ) and the Sum of all the Redan - gles on the Left of C, will be BD: Whence it is evident, that the Preponderancy is toward the Left Hand, and is equal to BD, which therefore is the Moment of all the Weights. . The Moment then of all the Weights being in this Case B D, and the Sum of all the Weights B D; ’ tis plain, if you divide the former by the latter, the Quotient - hr D will be ( by Princip.. ) equal to the Distance of the Common Centre of Gravity of all the Weights from the Point C. . When the Weights B, B, and B, hang all on the fame Side of C, the Sum of their Mo - ments is B D, as the Sum of the Weights is B Wherefore one Weight B, and hung at - f - - D distant from C, will gravitate in the fame manner as the separate Weights did before at their respective Distances: That is, the said Point is the Common Centre of Gravity of thole Weights, since it is that Point in which all their Forces unite and whereat, if they were al Joint - iy suspended, they would produce the fame EfFed as before they did separately. . Let the Line A B be suspended at A, and suppose it divided into an infinite Number of hea - ? y Points j ’ tis then plain, that the farther any Point is from A, the more it will gravitate; and the Moment of each Point will be a Rectangle under its Distance from A, multiplied by its ielf or Unity: Wherefore the Moment of all the Points must be equal to the Sum of all the said Rectangles; and therefore if the whole Moment be divided by the whole Gravity of all the Points, or by the Gravity of the whole Line A B, the Quo - tient ( by Princip.. and. ) will be equal to the Distance of a certain Point from A, at vhich, if all the Points be suspended, their Moment will be the fame as it is now j that is, that Point shail be the Common Centre of Gravity of the Line A B. . If a Line, Plane or Solid, be bifleded so by a Line or Plane, as that all the Parts in one Seg - ment be equal to the respective Parts in the other, and also equi - distant from the said Line or Plane; ’ tis then clear, that the Centre of Gravity of all such Figures must be in that Line or Plane. And from hence it naturally follows, Prop. General, That to find the Centre of Gravity of any Line, Plane or Solid, you must ima - line Lines to consist of an infinite Number of Points, Planes of an infinite Number of Lines, and Solids of an infinite Number of Planes or Surfaces; and then that all these are fuf - bended to the fame Arm of a Balance com - mon to them all: And let the Point of Suf - pension be as in A, at the End or Extreme of the said Line in the Edge of the Surface, or in the Surface of the Solid; and then find the Sum of the Moments of all those Points; which Sum divide by the Sum of the Weights, or the Weight of all the Parts, and the Quo - tient will be the Distance of the Centre of Gravity or the Line, Plane or Solid, from thd Point or Axis of Suspension. centrifugalforce.c: CENTRIFUGAL Force, is that Force by which all Bodies which move round any other Body in a Circle or an Ellipsis do endeavour to fly off from the Axis of their Motion in a Tangent to the Perip - hery of it. And this Force, as Mr. Hugens demon - states is always proportional to the Circumference of the Curve in which the Revolving Body is car - ried round. The Centrifugal Force of any Body to the Cen - tripedal, is as the Square of the Arch which the Body describes in a given Time, divided by the Diameter, to the Space through which an heavy Body moves in falling from a Place where it was at reft in the fame time. If any Body swim in Medium heavier than it self, ( and in one lighter it cannot do so ) the Centre - sugar Force is the diffrenee between the Specificfc Weight of the Medium and the Floating Body. What the Centrifugal Force in the Planets is, or the Conatus Becedendi ab Axe motus, the endeavour to recede from the Axis of the Motion; you will find explained under Planets; where the Reason of all their Motion is expounded.

CENTRIFUGAL Force. All moving Bodies endeavour, after a redilinear Motion, becaufethat is the eafieft, shortest, and most simple. When - ever therefore they move in any Curve, there must be something that draws them from their redili - near Motion, and retains them in the Orbit. When - ever this Force, which is called Centripetal, ceases, which artrads them towards a Centre, the mo - ving Body wou ’ d strait go off in a Tangent to the Curve in that very Point, and lo wou ’ d get still farther and farther from the Centre or Focus of its former Curvilinear Motion: And that endeavour so fly off in the Tangent, is the Centrifugal Force. The Efied of this Force is luch, that if a moving Body were to describe a Circle, it wou ’ d cause it to describe the largest possible, because a great Circle is less curved, and differs less from a Right Line than a small one: A moving Body therefore will suffer more Violence of Attradion, and con - sequently will exert more of its Centrifugal Force when it describes a less Circle, than in a greater. It is much the fame in ocher Curves as in the Cir - cle for every Curve may be considered as com - posed of an Infinity of Arks of infinitely small Circles, all described by different Radii and so, that, where the Curve hath the greatest Curvature, there it is com posed of such Arks as are Portions of theleaft Circles, or which are described by the shortest Radii. A Body therefore moving in a Curve, doth every Moment endeavour by the Centrifugal Force to get off from a Point which is the Centre of the Ark of an infinitely small Cir cle then described. And this Endeavour is so much the greater, by how much the Ark of the infinite - ly small Circle is the Portion of a lesser Circle so that in one and the fame Curve the Centrifugal Force of the revolving Body may vary according to the different Points of the Curve in which it may at any time be. It may be therefore, that in a Curve where the Force of Gravity in the desert - bing Hedy is continually variable, the Centrifugal Force may also continually Vary in the fame man - ner, and fb that one may always supply the Defed:, or abc e for the Excess of the other, and Consequent - ly the Effect be every - where equal to the absolute Gravity of the revolving Body. And this as a Problem, vi. To find such a Curve in a Vertical Plane, hath been proposed by Mr. Bernoulli of Gronirgucn., Vid. His. de I ’ Academ. fipyal, P,. for the Year, CENTRUM Phonicum T c

ceratias.c: CERATIAS, according to some Writers, is a Horned Comet, sometimes appearing Bearded, and sometimes with a Tail or Train. Some ( comets of this kind they will have to resemble the Figure of a New Moon; others that are Tailed, have a crooked Tail, bending either upward or downward; and others have their Tail of an equal Breadth or Thickness.

ceratoglossum.c: CERATOGLOSSUM, is the proper Pair of Muscles belonging to the Tongue, proceeding from the Horns of the Bone called Hyoides, and joined to the sides of the Tongue: Their use is to move or draw the Tongue straight into the / Mouth, when they ad joyntly; but if either the one or the o - ther be contra & ed singly, they move it to the Right or Left - side.

ceratumorcerecloath.c: CERATUM or Cerecloath, is a Medicine apply - ed outwardly, made of Wax, Oyls, and sometimes Dull intermixed, thicker than an Ointment, and lester than a Plaister.

cerchnos.c: CERCHNOS, is a certain Asperity of the La - lynx, which to touch feels like a Collection of Ju - per - berries, whence proceeds a little dry Cough. Blanchard

cercis.c: CERCIS, is the second Bone of the Cubit, cal - led Radius because it ’ s like the Spoke of a Wheel. Blanchard

cere.c: CERE, are the Horns of the Womb in Brutes, wherein xht Foetus is usually formed.

cerebellum.c: CEREBELLUM, is the hinder part of the Brain, consisting like the Brain it self, of an Ashy or Barkilh, Substance and a white Marrowy o. ne, wherein the Animal Spirits which perform into - lunary and meer Natural Actions, are supposed to be generated in Man; but not so in Beasts; seems consist of a great many thin Plates that lay up - on one another.....,.,

cerebrumthebrain.c: CEREBRUM, the Brain, is ftridly taken for the foremost part of the Substance, which is within the Skull; and it is a Substance of a fort peculiar to it self. Outwardly it is covered with the Skin called Pia Mater. It is wrought with many Turn - ings and Windings. Its exteriour Substance is Ashy, wherein, the Animal Spirits are thought to be generated: The Interior is white, which re - chives the Animal Spirits from the former, and discharges them by the Corpus Callofum, and the Medulla Oblongata into the Nerves, upon which voluntary Adions do chiefly depend. Likewise the Brain is the Subject of Imagination, Judge - ment, Memory, and Reminiscence; for the Ideas or Species of things being received from the Or - gans of the External Senses, are carried to the com - mon Sensory, or the Beginning of the Medulla Ob - longata, and then by the Corpora Strata, and the Corpus Callofum, there the Judgment and Image - nation are probably formed: but the Seat of the Memory is said to be in the Cortical Part of the Brain; and if the Idea's after some time chance to be called for out of the Place of the Memory, then it s properly said to be Reminiscence or Remem - bring. Sleep is likewise tranfaded in the Brain concerning which see in its proper Place. Blan chard. See Brain.

certificate.c: CERTIFICATE ( in Law ) is used for a Writ - ting made in any Court, to give Notice to another Court of any thing done therein.

certificationofaffileofnoveldiffsifinl.h: CERTIFICATION of Affile of Novel Diffsifinl
certificationofaffileofnoveldiffsifinl.c: CERTIFICATION of Affile of Novel Diffsifinl &c. is a Writ granted for the re - examining, or Review of a Matter palled by Assize before any, Justices, aqjl is called Certification of new Dr - fcoveries.

certificandoderecognitionsscapula.c: CERTIFICANDO de Recognitions Scapula, is a Writ directed to the Mayor of the Staple, &c, commanding him to certify the Chancellor of a Statute of the Staple, taken before between such and such, in Case where the Party himself retain - ed ! it, and refuseth to bring it in.

certiorari.c: CERTIORARI, is a Writ out of the Chancery to an inferiour Court, to call up the Records of a Cause therein depending, that conscionable Ju - ftice may be therein administred, upon Complaint made by Bill, that the Party which seemeth the said Writ, hath received hard Dealing in the said Court.

cervicalorvertebralvessels.c: CERVICAL or Vertebral Vessels, are the Arte - ries and Veins that pass through the Vertebra and Muscles of the Neck up to the Skull.

cerumina.c: CERUMINA, is the Filth or Wax of the Eai which seems to befweatoutfrom the Cartilages s Others th: nk it comes from the Glandules which border upon the Ears. It serves to hinder Dust, Motes or little Animals from getting into the Bar

cerusseorwhite.c: CERUSSE, or White - Lead, is Lead turned into a white Form by the Means of the Smoak or Va pours of boiling Vinegar. C / ftSARlAN Section or Operation, is the cut - ting open the Womb of the Mother to preserve the Child: And the

cesareanbirth.c: CESAREAN Birth, is that of a Child which is born this way and thole that were lo, as Cue - far, Seipio, Africanus Manlius, Sc. were called Cafares, and Cafones; a Cafo matris utero.

cessavit.c: CESSAVIT, is a Writ that lieth upon this ge - neral Ground, that he against whom it is brought hath neglected to pay luch Rents, or to perform such Service as he is tied to by his Tenure, and hath not upon his Land or Tenement fuffleient Goods or Chattels to be distrained.

cetusthewhale.c: CETUS, the Whale, a Southern Constellation consisting of Stars.

chaconne.c: CHACONNE ( in Musick ) is a kind of Sard - brand, whose Measure is always Triple Time.

chafeseamen.c: CHAFE, Seamen lay a Rope chafes, when it galls or frets by rubbing against any rough and hard thing. Thus they fay the Cable is chafed in the CH A the Hawse, when it is fretted or Begun to be worn out there.

This Chain of all others is the most commode - ous for Land - measure.
