Thus, suppose i - - h h milltiply air by d, and it will stand thus, d a db a a - u CCCONVER m. w led by Vi,, a - V rU.

conversionofproportions.c: CONVERSION of Proportions, in Logick, is the changing of the Subject into the Place of the Praedicate, and the Predicate into the Place of esse Subject and yet always retaining the fame Quan - tity of both Propositions, as every Right - linedTri - angle hath the Sum of its Angles equal to two Right ones; every Right lined Figure that hath the Sum of Angles equal to two Right ones, is a riangle.

convexity.c: CONVEXITY, signifies any Protuberance or swelling out of any thing; as Glasses are said to be Convex, when they are thicker in the Middle than at the Edges; or rather, when their Surface rises up regularly ( so Vitelho defines it above the Plane of the Base; as they are Concave, when the Surface finks down regularly, or with a regular Curvity below it; so that, the fame thing may be, and of - ten is, Concave within, and Convex without. Here follow some Properties o f Convex Glasses. ] “ a " bjed be in the Focus of a Convex Glass and the Eye on the other Side the Glass the Ob - ' jed will appear ered and distend. . If asiy Object be in the Focus of a Convex Glass and the Eye in the oppose Focus on the o - ther Side, it will appear under the fame Angle, as if if the Eye were in the Place of the Glass and consequently the Distance being double in that Po - sition of the Eye and Object, it will appear thro ’ the Glass magnified under an Angle almost double of what it would appear to the naked Eye; but the Eye can fee no more of its Area than the Breadth of the Glass will permit. Mr. Molyneux, in his DioptricaNova, ( hews how to determine the visible Area of an Object in the Focus of a Convex Glass from the Distance of the Object, and of the Eye from the Glass, and the Glass s Breadth. P.. Prop.. . If an Object be farther from a Convex Glass than the Focus, and the Eye on the other Side be nearer than the distend Base of the Glass, it will see the Object ered but confuted; and it will be must confused when the Eye is placed in the di - stand Base. . But if the Object being placed as before, the Eye be farther from the Glass than a distend Base, It begins to see the Object Inverted, and at a due Distance distend. . If the Object be nearer than the Focus, it will appear ered and distend to an Eye placed on the other Side the Glass, at any Distance within the Eye ’ s Power to discern it.

convict.c: CONVICT, in the Common Law, is he that Is found guilty of an Offence by the Verdid of a Jury: But Crompton says, that Conviction is either when a Man is Out - lawed, or appeareth and con - fefieth, or else is found Guilty by the Inquest.

convocation.c: CONVOCATION, is commonly taken for the General Assembly of the Clergy, to consult of Ec ciefiaftical Matters in Parliament; and as there are two Houses of Parliament, so there are two Places called Convocation Houses, the one called The Higher, where the Archbifliop and Bishops lit severally by themselves; the other. The Lower Convocation House, where all the reft of the Clergy fit. ' An English Convocation or Synod, as it now stands for the Province of Canterbury, consists of a President ( the Lord Archbijhcp ) and Bishops, Deans, Archdeacons, Prodors of Chap - ters, Prodors for the Diocesan Clergy ( for each Diocese ) and one Precentor. Cowell j Inter - preter:

convolution.c: CONVOLUTION, is a winding or turning Motion which is proper to the Trunks of some Plants, as the Convolvuli or Bindweeds, and to the Claspers of Vines and of Briony; and Dr. Grew thinks that all those Plants whose Roots are twisted have such a Convolution; and he assigns two great Effi - cent Causes of this winding Motion, the S and the ' Moot: Methinks ’ twere worth the while, as Ais very easy, to try whether there be any such Convolution, or not in the Trunks of Plants, which may easily be done, as he hints, by tying a little Bit of Paper to any of the Branches which are exactly South, North, &c. and then seeing whether it will change its Position or not, in Refped of the Point of the Compass.

conusfuforitis.c: CONUS Fuforitis, is a fort of Crucible made to melt Iron or any other Metal. Blanchard.

conlsant.c: CONLSANT, m the Common Law, signifies Knowing or Undemanding as if the Son be Com - fant, and agrees to the Feoffment. Cook upon Lit - tleton. Sol.. b.

convulsion.c: CONVULSION, is a - Motion whereby the Nerves, Muscles and Members are contraded or remitted against the Will, or without it, as in the Cramp, Epilepjy, &c. Blanchard.

convulsivemotions.c: CONVULSIVE Motions, are sudden and swift Concuffions or Shakings that cease and return al - ternately,

cook.c: COOK - i cow ?, in a Ship, is variously feared in some, and generally in great Ships it is in the Fore - Castle in some other Ships it is feared in the Hatch - way, upon the first Orlope; and for Ships of War ( " which are termed Men of War ) it might most properly be there, in regard of Danger by Fire, and the freer Ule of the Guns that lie in the Fore - Castle, especially if this Cool Bpom ( as some conceive ) may be contrived to be movable, and lo in a Fight be struck down into the Hold of the Ship. But after all, I cannot apprehend how it can be otherwise placed than in the Fore - Castle in great Ships, by reason of the Multitude of Men, which require, necessarily, the dressing of much Meat, and as necessarily a large and private Room to dress it in.

copercenters.c: COPER CENTERS, or Parceners, in Common Law, are such as have equal Portions in the Inhe - ritance of their Ancestors; and as Littleton in the Beginning of his Third Book, faith, ' Parceners be either by Law or by Custom Parceners by Law are the I slue Female, which no Heir - Male being come in Equality to the Lands of their Ancestors. Par - centers by Custom, are those that by Custom of the Country challenge equal Part in such Lands; as in Kent, by the Custom called Gavel - kind: This, amongst the Feudifts, is called Ad equation.

copernicansystem.c: COPERNICAN System, the fame with the most Ancient or Pythagorean System of the World, which Copernicus revived; and it is since improve - ed, and now generally adhered to by Astronomers, and is as follows. . The Sun is supposed to be placed in the Mid - dle, very near the Center of Gravity of the intire System, in the common Focus of every one of the Planetary Orbits. Next to him Mercury, in about three Month s Time, describes his Ellipsts, and that so near, that we on the Earth rarely obtain a distend View of him. Next to Mercury is the EUiptick Orbit of Venus, whose Peritid is Months f; and next to Venus our Earth, with its Attendant the Moon perform a joint Course, and mcafurcs out the Annual Pe - rod. Next to the Earth, Mars alone, without any visible Guard or Satellite accompanying him, re - valves about the fame Center in about two Years Time. Next to Mars, tho " at a mighty Distance from him, the largest of the Planets Jupiter, with his four remarkable Satellites, takes his Round in Years. COP COP -. -...... - - n u - And Lastly, Saturn with his five little Moons, about him, according to Caffmi, deieribes in Years time, the farthest and most remote Orbit; and compleats the intire Planetary Chorus, as the Figure represents. Besides the Planets, whole Orbits are not very different from Circles, there are another Species of Bodies which are called Comets, revolving about the Sun in such Ellipsis, as may pass almost for Parabola's, they are so exceeding Eccentrical; but as regularly retaining their leveral Periods and Or - bits as the Planets themselves, of which fee Co - mets.

cophosis.c: COPHOSIS, is a Deafness in the Ears. Blan - chard.

codiali.c: CODIA Li be Hi deliberando, is a Writ that lieth, in Case when a Man cannot get the Copy of a Libel at the Hands of a Judge Ecclesiastical,

copos.c: COPOS, is a Weariness of the Body, when the Muscles, or their Fibres rather, are loaden and ob - ftrudted with such viscous Humours, that they are rendred unfit for Motion, Blanchard.

coprocritica.c: COPROCRITICA, are Medicines which purge away the Excrement in the Guts.. Blan -

copulainlogic.c: COPULA, in Logic k, is the Verb that connects any two Terms in an Affirmative or Negative Proposition; as God is Good, where ( is ) is the Co - pa. Riches alone make not a Man Happy, where ( make ) is the Copula..

copulativeproportions.c: COPULATIVE Proportions, are thole that in - crude several Subjects or several Attributes joyn ’ d together by an Affirmajiveor Negative pon juncti - on; that is to fay, and ( not ) or ( neither: ) For ( new - ther ) does the fame thing as ( and ) in these forts of Propositions, for that ( neither ) signifies ( and ) with a Negative, which falls upon the Verb, and not up - on the Union of the two Words which it joins; as if I should fay, That Knowledge and sithes done make a Man happy: Here I unite Knowledge and Riches, affirming of both that they don ’ t make a Man happy.

copy.c: COPY - hold, is a Tenure for which the Tenant hath nothing to ffie but the Copy of the Rolls made by the Steward of the Lord ’ s Court; for the Steward as he doth enroll and makeRemembrances of all other things done in the Lords Court; so he doth also of such Tenants as he admitteth into the Court, to any parcel of Land or Tene - ment belonging to the Mannor; and the Transcript of this is called The Copy of the Court foil, which is all the Tenant taketh sion him, and keeps as his own Evidence: This Tenure is call ’ d A Base Te - nure, because it holdeth at the Will of the Lord: It is wont to be called Tenure in Villaruige by some, who also fay, that Copy - hold is but a new Name, ye & it is not simply at the Will of the Lord but ac - cording to the Custom of the Mannor: So that if a Copy - holder break not the Custom of the Mannor, and thereby forfeit his Tenure, he seemeth not so much to stand at the Lord ’ s Curtesie for his Right, ' that he may be displaced hand overhead at his plea - sure. These ’ Customs of Manners be infinite, va - rying in one Point or other almost in every several Mannor. Fir ft, Some Copy - holds are fine able at Will, and fame certain: That which is fineabh at Will, the Lord Lord raketh at his Pleasure, but if it exceed two Years Revenue, the Chancery, Kjngs - Bench, Com - mon - Pleas, or Exchequer, may reduce them to Rea - fon. That which is certain is a kind of Inheri - tance, and called in many places customary, be - cause the Tenant dying, and the Hold being void, the next of Blood, paying the customary Fine ( as a j. for an Acre, or such like ) may not be denied his Admission.. Secondly, Some Cop - holders have, by Custom, the Wood growing upon their own Land, which by Law they could not have. Thirdly, Copy - holders, some be such as hold by the Verge in ancient Demesne; and although they Jiold by Cop, yet are in Account a kind of Free - holders, for if such a one commit Felony, the King hath Annum, Diem & Vaflum, as in the Case of Free - hold. Some other hold by Common Tenure, called Meer Cop - hold, and they committing Felony, their Land efcheateth to the Lord of the Mannor.

cortheheart.c: COR, the Heart, is a fleshy fibrous Substance made up of several Muscles and Tendons it has two Auricles or Ears, and as many Ventricles: the Vena Cava, or great Vein, is fallen d to the Right Auricle, and the Pulmonary Vein to the Left; the Pulmonary Artery is joyn ’ d to the Right Ventri - cle, and the great Artery to the Left. It is cloath - ed with a little Membranous Bag, called the Pe - ricardium, wherewith it is joyned to the Mediafti - num, and the Diaphragm; its Balls is upwards, and Point downwards, and it is placed in the Mid - dle of the Chest amongst the Lobes of the Lungs. Its Use is to receive and dilperie the Blood to all Parts in the Body. The Base of the Heart is en - ironed round with a Plexus of Veins and Arteries,, Our Excellent Dr. Lower was the first that gave us the true Mechanical Structure of the Heart, and a very good rational Account of its Action: He ex - plains the Systole of the Heart, by the natural Me - tho of muscular Contra & ion; but in order to ac - count for its Diastole, he hath recourse to a certain unaccountable Motion of Eeftitntion, which seems not to be so well grounded. The Heart being a single Muscle without an Antagonist, appears to be of the Spinier kind; and Borellus in his Oeconomia Animalis, computes ! the Motive Power of a Man ’ s Heart to be more than that of a Weight of lb. The Obstacles to the Motion of the Blood through the Arteries, he judges equivalent to lb. i. e. times as much as the Power of the Heart: He estimates the Power of the Elajlick Coat of the Arteries at lb. whole Adventitious Help to move the Blood being deduced, he leaves the Heart with a force ’ but of lb. to surmount a Resistance of lb. that is, with to move - and ’ this mighty Power in the Heart he ascribes to the Force of Percussion. Dr. Drake, in his Discourse of the Motion of the Heart in Phil. TranfaEl. N., o. supposes that Respiration hath a great Influence to assist it; and that even the Systole or Conftri & ion of the Heart is occasioned in some measure by the help of the Diaphragm and Intercostal Muscles, by whole Means the Blood hath a Passage opened for it into the Lungs, which denied would be an Invincible Obstacle: And he thinks also that the Systole is furthered by the Situation and Capacity of the Blood Vessels of the Lungs, ih the several Times of the Elevation and Depression of the Ribs; for by this Means a Passage is opened to the Blood to flow from the Right Ventricle of the Heart to the Left thro ’ the Lungs, to which it could not o otherwise pass, and the Opposition which the Blood contained in that Ventricle must otherwise have made to its ConftriBion, is taken off. And thus the Dr. with great probability, suppos the Systole of the Heart to be much facilitated by the Acftiofa of the Thorax But he faith, that neither the Dia - phragm nor Intercostal Muscles can contribute a - ny thing towards the Diastole, the Cause of which, be it what it will, must be equal to that of the Heart, the Intercostal Muscles, and the Diaphragm, to all. which it rests as an Antagonist, dilating the Heart, as they conftridl or dole it. The Drv thinks such a Power or Cause is not to be found any where in an Animal Body, and therefore it must be lought without it; and he concludes that this Cause is the Weight of the incumbent Anno - sphere pressing upon the Thorax and other parts of the Body, which he proves from Mr. Boyle's Expe - riments upon Animals in Vacuo, where, as soon as the Pressure of the Incumbent Atniofphere is re - moved, the Intercostal Muscles and Diaphragm are contracted, and the Ribs elevated in an In - stant, and can ’ t by any power of the Will be made to subside, till the Air is let in again to bear them forcibly down: And as in the Elevation of the Co - fta, the Blood is in a manner solicited by the Pas - sage now opened for it to flow into the Lungs; so in the Depression of them by the Subsidence of the Lungs, and the Contraction of the Blood Ves - self ( both which are consequent thereupon ) the Blood is forcibly driven, as it were by an Embo - lus, through the Pulmonary Vein into the Left Ventricle of the Heart; and that, together with the general Compreffton of the whole Body, by the Weight of the Atmosphere, which surrounds and gravitates upon the whole Surface of it, is that Power which causes the Blood to mount in the Veins, after the force impress ’ d upon it by the Heart is broken and spent, and which is fufScient to force the Heart from its Natural State to Dilata - tion. And thus by the Contraction of the Heart ( the proper Action of all Muscles ) and its Dilatation again this way is the Circulation of the Blood fee forward and kept going on.

corcaroli.c: COR Caroli, an Extraconftellated Star in the Northern Hemisphere, situated between the Coma Berenices, and Vrfa major, so called in Honour of King Charles.

corhydra.c: COR Hydra, a fix ’ d Star of the first Magnitude in the Constellation of Hydra - its Longitude is deg. min. Latitude zz deg. min. COR Leonis See ftegulus or Baftlicus,

coragobrachialisorcoracobrachieus.c: CORAGOBRACHIALIS, or Coracobrachieus, is a Muscle so called from its Origination and Infer - tion: It arises partly fleshy, and partly tendinous, from the Extremity of the Precejftus Coracboides Sca - pula, and in its Descent it becomes larger strictly adhering to the Internal Tendinous Beginning of the Biceps, and parts from it near its Tendinous Insertion at the Middle of the Internal Part of the Os Humeri: Thro ’ this Muscle passes a large Nerve, wherefore by some it is called Perforatus. When it acftethj the Arm is moved upwards, and turned some Arhat obliquely outwards.

coracohyoides.c: CORACOHYOIDES, are Muscles which pro - ceed from the Process of the Shoulder - bone, call ’ d C C Cor v ". Coracoides, and go on as far as the Bone Hyoides; their Use is to move obliquely downward.

coracoides.c: CORACOIDES is the Processes the Shoulder - blade, in form of a Beek.

coram.c: CORAM non Judges, is a Term in the Com - mon Law, when a Cause is brought into a Court - wherein the Judges have no Jurisdiction.

corbeilsinfortification.c: CORBEILS, in Fortification, are little Baskets about a Foot and a half high, eight Inches broad at the Bottom, twelve at the Top; which being filled with Earth, are frequently fet one against another upon the Parapet, or elsewhere, leaving certain Port - holes, from whence to fire upon the Enemy under Covert, without being seen by them.

cordageatsea.c: CORDAGE at Sea, Signifies in general all the Ropes belonging to the Rigging of a Ship.

cordialia.c: CORDIALIA, are Medicines which are com - monly thought to strengthen the Heart; but they only put the Blood into a fine gentle Fermentati - on, which corroborates and facilitates the Motion of the Heart. Blanchard.

cordoninfortification.c: CORDON, in Fortification, is a Row of Stones made round on the outside, and fet between the Wall and the Fortress which lies in T ' alu, or a Slope, and the Parapet which stands perpendicular after such a manner, that this Difference may not be offensive to the Sight; so that those Cordons serve only as Ornaments ranging round about the Place; neither are they used but in Fortifica - tions made of Mason ’ s Work, the void Space be - ing filled up with pointed Stakes in those that are - railed with Earth.

cordsinmusick.c: CORDS, in Musick, properly signifies the Strings of a Harp, Violin, Lute, or any other Musical Instrument: But the Term is also apply - ed to denote the Sounds which proceed from such Instruments, even from those that have no Strings..

corinthianorderofarchitecture.c: CORINTHIAN Order of Architecture, is so called from Corinth, the Place of its Invention. It observes the fame Measure with the Ionic h, and the Difference between them is chiefly in the Capital: See Order and Column. Vitruvius makes the Height of the Capital to be two Modules, and this he divides into leven parts, of which the first is for the Abacus, and the other fix downwards is for the Ornament.

corneaoculitunica.c: CORNEA Oculi Tunica, which is also called Sclerotes, and Dura, the hard Turned, proceeds from a Tunicl in the Brain called Dura Meninx; it is pellucid forwards, that it may transmit the visible Species: Its Sides are covered with the Al - bugineous Tunic inwardly it contains the Aque - ous Humour.

cornice.c: CORNICE, or as we pronounce it Cornijh, in Architecture, is the third and highest part of the Entablature, and is commonly used to signifie the uppermost Ornament of any Wainscot, ( c. In reference to the Pillar, ’ tis different according to the different Orders of Architecture. In the Tuscan his without Ornaments, and this Pillar of all others hath the least Mouldings, The Dork is adorn ’ d with Dentils like the Ionic t, and which sometimes hath its Mouldings cut into it. The Corinthian Pillar hath of all others the most Moul - dings, and those very often cut with Midi Hons and sometimes Dentils, The Compofiie hath its Dentils and its Mouldings cur, with its Channels or Chamferings under its Platfond.

Silipua: This kind is called also Multiflimom - such as the Sedurn or Sempervivum, Telephium, Sedum Stellatum, Juncus Floridus, Helleborus Niger, Fra - xinella, Aconitum ( or Napellm ) Aquilegia, Del - phinum, Pceonia, Caltha Palu ( lris, Althaa Lutea &c.

cornishring.c: CORNISH Ring Of a Gun, is the next from the Muzzle Ring backwards: See Ordnance.

corneauteri.c: CORNEA Uteri, are two lateral parts of the Womb in some Brutes, as Cows, Harts, Sheep Goats, c. yet some Authors have attributed the fame parts to a Woman ’ s Womb from something which imitates them there; for at the Sides of the Bottom of the Womb, there is a fort of Protube - range on both Sides, where the Vasa Deferentia are inserted; yet a Woman s W womb is rarely Bipar - tite, as it is in Brutes. x "

corodiohabendo.c: CORODIO Habendo, is a Writ whereby to exact a Corody of an Abby, or Religious House.

corodyhabendo.c: CORODY Habendo, in Common - Law, fignh lies a Sum of Money, or Allowance of Meat Drink, and Cloathing, due to the King from an Abby, or other House of Religion, whereof he is Founder, towards the reasonable Suftenence of such a one of his Servants, being put to his Penfi on, as he thinketh good to bestow it on. And the Difference between a Corody and a Pension seems to be, That a Corody is allowed towards the Main - tenancy of any of the King ’ s Servants that livetfc in an Abby; a Pension is given to one of the King ’ s Chaplains, for his better Maintenance in the King ’ s Service, until he may be better provided of a Be - nefice. It appears in Weft.. Cap.. That an Assize shall lie for a Corody; and in others, That Corodies belonged sometimes to Bishops from Mo - nafteries; and also. That a Corody may be due to a common Person, by Grant from one to another; or of common Right, to him that is a Founder of a Religious House, nor holden in Franc - ' Almoine, for that Tenure was discharged of all Corodies in it self. And a Corody is laid to be either certain or uncertain, and that it may be for Life, for Years in Tail, or in Fee.

That a Triangle which has two equal sides has also two Angles equal; you should draw this Consequence, That a Triangle which has the three Sides equal, has also its three Angles equal.

Newton was the first who ( hewed bf most plain Experiments, that the Rays of Light do not come uniform and Ample out of the Luminous Body; but that the pure white Light which we fee, is compounded of the Corpuscles of all manner of Colours, blended one with another, by the most: rapid Motion; and, That the Colours of all Bo - dies arise from their different Dispositions to rcfrad or reflect some peculiar Species of Light. This is principally proved from If frail ions, by which these difincl Species are separated one from another; for Blue or Purple Light is for Instance more refracted in passing through a Diaphanous Body, then Yet - low or Red. See the Words Light and Colours, where I have given you a large Account of Sir If Newtons Experiments, as mentioned in his Letter in the Phil. Trans. N., Qjc. After this, Mr. Halley shews how, having the Distance of the Iris from the Sun, to find the Ra - tio of the Refraction; and this by a very easie, but molt accurate Observation. Take a small Glass Tube, and ere & ing it per - pedicular to the Horizon, suspend in its lower Orifice a small drop of Water, or some such clear Fluid and then at some time when the Sun is near the Horizon, and Ihines very bright, let it be observed under what Angle cum Oppofito Solis, the Colours of the Iris are seen in the pendulous drop; for then the Ratio of the Refraction may be had by an easie Calculation. COROLLARY, And from hence ’ tis plain, That if any two TrL angles. Parallelograms, Prisms, Parallelepipeds,, Pyramids, Cones, or Cylinders, have their Bases and Altitudes Reciprocally proportional, those two Figures or Solids are equal to one another and vice versa, if they are equal, their Bases and Alti tudes are Reciprocally proportionable.

coronainarchitecture.c: CORONA, in Architecture, is properly the flat and molt advanced part of the Cornice, cal - led by the French Larmeir, and by us the Drip, because it defends the reft of the Work from Wind and Weather; but it is often taken by Vitruvius for the whole Cornice.:. Corona, or the Flat - Crown, is also a particular Member in the Dorick Gate, made by so extra - ordinary an Enlargement of the Larmier or Drip, that it hath fix times more breadth than Prove - dure. This fort of Corona is no where found a - amongst amongst the Ancients, except only in the Writings of Vitruvius.

coronaborealis.c: CORONA Borealis, or the Northern Garland, a Constellation in the Northern Hemisphere, - con - sifting of about Stars.

coronameridionalis.c: CORONA Meridionalis, a Southern Conftella - tion confi sting of Stars.

coronalissutura.c: CORONALIS Sutura, is a Cleft in the Head made like a Comb, and joins as if the Teeth of two Saws were closely compacted into one ano - ther: It is placed in the upper Part of the Skull from one Temple to another, and ' is circumscribe ’ d with the Bones of the Forehead, and that parti - cularly called Bregma; in the Middle whereof the Suture, ftiied Sagittalis, is terminated.

coronariavasa.c: CORONARIA Vasa, are the Veins and Arte - ries which surround the Heart to nourish it: They arise out of the Aorta before it comes out of the Pericardium; they incompais the Basis of the Heart like a Garland; in their Circuit fend down divers Twigs length - ways of the Heart, and when they have incompalTed the Basis and meet, they in - oculate with one another, but not with the Veins.

coronatoreeligendo.c: CORONATORE Eligendo, is a Writ which, after the Death or Discharge of any Coroner, is di - erected to the Sheriff out of the Chancery, to call together the Free - holders of the County for the choice of another Coroner; and to certify into the Chancery both the Election and Name of the Party eleCted, and to give him his Oath.

corone.c: CORONE, is an Acute Process of the lower Jaw - bone, from its Likeness to the Beek of a Ra - ven called Roftri for mis, in the Form of a Beek.

coroner.c: CORONER, is an ancient Officer of this Land, so called, because he dealeth wholly for the King and Crown: There be four of them commonly in every County, and they are chosen by the Free - holders of the fame upon Writ, and not by Patent. His Office especially concerneth Pleas of the Crown. There be also certain special Coroners within divers Liberties, as well as those ordinary Officers in eve - ry County; as the Coroner of the Verge, which is a certain Compass about the King ’ s Court: And there are certain Charters belonging to Colleges and other Corporations, whereby they are licen - ced to appoint their Coroner within their own Pre - cinCts,

corporacavernofapenis.c: CORPORA Cavernofa Penis ( by D ’ Graaf cal - led Nervofa, and by others Nervea Spongiofa ) are two Capsul re or oblong Folliculi, fenced every where without with a thick Membrane: They spring with two distinct Originals from the lower Side of the OJfa Pubis, whence stretching forwards, they meet one another, leaving an Interstice before their Conjunction, in which the Urethra is conveyed: Where they leave the Off a Pubis they are each co - vered with a Membrane, and afterwards joined to each other by the Intervention of a Septum In - termedium, which, the nearer it comes to the Gians, is the more diminished.

corporapyramidalia.c: CORPORA Pyramidalia, are Protuberances of the under Part of the Brain, they are in Length of about an Inch.

CORPORA Pyramidalia, when the Blood hath difeharg ’ d it self of the Seed into the Testicles, it returns by the Veins, which rising in several Bran - ches from the Testes, fend towards the Abdomen in the Production of the Peritoneum the fame way the Arteries came down. In their Progress their Bran - ches frequently Inosculate and Divide again, till they come near the Abdomen, and then they all Unite in one Trunk, and therefore because of their Shape are called Corpora Pyramidalia, Gp U

corporastrata.c: CORPORA Strata, are Protuberances upon the Crura Medulla Oblongata.

corporal.c: CORPORAL, is an inferior Officer in a Foot Company, who hath charge over one of the Divi - signs; places and relieves Centinels, and keeps good Order in the Corps de Garde. He receives the Word of the Inferior Rounds that pass by his Corps de Garde.,

CORPORAL of a Ship, is an Officer that hath the Charge of letting the Watches and Gentries, and relieving them; and who lee that all the Solid - ers and Sailers keep their Arms neat and clean he teaches them also how to use them, and hath a Mate under him.

corporation.c: CORPORATION, is a Body Politick author - rifed by the King ’ s Charter, being of Capacity to take and grant, having a Common Seal, ( c, These are constituted either by Prescription, by Let - ters Patent, or by Ad of Parliament, and are ei - ther Spiritual or Temporal.

corporeitytheschoolterm.c: CORPOREITY, the School Term for the Nature of a Body.

corpsdegarde.c: CORPS de Garde, is a Poll in an Army some - times under Covert, sometimes in the open Air, to receive a Number of Men ' who are relieved from time to time to watch in their Turns for the Seen city of some more conilderable Poll; and it often also is taken for the Men thus watching, who are called the Corps de Garde.

corpuscumcausa.c: CORPUS cum Causa, is a Writ issuing out of the Chancery, to remove both the Body and the Record touching the Cause of any Man lying in Execution upon a Judgment for Debt, into the King ’ s Bench, &c. there to lie till he have fatisfi - ed the Judgment.

corpuscallofum.c: CORPUS Callofum, is the upper Part or Cover - ing of a Space made by the joining together of the ' Right and Left Side of the internal Substance of the Brain. This Space forms the three Ventricles or Foramen Oval, and its Bottom is the Internal Substance of the two Sides of the Cerebrum gather ’ d as it were into two Bundles, and are called the Crura of the Medulla Oblongata

corpusglandulosum.c: CORPUS Glandulosum, the fame with the Pk ftata.

corpusclesinnaturalphilosophy.c: CORPUSCLES, in Natural Philosophy, figni - fy the Minute Parts, or Particles, or Physical A - toms of a Body and by this Word is not meant Elementary Parts, nor the Hypostatical Principles of the Chymifts, but such Particles, whether of. simple or compounded Nature, whose Parts will not be dissolved, disjoined or dissipated by ordinary Degrees of Heat. And that way of Philosophizing which ended - vours to explain things, and to give an Account of the Phenomena of Nature by the Motion, Figure, Reft, Position, I c. of Corpuscles or Minute Par - titles of Matter, is by the Honourable Mr. Boyle called very properly the

corpuscularphilosophy.c: CORPUSCULAR Philosophy j which was so very Ancient, that both before Epicurus and De mocritus, and even before Leucippus taught in Greece, there was a Phcenecian Philosopher that ex - plained Natural Phenomena by the Motions and Affections of the Minute Corpuscles of Matter, as very old Writers inform us; and therefore this kind of Philosophy should rather be called Phoenicia ah than Epicurean. - The chief Principles of the Mechanical Hypothecs of Corpuscular Pbihfopby, Mr. Boyle sums up in these Particulars; , i. They suppose that there is but one Catholick or Universal Matter, which is an extended, im - penetrable and divisible Substance common to ail Bodies, and capable of all Forms. . That this Matter, in order to form the vast Variety of Natural Bodies, must have Motion in some or all its designable Parts; and that this Mo - tion was given to Matter by God the Creator of all things, and has all manner of Directions and Ten - denies. . Matter must also actually be divided into Parts, and each of these Primitive Particles, Frag -. C c ments taents or Atoms of Matter must have its proper Magnitude or Size, as alfoits peculiar Figure and Shape. . They suppose also, that thcfe differently fiz ’ d and ship ’ d Particles may have as different Orders and Positions, Situations or Pojlures, from whence great Variety may arise in the Composition of Bo - dies.

corrector.c: CORRECTOR of the Staple, is a Clerk be - longing to the Staple that Writeth and Recordeth the Bargains of Merchants made there.

corridorinfortification.c: CORRIDOR, in Fortification, is the Covert - way lying round about the whole Compass of the Fortifications of a Place, between the Outside of the Moat and the Pallifado ’ s.

corrosibility.c: CORROSIBILITY Y, is the Power of being cor - roded, eaten or dissolved by any Corrosive Mtnftru - m or Liquor; and the Honourable Mr. Boyle reckons these Qualifications necessary to render any Body Corrosible. . That it be furniftied with Pores of such a Bigness and Figure, that the Corpuscles of the Men - Jlruum or Solvent may enter them, and yet not be much agitated in them, without also giving brisk Knocks or Shakes to the solid Parts which confti - tute the Pores or Cavities: For sometimes, though the Pores of a Body may be large enough to let in some gross Corpuscles, yet if these, for want of Solidity or Rigidity, are too flexible, or are of an Incongruous Figure to those Pores, a Dissolution may not ensue; as it happens when pure Spirit of Wine is in the cold put upon Salt of Tartar; or when Aqua Fort is is put upon powdered Sul - pour. . That its consistent Corpuscles be of such a Bulk and Solidity as doth not incapacitate them from being dis - joined by the Action of the infinua - ting Corpuscles of the Menjlruum. . That the Cohesion of the Parts of the Corro - edible Body be not so stri, as that they are not fe - parable by the Action of the Dissolvent.

corrosionchymica.c: CORROSION Chymica, is a Dissolution of mix - ed Bodies by Corrosive Menstruums.

corrosivemedicine.c: CORROSIVE Medicine, is one that has a Pow - er of Corroding, as Lime, Lapis Infernal is, and o -

corrosiveness.c: CORROSIVENESS, is the Quality that some Liquors which are called Menstruums have of dis - solving or corroding Bodies..., And the Attributes or Qualifications which seem proper to render any Liquor Corrosive, Mr. Boyle, in his Mechanical Original of this Quality, rec - kons to be such as these: . That the Menflruum or dissolving Liquor con - fist of, or abound with such Particles as are not too big to get in at the Pores or Comminutes the Body to be dissolved; nor yet so small, as rea - dily to pass through them, as the Rays of Light do through Glass; nor must they be unable, by reason of their great Slenderness and Flexibility, to disjoin the Parts they invade. . That thele Corpuscles be of a Shape fitting to insinuate themselves more or kfs into the Com - fissures or Pores of the Body, m order to diffoci - ate its solid Parts. That these Particles have also a competent degree of Solidity; in order to disjoin the Panicles of the Body to be dissolved: And this Solidity dis. fers much from the Bulk of the Corpufile, mention - ed in the first Requisite; for one thing may be much more solid than another, tho it have, as to Bulk, me lame jLiimennons: xnus the iralk of a Plant may be as big as a small Iron or a Steel Rod, but the Latter is much slider than the Former. . That the Particles of the Menjlruum be Agile; and advantaged for Motion, in respect of their Shape, or their Smallneifs, or their Fitness, to have their A & ion befriended by the Pressure of the Atmo - sphere, which may help to drive them into the Pores of Bodies, or by the Agitation which these intruding Particles may be fitted to receive in ' those Pores by the Transcursion of some subtile Ethere - al Matter.

corrodentia.c: CORRODENTIA: Cotroding things are things which eat up and consume Excrefent Flesh with their ( harp Particles.. Blanchard.

corrugantmuscles.c: CORRUGANT Muscles, according to some, ’ are those that help to knit the Brows when one frowns; but they seem to be only a Part of the Frontal Muscles that have their Fibres running in this Place somewhat obliquely.

corrugatorsupercilii.c: CORRUGATOR Supercilii, is by some Anato - mists reckoned as a Muscle of the Eye - brows, help - ing to knit them when we frown; but it seems to; be only a Part of the Frontal Muscles, having Fi - bres in this Place a little obliquely.

corruption.c: CORRUPTION ? is the Deftrudtion, Extincti - on, or, at least, the Cejfation, for a Time, of the proper Mode of Existence of any Natural Body: For whenever any Body loses all, or any of those Accidents which are essentially necessary to the conftitutingit of such a kind, itisthen said to be corrupted or destroyed, and loses its former Deno - omination, being not now a Body of the Kind it was before. But, as in Generation, nothing Sub - Jlantial is produced, so here nothing Subjlantial is loft or destroyed, but only that Modification of the Body which was its Form, and made it be of such a Species.

corticalpart.c: CORTICAL Part of the Brain, is the outward Substance of the Brain, full of Labyrinths and Meanders in the Outside; it is covered with a thin Skin, and is of an Ash - grisly Colour, being, as Malpighius faith, only an Heap of little Oval Glands, and full of little Vessels; inwardly the Medullary Substance is next to it. Its Use is thought by some to be for the generating Animal Spirits from the Blood, and hence they are conveyed by, the Medullary Substance to the Nerves, and diftri - buted through the whole Body: And the Seat of the Memory and Sleep is placed there by many A - anatomists.

cortininfortification.c: CORTIN, in Fortification, signifies the Wall or Distance between the Flanks of two Bastions.

coruscationorflajhing.c: CORUSCATION or Flajhing, is ( by the Cartesians ) an Exhalation spread under a Cloud; which rushing downwards is fet on Fire and flafheth.

corvusasouthernconstellation.c: CORVUS, a Southern Constellation in the Hea - vens, consisting of seven Stars.

corymbus.c: CORYMBUS, in general, signifies the Top of any thing; but among the old Writers about Plants, Cofymbi were the Bunches or Clutters of I - vy Berries: Some also call the Top of the Stalk of a Plant, when ’ tis so subdivided and adorned with Flowers or Fruits that its makes a round Spherical Figure, by this Name Corymbus, as the Tops of Leeks, Onions, and of the Sambucus Aquatica; &c. and others confound the Word with VmbeUa which expresses the Flowry Top of such Plants as have their Branches and Flowers spread round into theForm of what ourWomen now call an Umbrella ! But eos cos But among our Modern Botanists it is used for a compounded dilcous Flower, whose Seeds are not Pappous, or do not fly away in Down; such are the Flowers of Daiftes, Coryi - Marygold, ( c. and therefore the Accurate Botanist Mr. ay makes one large Genus of Plants to be such as have a com - pound difeous Flower, but without any downy Wings to carry off their Seeds, and these he pro - perly calls Corymbiferous Plants and these he distinguishes into, . Such as have a Radiate Flower, as the Flos Solis, Calendula, Caltha, Flos Africanus, Chry - santhemum Sagetum, Buthphalmum, Ptarmica, Abfinthinm Vmbelliferum, Millefolium, Beilis Major ( Minor, Parthenium, Chnmamelum, ( c. . Such as have a Naked Flower, as the Abro - tanum Fcemina, Eupatorium Caunabinum fce - vnina, Coftus HortorUm, Ageratum, Abjinthium, Artimefut, ( c. To which he adds such as he calls Corymbiferis Afftnes, i. e, such Plants as seem a - kin to the Corymbiferous Kind, as Scabiofa, Dypfacus, Carduus, Sphceroeephalus, Eryngium, ( c.

coryphe.c: CORYPHE, is the Crown of the Head; also the interior Extremity of the Fingers near the Nails. Blanchard.

coryzaorgravedo.c: CORYZA or Gravedo, is a Defluxion of a sharp Salt and thick Humour into the Mouth, Lungs and Nostrils from the Ventricles of the Brain by the Ossa & ory Nerves; for when it grows thick, it can neither be Percolated by the Reins, nor pass from the Pituitary Glandule through the Infundibulum into the Veins, and therefore it distils into the Nostrils by the aforesaid Nerves. Blanchard. CO - SECANT, is the Secant of an Arch which is the Complement of another to. CO - SINE, is the Right Sine of an Arch, which is the Complement of another to Degrees.

chosenage.c: CHOSEN AGE, or Cognatione, is a Writ that lies where the great Grandfather is fenced in his De - mesne, as of Fee, at the Day of his Death, of cer - tain Lands and Tenements, and dieth, and then a Stranger entreth and abateth; for then shall his Heir have this Writ of Cosenage.

coshering.c: COSHERING, in the Feudal Laws; as there were many Privileges inherent by Right and Cu - stom, so were there several then grievous Exact - ons imposed by the Lords, by a fort of Preroga - tive or Seignioral Authority, as to lie and feast themselves and their Followers ( called Cojhering ) at their Tenant ’ s Houses.

cosmeticks.c: COSMETICKS, are Medicines which whiten and soften the Skin, or, in general, any thing that helps to promote the External Beauty or good Ap - pearance of the Person that useth it.

cossical.c: COSSIC AL, a Term in Astronomy, express - sing one of the Poetical Riftngsof a Star; for a Star is said to rife CofmicaUy, when it riles together with the Sun, or with that Degree of the Ecliptic wherein the Sun then abides; and the Coftmical Setting is when a Star sets or goes down in the Weft, at the fame time as the Sun rises in the East.

cosmography.c: COSMOGRAPHY, is a Description of all the several Parts of the visible World, delineating them according to their Number, Positions, Motions, Magnitudes, Figures, and their other Properties. The Two Parts of which are Astronomy and Geo - grapy.

cosseandcoftick.c: COSSE and Coftick., the old Word for Algebra.

cost.c: COST, ( in the Plural Number Cotiqes ) a Term in Heraldry, signifying a Fourth Part of a Bend. COSTjE, the Ribs, are those Bones which, with other Parts, makes the Chest or Thorax - Backward they are connected with the Vertelres of the Back Forward with the Cartilages of the Breast Bone: They are Twelve in number on each Side, the Se - ven upper are called Costa Vera, True, because their Cartilaginous Ends are received into the Sinus of the Sternum; the Five lower Spurious, because they are fliorter and softer; the broader Part of the Rib is called Palmula, the straighten towards the Vertebres, ftemulus. The Ribs are crooked like the Segments of Circles, and grow flat and broad as they approach the Sternum, but nearer the Verte - bra they are rounder and thicker, and at those Ends have each a round Head, which being covered with a Cartilage, is received into the Sinus in the Body of each Vertebra; and at the Neck of each Head there is a small Tubercle, which is also received into the Sinus of the Transverse Processes of the Vertebra; and as they are thus articulated, the Ribs make an Acute Angle with the lower Verte - bra. Each one hath a small Canal or Sinus run - ning along the under Side, - in which lies a Nerve, Vein and Artery: Their Extremities, which are fastened to the Sternum, are Cartilaginous, and the Cartilages make an Obtuse Angle with the Bony Part of the Rib. These Cartilages are harder in Women than Men, that they may the better fii - stain the Weight of the Breasts. Dr. Keil observes very well in his Anatomy, PV. That if the Ribs had been articulated with the Bodies of the Vertebra at Right Angles, the Cavities of the Thorax could never have been en - larged in breathing: If each Rib had been a rigid Bone articulated at both Ends to two fix ’ d Points the whole Chest had been immoveable. If the Ribs had not been articulated to the Transverse Processes of the Vertebra, the Sternum could not have been thrust out to that Degree it is now, nor the Cavity of the Thorax increased so much as is requisite in Inspiration; for when the Ribs are pull ’ d up by the Intercostai Muscles, the Angle which the Cartilages at the Sternum make with the Bony Part of the Rib must be increased, and confequentlyits Subtense, or the Distance between the Sternum and the Transverse Processes lengthen - ed; Now because the Rib can ’ t move beyond the Transverse Process, on the account of its being ar - ticulated with it, therefore the Sternum moist ei - ther be thrust to the other Side, or else outwards It cannot move to the other Side because of an e - qual Pressure upon the fame Account there, and therefore ’ tis thrust outwards, or the Distance between the Sternum and the Vertebra is increai - ed: The last Ribs, which do. not reach the Ster - num, and consequently conduce nothing to this Atftion, are not articulated with the Transverse Processes. If we suppose the Cavity of the thorax to be half a Spheroid, whose Semi - Axis is equal to the Height coil cou Height of the Thorax, or about Inches, and the Diameter of its greatest Circle Inches, then the Cavity of the Thorax will contain about Cu - back Inches; but in an easy Inspiration the Ster - num is raised of an Inch ( as I am allured by an exatft Experiment ) and therefore on that Ac - count the Thorax is enlarged to the Capacity of Cubick Inches. To this, if we add. the Space which the Diaphragm leaves which is the Segment of a Sphere whole Diameter is about Inches, and the Solidity of that Segment In - ches, we shall have Inches more, if the Dia - phragm descends but one Inch; but if it descends an Inch and it then leaves room for Inches of Air more to enter j and if it descends two In - ches, the Cavity of the Thorax will be increased on the Account of the lylotion of the Diaphragm alone to Inches; so that in the least infpirati - on which we can fairly suppose, the Lungs are distended with Inches of Air, and sometimes may receive above or. CO - TANGENT, is the Tangent of an Arch, which is the Complement of another to De - grees.

cotyle.c: COTYLE, the fame with Acetabulum, is the Cavity of the Huckle Bone, which is appointed to receive the Head of the Thigh Bone. . COTYLEDON, the fame with Cotyle.

cotyledonesoracetabulavterina.c: COTYLEDONES, or Acetabula Vterina, are Glandules dispersed up and down the uttermost Membrane investing the Foetus, called Chorion, which separate the ' Nutritious Juice from the. Womb to nourish the Foetus; but this is found on - ly in some Animals the Placenta in the Womb supplies their Place in Women: The gaping meet - ing of the Veins in the Womb also are called Co - tyledones and Acetabula These Glandules are lo called from the Resemblance they bear to the Leaves of the Herb Pennywort, in Latin Cotyledon. ' COUCHANT, the Term in Heraldry for a Lion born in any Coat of Arms, lying on his Bel - ly, but with his Head eredb

covenant.c: COVENANT, is the Consent of two or more to one thing, to do or give somewhat. Covenant is either in Law or in FaSl; A Covenant in Law, is that which the Law intendeth to be made, though in Words not to be expressed, as if the Lessee do demise or grant, &c. to the Lessor for a certain Term, the Law intendeth a Covenant on the Les - for ’ s Parr, that the Lessee shall quietly enjoy his Lease for his Term against all Incumbrances. Covenant in FaEt, isthat which is expressly agreed between the Parties. There is also a Covenant Real, and a Covenant meerly Personal; A Covenant ' al is whereby a Man tieth himself to pass a thing Beal, as Lands or Tenements, as a Covenant to levy a Fine or Land, &c. A Covenant meerly Per - synal, of the other Side, is where a Man covenant - ed with another by Deed to build him a House, or any other thing, of to serve him, or to infeoff him,
COVENANT is also the Name of a Writ: See Convention. CO - VERSED Sine, is the remaining Part of the Diameter of a Circle, after the Versed Sine is taken from it.

covertureinlaw.c: COVERTURE, in Law, is particularly ap - plied to the Estate and Condition of a married Woman, who, by the Laws of our Realm, is fub foteftate viri, and therefore disabled to make Bar - gains with any, to the Prejudice of her Self or her Husband, without his Assent and Privity, or at least without his Allowance and Confirmation; and if the Husband alien the Wife ’ s Lands dm ing the Marriage, she cannot gain - fay it during his Life.

covert.c: COVERT - WAY, in Fortification, is a Space of Ground level with the Field, on the Edge of the Ditch three or four Fathom broad, ranging quite round the Half - Moons and other Works toward the Country: It is otherwise called Corridor, and hath a Parapet railed on a Level, together with its Banquets and Glacis, which from the Height of the Parapet ought to follow the Parapet of the Place till it is insensibly loft in the Field: It hath also a Foot Bank. One of the greatest Difficulties in a Siege is to make a Lodgment on the Covert - way, because usually the Besieged Pallifade it a - long the Middle, and undermine it on all Sides t This is sometimes called, and that commonly, the Counterfcdrp, because ’ tion the Edge of it. CO VINE, ( in Law ) is a deceitful Assent or Agreement between two or more, to the Preju - dice of one another.

count.c: COUNT, ( in Law, ) signifies as much as the Original Declaration in a Process, though more used in Real than in Personal A & ions, as Decla - ration is more apply sd to Personal than Real.

COUNT - WHEEL, is a Wheel in the striking Part oi a Clock, moving round once in or Hours. It is by some called the Locking T / Wheel, be - cause it hath commonly Notches in it at one - qual Distances from one another, in order to make the Clock strike,,,, &c. tis driven round by the Pinion of Report.

counter.c: COUNTER - APPROACHES, in Fortificati - on, are Works made by the Besieged to hinder the Approach of the Enemy; and when they design, to attack them in Form,
COUNTER - BATTERY is one raised to play against another.

COUNTER - BREAST - WORK, a Term in Fortification, the fame with False Bray. COUNTER - CHANGED, is a Term in He - raldry, when there is a mutual changing of the Colours of the Field and Charge in an Escutcheon, by Reason of one or more Lines of Partition. Thus in the Coat of the Famous Chaucer, he beareth Party per Pale, Argent and Gules, a Bend Counter - changed, i. e. that Part of the Bend which is in that Side of the Escutcheon which is Argent, is Gules, and that Part of it which is in the other Side, is Argent.
COUNTER - COMPONED; the Herald ’ s Term for a Bor dure, or any Ordinary which hath two Rows only of Checkers of two different Co - lours; but when it hath three or more, they call it Cheeky.

COUNTER - FORTS, are certain Pillars and Parts of the Walls of a Place, diftantfrom to Foot one from another, which are advanced as much as is possible in the Ground, and join ’ d to the Height of the Cordon by Vaults to support the Way of the Rounds and Part of the Rampart; as also to fortify the Wall, and strengthen the Ground; nevertheless they are not at present much used, except in large Fortifications.
COUNTER - FUGUE, in Musick, is when the Fugues proceed contrary to one another, COUNT cou CO u

COUNTER - GUARDS, or Envelopes, in For - tification, are large Heaps of Earth in Form of a Parapet, raised above the Moat before the Faces and the Point of the Bastion to preserve them and then they consist of two Faces, making an Angle Saliant, and parallel with the Faces of the Bastion. If they are designed to cover one of the Faces of the Bastion, they are shaped like a Demi - Bastion, with a Parapet on the Face and Capital, but none on the Flank, which must lie open and be exposed to the Fire of the Place but there are few Places now Fortified after this Manner, by reason of the excessive Charge it requires.
COUNTER - MARCH, in the Art of War, signifies changing the Face or the Wings of a Bat - talon, and this is done either by Files. or by Banks.
COUNTER - MARCH by Banks, is when the Wings or Flanks of the Battalion change Ground with one another.

COUNTER - MINE, in Fortification, is a Sub - terraneous Passage made by the Besieged in search of the Enemy ’ s Mine, to give Air thereto, to take away the Powder, or by any other Means to fru - ftratethe Effedl of it, t hough it should even happen to be fired by the Affailants.
COUNTER - PART, a Term in Musick, only denoting one Part to be opposite to another as the Base is laid to be the Counter - part of the Treble.
COUNTER - PASSANT, when two Lions are born in a Coat of Arms, and one appears to be pasting or walking quite the contrary way with the other, the Heralds call it by this Term Count er - V off ant.

COUNTER - PLEA, in Common Law ' figni - fies that which the Demandant allegeth against a Tenant in Courtesy or in Dower, who prayeth in Aid of the King; or him who hath the Reversion for his better Defence.

COUNTER - POINT, in Musick, is a Term whereby is understood the old Manner of compo - ( ing Parts, before Notes of different Measure were invented which was to let Pricks or Points one against another to denote the several Concords the Length or Measure of which Points was sung according to the Quantity of the Words or Sylla - bles whereto they are apply ’ d so that in regard that in composing our Descant we fet Note against Note, as the Ancients did Point against Point the Term Counterpoint is still retained in thele Compofirions.
COUNTER - SAILIENT, is when two Beasts j are born in a Coat of Arms in a Posture of leaping from each other directly the contrary way.
COUNTER - TENOR, one of the mean or middle Parts of Musick, so called as it were oppo - site to the Tenor.

COUNTER - TRIPPING when two Staggs, or other Beasts, are born in a Coat of Arms trip - king, i. e. in a walking Posture, and the Head of one is to the Tail of the other, the Heralds fay they are Counter - Tripping.

countermand.c: COUNTERMAND, is where a thing former - ly executed, is afterwards, by some Ads or Cere - many, made void by the Party that had first done

countermarchbyfiles.c: COUNTER MARCH by Files, is when those Men that are in the Front of the Battalion go into the Fear.

counterscarpinfortification.c: COUNTERSCARP, in Fortification, is that I Side of the Ditch which is next the Camp, or pro - perly the Talus that supports the Earth of the Co -; vert - way although by this Term is often under - stood the whole Covert - way, with its Parapet and Glacis; and so it is to be understood when tis said, T he Enemy lodged themselves on theCounterfcarp.

counterswallowstail.c: COUNTER Swallow's Tail, is an Out - work in Fortification, in the Form of a single Tenaile, wi - der next the Place, A e. at the Gorge, than at the Head, or next the Campaign: The Sides of this Counter Swallows Tail are not so well slank'd from the Place as those of the true Swallow's Tail, and therefore ’ tis not so good.

counters.c: COUNTERS, are Two Parts of a Ship the upper Counter is reckoned from the Gallery to the lower Part of the straight Piece of the Stern The lower Counter is between the Tranfbm and lower Part of the Gallery.

counting.c: COUNTING - HOUSE, in the King ’ s Houf - hold: See Green Cloth.

county.c: COUNTY - COURT, is a Court held ever f Month by the Sheriff, or his Deputy the Under Sheriff.

couped.c: COUPED, is the Herald ’ s Word for any thing in an Escutcheon which is born cut clear and even - ly off, in opposition to its being torn off, which they call Erased: Thus the Arms of Differ which all Baronets carry, is a Dexter Hand. Condor cut off at the Wrist.

coupleclose.c: COUPLE Close, a Term in Heraldry, signify - ing the th Part of a Chevron r These are never born but in Pairs, except a Chevron be between - them, faith Guillim, but Bloom gives us an Instance to the contrary.

courseinnavigation.c: COURSE, in Navigation, is that Point of the Compass or Coast of the Horizon on which the Ship is to be fleered from Place to Place or rather the Angle between the Bumb - Line and the Me - ridian.

courses.c: COURSES, in a Ship, are her Main - fail and Fore fail when file fails under them only without lacing on any Bonnets, they fay then Die goes under a Pair of Courses.

court.c: COURT, is a Word that has divers Significati - ons, but in Law ’ tis the Place where Justice is ju - dicially administred, of which you findThirry Two several forts in Cromptons Book of JurifdiSlions well described, and of them most are Courts of Re - cord some be nor, and therefore are accounted Base Courts in comparison of the reft. Besides these, there are also Courts Christian, which are so called, because they handle Matters especially ap - pertaining to Chriftianity and such as, without good Knowledge in Divinity, cannot be well judge - ed of and therefore the Judges are divines as Archbifhops, Bishops, Archdeacons, and the like.

COURT - BARON, is a Court that every Lord of a Mannor hath within his own Precindls: And this Court is twofold as if a Man having a Man - nor in Town, to grant the Inheritance of the Co - py - holders thereunto belonging to another this Grantee may keep a Court or the Customary Te - nants, and accept Surrenders to the use of others and make both Admittances and Grants. The ! ther Court is of Free - holders, which is properly called the Court Baron, wherein the Suitors that is, the Free - holders, be Judges, whereas of the o - ther, the Lord or his Steward is Judge.

COURT - Chriflian, or Ecdefiaftical, is so call ’ d in Opposition to the Civil Court, or Lay Court, or Curia Domini Regis i These Courts of Chriftianity were not only held by the Bishops in Synods, and the Arch - Deacons and Chancellors in Gonfiftoriest Bat they were also the Rural Chapters where the Dura ! C R I Rural Dean or Dean of Chriftianity preside, and the Clergy were AfFeffbi's and Afilftants. Dh jqknet s Glossary. ' CRASIS - MzV /; See Cra e - MilL CRAYONS, are Pencils of several Colours made purposely to paint withal: They are chiefly used in Portraits and Pidures done after this way of Painting, are said to be done with Cray - ons

courtofchivalry.c: COURT of Chivalry, or the Marshal's Court - the Judges are the Lord High Constable and the Earl Marjhal of England. This Court is the Fountain of Martial Law, ' and the Earl Marjhal is riot only ona CR A CR A one of the Judges, but also to fee Execution done.

courtofpeculiars.c: COURT of Peculiars, is a Spiritual Court held in such Parifhes as are exempt from the Juris - di & ion of the Bishops, and are peculiarly belong - ing to the Archbishop of Canterbury.

courtofrequejh.c: COURT of Requejh, is a Court of Equity of the fame Nature with the Chancery, but inferior to it,, being principally instituted for the Help of such Petitioners as in Conscionable Cafes deal by Sup - plication to His Majesty. This Court had a ( sum - ed so great Power to it self, that it grew Burthen - som and Grievous and therefore was taken away with some others by a Statute made and Car. I. Cap. o.

courtesyorcurtifyofengland.c: COURTESY, or Curtify of England, signifies, with us, a certain Tenure, whereby a Man mar - rying an Inheritrix, that is, a Woman, seised of Lands offer - simple or Fee - tail General; or seised as Heir of the Tail Special, and setteth a Child by her that cometh alive into the World, though both it and his Wife die forthwith; yet if ( he were in Possession, he ( hall keep the Land during his Life; and is called Tenant per legem Angliae, or Tenant by the Cur tery of England, because this Privilege is not allowed in any other Country except Scotland, where ' tis called CurialitasSc otke.

couteutlaugh.c: COUTEUTLAUGH, he that willingly receive - ed ! and cherifheth, or hidethan Out - Law.

coward.c: COWARD; when a Lion is born in any E - scutcheon with his Tail doubled or turned in be - tween his Legs, they call it a Lion Coward. COXiE Os, the Hip Bone, called other wife In - nominatum, and Ilium Coxendicis, because it con - tains the Gut called Ilium; it is annexed to the Sides of the Os Sacrum: In Infants it consists of three Bones, Ilium, Ischium and Os Pubis, which are joined together by Cartilages till seven Years of Age, then it is distinguish ’ d by a Triple Line: It grows into one continued Bone in Adult Persons.

coxendix.c: COXENDIX, the fame withCVx / ?, and the Or Ischium, is the Third and Inferior of the Off a Into - minata, having a large Cavity called Acetabulum Coxendicis, which receives the Head of the Thigh Bone -; the Circumference of this Cavity is tipt with a Cartilage called its Supercilium: Where it joins the Os Pubis; it hath a large Hole called the Foramen ischium and Pubis, about whose Circum - ference the Muscles called Obturator Ext emus and Internus do arise. At its lower End it hath a large Protuberance, on which we fit, and from whence the Benders of the Legs arise; and a little above this behind, it hath a ( mall acute Process, between which and the former Protuberance lies the Sinus of the Ischium, through which the Tendon of the Obturator Internus pa ( fes.... e

crabbanengineofwood.c: CRABB, an Engine of Wood with three Claws placed on the Ground like a Capftern, which is used to launch Ships, or to heave them into the D CRADLE, so the Ship - wrights call a Frame of Timber raised along the Outside of a Ship by the nil doe serving the more securely and commode - oxfly to help to Launch a Ship: This is much used in Italy, Spain and Turkey, where, for Safety s fake, they also trim a great Ship in be Cradle.

cramacroma.c: CRAM A, Croma, Chrama, is a Mixture of any whether Medicines or Elements. Blanchard.

cranage.c: CRANAGE, ( in Law ) is a Liberty to use a Crane for the drawing up of Wares from the. Ves - sols at in Crick of the Sea or Wharf unto the Land, and to make Profit of it: It signifies also the Money taken and paid for the fame.

cranelines.c: CRANE Lines, in a Ship, are Lines going from the upper End of the Spric - Sail - Top - Mast to the Middle of the Fore - stays; they serve to keep the Spnt - Sail - Top - Mast upright and fteadyin its Place, and strengthen it, in order that it may bear its Yard and Sail the better.

crane.c: CRANE ’ Bill, a fort of Bor ces used by Surge - ons, so Named from its Figure.

cranium.c: CRANIUM, is the Comp ages of the Bones of the Head, to which belongs the Bones of the Fore - head, of the Sides of the Head, of the hinder Part of the Head, of the Temples, the Bone called Sphenoides, and another called the Os Cribriforme ?, It is like a K prot or Helmet to the Head, which defends it from external Injuries; its upper Part is double: Some call it Calva and Calvaria. -. See Calva. Each Bone in the Cranium is made up of two Tables or Lamina, between which there is a thin and spungy Substance made up ot some Bony Fi - bres which come from each Lamina, called in Greek Diploe, in Latin Meditullium, In it there are a great number of Veins and Arteries, which bring Blood for the Nouriftiment of the Bones. The Tables are hard and ( olid, because in them the Fibres of the Bones are close to one another. The Diploe is fofr, because rhe Bony Fibres are at a greater Distance one from another, by which - Contrivance the Cranium is not only made lighter,, but is also le ( s Subject to be broken. The Enter - nal Lamina is smooth, and covered with the Peri - carnium; the Internal also is ( mooth, but on it - there ’ are several Furrows made by the Pulse of the Ar - teries and the Dura Mater, whilst the Cranium was soc and yielding. The Bones of the Cranium are joined by four Sutures, the Coronate, the Lambdoidalis, the Sa - gittate, and the Squamofa; the three First of which are called Suturce ver e, the Last Falfa. The Bones of the Cranium are fix proper, as the Os Frontis, making the Front of the Skull; the Os Occipitis, which makes the hinder Parr; the OJfa Parietalia and Temporum, which constitute the Sides; and two Common Bones, as the Os She - noides, and the Os Ethmoides all which fee under those Words.

cranktheseaterm.c: CRANK, the Sea Term for a Ship that cannot bear her Sails, or can bear but a small Sail for fear of overfetting; and they fay ( lie is Crank, b the Ground, when ( lie cannot be brought on Ground without Danger ot overthrowing ' her.

crapula.c: CRAPULA, is an Head - ach proceeding from too much Wine. Blanchard.

crasis.c: CRASIS. in Grammar, is the fame with Synerefisl and draws two Letters belonging to different Syl - tables into one Syllable, as Vement for Vehement.

crasisortemperamentum.c: CRASIS, or Temperamentum, is a convenient Mixture of Qualities in an Animal Body. Blan - chard.

craterthename.c: CRATER, the Name of one of the Southern Constellations confiding of u Stars, CRA -

craticula.c: CRATICULA, is a Chymical Instrument made of square Pieces of Iron as thick as one ’ s Finger, placed so near one another in Acute Angles, that there ’ s half a Finger s Space betwixt then !: It is u - fed in making of Fires to keep up the Coals. Blan - chard.

creamoftartar.c: CREAM of Tartar, isTartar boiled in a great deal of Water, so that as much of it as can may be there dissolved; then the Dissolution is passed hot through Hippocrates his Sleeve, and about half the Liquor being evaporated, the Remainder is fetinacool Place, and the Tartar will hoot into Chrystals, and some of it be like a Cream on the Top of the Water: This Latter is properly the Cream of Tartar, and the Former are Chrystals of Tartar, though both are of the fame Nature and Use. Sometimes the Rust of Iron powdered is boiled in the Water along with the Tartar, and then the Chrystals are called the ChalybeateChryftals of Tartar.

cremasterthename.c: CREMASTER, the Name of a Muscle, other - wile ( from its use ) called Juftpenfor Tefticuli: ’ Tis designed ro keep the Testes from hanging down too much, and alio to raise them up in Coitu.;

crenelleaterminheraldry.c: CRENELLE, a Term in Heraldry, signifying the fame as Embatteled: Which fee.

crenyles.c: CRENYLES, in a Ship, are small Ropes spliced into the Bolt - ropes of the Sails of the Main - Mast and Fore - Mast; they are fattened to the Bowling Bridles, and are also to hold by when a Bonnet is Ihaken off.

crepusculum.c: CREPUSCULUM signifies Twilight, either Morning or Evening: See Twilight.

crescent.c: CRESCENT; the Herald ’ s Term for an Half Moon, which they draw of this Figure, and though it be sometimes born as Coat Armour, yet is usually the distinguishing Mark of the ad Brother or Family from the First.

crestinheraldry.c: CREST, in Heraldry signifies that Represent tation, whatever it be, whether Animal, Vegeta - ble or other Artificial things, which is born on a Wreath Chapeau, &c. on the Top of the Helmet in any Atchievement: This they call also the Cogni - since.

cribrationthechymist.c: CRIBRATION, the Chymist ’ s Word for fitting any Powder, or palling through a fine Sieve.

cribrum.c: CRIBRUM benediftum anti quorum, the Anci - ents fancied two Cavities placed long ways in the Reins; one uppermost, wherein the fefous Blood was poured from the Emulgent Arteries; another lowermost, which they fancied was distinguished with a certain Transverse Membrane full of lit - tle Holes like a Sieve; whence they called it Co - latorium, a Strainer; and Benediftum Cibrum, a blessed Sieve, through which they would have the Serum percolated into the Vreters, and the good Blood stay behind for the Nourishment of the Reins. Blanchard, CRICOARYTiENOIDES, areMufcles which proceed from the Cartilage Called Cricoides lateral - ly, and are inferred into the Arytanoides, which, whilst they draw the Arytcenois sideways and out - wardly, the Opening or Rimula of the Larynx is dilated. Blanchard.

cricoides.c: CRICOIDES, is the Cartilage of the Larynx or Windpipe in Fashion of a Ring.

cricothyroidesapairofmuscles.c: CRICOTHYROIDES, a Pair of Muscles which proceed from the Cartilage of the Larynx like a Ring from the Fore - part of the Cricoides, and are terminated in that which is call ’ d the Scuti formis; they dilate the opening of the Larynx by - moving a little obliquely: Its use is to pull up the Annularis.

crimnoidesorcrimoid.c: CRIMNOIDES, or Crimoid. es, is Urine with thick Sediments at the Bottom like Bran. Blan chard.

crisis.c: CRISIS, is a sudden change in a Disease either towards a Recovery or Death: It sometimes fig - nifies a Secretion of Humours, but is more fre - quently taken for a Judgment passed upon a Dil - ease; one C rifts is called persist, another imp erf eft; the Perfect is that which frees the Patient perfect - ly from the Distemper, and it is either Salutary or Deadly; an Imperfect Crifish that which does not dearly determine the Tendency of the Disease, but leaves Room for another Crifts; and this is two - fold, either for the Better, or for the Worse - the Former is that which does not quite take away the Disease, but enables the Patient to bear it bet - ter; the latter is when the Disease become more violent and dangerous. Blanchard.

cristagall.c: CRISTA Gall., is the Third Part of the Bone Ethmoides, or the inner Process, not much unlike the Comb of a Cock; it arises betwixt the Olfac - tory Nerves, and has the Extremity of the third Cavity of the hard Skin of the Brain; called Durd Mennix, implanted in it.

crist.c: CRIST., are Excrefcencies of Flesh growing about the Fundament, the Roots whereof are of - ten chapt and cleft. Blanchard,

criteriumorcriterion.c: CRITERIUM, or Criterion, is a Judgment made of the Truth or Falfhood of a Proposition, the Nature or Qualities of any EffeCt, c,

crock.c: CROCK, is a Word the Botanists use sometimes for the Apices of Plants. Which fee.

crocusmar.c: CROCUS Mar tis, or Saffron of Steel, so cal - led from its reddish Colour: Of this there are fe - vefal kinds, and diverse ways prepared.

crocusmartisaperient.c: CROCUS Martis Aperient, opening Saffron of Mars: Mr. Lemery, with great probability, asserts the belt way of preparing this; is only to wafli Iron Plates, and then expose them to the Dew till they have contracted a Rust, which Rust is the Crocus, and may be scraped off, and the Plates washed and exposed for more. He gives another good Way, which is, to expose Filings of Iron ( Tor Steel is not so fit for Medicinal Uses ) in ah Earthen Pan to the Rain, till they become a kind of Paste, which is dried and powdered, and exposed again to the Rain, and this for twelve times. Others calcine Filings of Iron or Steel with an equal Weight of common Sulphur; and some heat a Bar of Iron Red or rather White Hot, and then clap it between two Rolls of Brimstone, and the Iron will melt and run down into a Vessel of Water below: Steel so prepared, Or by the former way, is called Mars cum Sulphurs preeparatus. Dr: Willis's Way was to mix Tartar with Steel Filings, and no doubt many other Processes cs this kind there are, Dd all of which may be good Aperitives; tho ’ many assert the giving Filings in Substance is as good a Way as any,

crocusmartiafiringens.c: CROCUS Marti Afiringens, Binding Saffron of Steel, is the Filings of Iron deprived of their more Saline Parts, which is done by washing them or times in strong Vinegar, and then calcining them or Hours in a strong Fire in a Pot, or up - on a Tile. There are many other ways of preparing this Afiringent Crocus, but this is a very good one.

crocusmetallorum.c: CROCUS Metallorum, is a kind of Impure and Opaque Glass of Antimony of a Liver Colour, whence often called Hepar, or Liver of Antimony, made by firing equal Parts of Powder of Antimo - ny, and Salt Petre well mix ’ d, in an Iron Mortar covered with a Tile. ’ Tis kindled by dropping in a Coal of Fire, a great Detonation ensue, which when over, strike the Mortar to make the Matter fall to the Bottom: The shining Part is the Crocus or Liver, which must be separated from the Dross, walked and kept for use. Of this usually is made the Emettick " Urine, or Vinum Bene di Slum, by in - filling an Ounce of the Crocus powdered, in a Quart of Wine for Hours.

cross.c: CROSS, one of the Honoura - ble Ordinaries in Heraldry, con - gaining one fifth of the Field. There is great Variety in its Form, according to the Lines that com - pose it; but a plain Cross is figured thus, by the Name of Ifainsford. He beareth Argent, a. Cross Sab let Sometimes there is a Line drawn parallel to the Out - line of the Cross, and then the Field is supposed to appear through; this is called a Cross voided, and born thus. He beareth Argent, a plain Cross voided Assure; and some - times the Cross is couped as well as voided.
CROSS - Bar - Shot, is a round Shot or great Bullet, with a Bar of Iron put through it.
CROSS - LETTS, are little plain Crosses, whose Ends also bear the Form of a plain Cross. They are thus Figured, and are frequently born Fitcbee, that is, pointed at Bottom: Vid. Fi thee.

CROSS - Staff, is an Instrument made of Box or Pear - Tree, commonly called the Fore - pass, be - cause of taking forward Observations; and may be made alio a Backoff, by adding a fourth Vane and Sight. ’ Tis used by Seamen to take the Me - ridian Altitude of the Sun or Stars in order to find the Latitude; ’ tis also by some used m Surveying, t CRo sj “ k, in a Ship, is a small Yard flung at the upper End of the Mizen - Mast under the Top; it hath no Halliards nor Tyes belonging to it. Its Use is to spread and hale out theMizemTop - Saii Sheets. This is alio called the Cross - Tree - Tard.
