CKOSSrStaff. The. Description and Use of this Instrument is as follows: The Staff is usually above Foot long, having Sides Square to one another about f an Inch o ver; and each is graduated like a Line of Tan - geiits, and to every Side belongs a peculiar Cross - piece. The Staff may be divided either by a Ta - ble of Natural Tangents, or Geometrically by the Divisions in the Quadrant of a Circle. Then the Half of the Cross - piece being supposed Radius, the Graduation on the Staff - will be the Natural Co - Tangents of the half Arches. The Uses of this Instrument are, to take the Al - titude of the Sun, or of a Star; to take the Di - stance between two Stars, or of any Star from the Moon, &c. and ’ tis us ’ d by some to take Distances by Land. To Observe the Altitude of the Sun or Stars. There ate four Crosses belonging to the Staff, one called the Tencrofs, which belongs to that Side where the Graduation begins deg. and end with deg. another called the T thirty - cross, belonging to that side of the Staff where the Divisions begin with o and end with deg. The Third is the Sixty - Cross, which belongs to that Side where the degrees begin at and end at deg. And the last is called the Ninety - cross, belonging to that Side where the Graduations begin at and end at deg. Now according as you can guess the Suns Al - titude to be, you mull use the proper Cross: If the Altitude be under deg. use the Ten - cross; if under, use the Thirty - cross; if under, the Sixty - cross; but if above that, use the Ninety - cross. And the Way of Obfervifig, is thus: Having fitted on your proper Cross, place the flat end of the Staff to the outside of your Eye, and as near to your Eye as you can: Then look at the Slip, or Star with the upper end of the Cross, and at the Horizon with the lower end, moving or Aiding the Cross to and fro ’ till you can do this exactly; for then the Degrees and Minutes cut by the inner Edge of the Cross, on the proper Side of the Staff for that Cross, will give you the preterit Altitude of the Sun of Star. Unless it be hazy and thick Weather, the Ob - serration can hardly be, made without Prejudice to the Eye: To prevent which, some put a co - loured Glal's on the top of the Cross; and then they observe the upper Limb of the Sun, and fub - ftracft his Semi - diameter from the Altitude. There is a Way also of making a Backward Observation of the Sun ’ s Altitude With the Cross - StafF, as thus: Fix a Horizontal Vane on the Eye - End of the Staff, and a Shoe of Brass to the End of any of the Four Crosses; which will serve in - stead of a Sight Vane. Having done this, and fit - ted the Cross on upon the Staff, turn your Back to the Sun, and looking through the Slit in the Brass Shoe, lift Up or down the End ofthe Staff, ’ till the Shadow made by the upper End of the Cross fall on the Slit in the Horizon Vane, and that likewise at the fame Time you can see the Horizon through M z the Horizontal Vane at the End of the Brass j then will the Degrees cut on the proper Side of the Staff, be the Sun's Altitude required. To observe the Distance between Two Stars, or the Moons Distance from a Star. Place the flat End of the Staff to the Edge, as in the First Observation, and looking to both Ends of the Cross, draw it to and fro, ’ till the Ends will cut the Two Stars, or One the Moon, and the o - ther the Star, then will the ' Cross cut the Distance between thole Objects on the proper Side of the Staff. Because there may be a Mistake in placing the Staff to the Eye, take fthis Rule to know when it is right: Put the Sixty - cross on Degrees on its proper Side of the Staff, and likewise the Ninety - cross on Degrees on ' its Out - side; and then when, by moving the Staff higher or lower, you have placed it so, that you can see the ' upper End of the Two Crosses in one and the fame right Line, and the Two ' lower Ends in another, the Staff is placed right.

crosspiece.c: CROSS Piece, is a great Piece of Timber go - ing a - cross the Bins of a Ship, and unto it is the Cable belayed when Ihe rides at Anchor.

crossfrees.c: CROSS Frees, in a Ship, are Pieces of Tim - ber bolted and let into one another a - cross at the Head of the Mast: Their Use is to keep and bear the Top - masts up, for the Foot of the Top - mast is always fattened into them. Thole who are more nice, call only those two of these Timbers which go athwart Ships, the Cross Trees; and then the others they call the Treffel Trees.

crosstreetard.c: CROSS Tree Tard, is a Yard ( landing square just under the Mizen Top, and to it the Mizen - Top - fail is fattened below.

crossiers.c: CROSSIERS, are four Stars in Form of a Cross, which serve to ( hew those that fail in the Southern Hemisphere the Antarticl l Pole.

crotaphickartery.c: CROTAPHICK Artery, so some erroneously call the Tendon of the Muscle called Crotaphites or Temporalis. CROTAPHITES: See Temporalis.

crotchetaterminmusick.c: CROTCHET, a Term in Musick: See Notes and Time.

crowningeometry.c: CROWN, in Geometry, signifies a plain Ring included between two concentrick Perimeters, and is generated by the Motion of some Parr of a Right Line found a Center, the said moving Part not be - ing contiguous to the Center. The Area of which will be had if you multiply, its Breadth by the middle Perimeter; for a Series of Terms in Arithmetick Progression being n x e - the Sum of thefirft and last multiplied by i the Number of Terms, the middle Element ct CO must be; wherefore that multiply ’ d by the Breadth or Sum of all the two Terms, will give the Crown.

crown.c: CROWN - WHEEL, of a Watch, is the upper Wheel next the Balance, which, by its Motion, drives it; and this in kpyal Pendulums is called the Swing - Wheel.

CROWN - WORKS, in Fortifications, are cer tain Bulwarks advanced towards the Field to gain some Hill or riling Ground, being composed of a spacious Gorge, and two Wings that fall on the Conn - terfcarp near the Faces of the Bastion, so that they are defended by them, and present on the Side of the Field an entire Bastion between two Demi - Ba - ftions, whose Faces look towards one another, ' Those Works have alio their Half - Moons, and are raised only to take up and secure some large Space of Ground, or to defend the Head of a Camp when it is intrenched.

CROWN - Po / ?, is a Post which in some Buil - dings stands upright in the middle, between Two principal Rafters, and from it there go Strutts or Braces to the middle of each Rafter. This is also by some called the King - piece, and the Joggle - piece

crownedhorn.c: CROWNED Horn - word, is a Horn - work. with a Crown - work. before it.

crow.c: CROW - FEET, in a Ship, are small Lines of Ropes put through the Holes of the Dead Mens Eyes, and divided by that Means into or, or sometimes more Parts: They are of no use at all, ’ but are there left hanging by the Boat - Swain to make a ( hew of small Rigging. They are placed at the Bottom of the Back - Stays of the Fore - Top - Mast, Mizen - Top - Mast, and Gallant - Top - Mast. There goes also a Rope divided into or Por - tions from the upper End of the Sprit - Sail - Top - Mast to the Fore - Top - Mast Stay, which they call the Sprit - Sail Top - Sail Crow - Foot.

crows.c: CROWS - FEET, ( called also Caltrops and Chaufft Trapes ) are Irons so made with Points of, or Inches long, that which way soever they fall, one Point may beuppermoft; the fhorterare to ( fiow on Bridges, the longer on the Ground, to gall the Feet of a Body of Horse.

cube.c: CUBE I, or the Vena, in Anatomy is a long hard Bone with a Cavity in its Middle, and lies on the Inside of the Arm, reaching from the El - d. bow ClIC bow to the Wrist; but Lome make it to consist of two Bones, the one called the Vena, and the other Radius., r. CUBITiEUS Intemus & Extemus, areMufcles of the Wrist, the one serves to bend, the other to extend it CUBITiEUS Extemus, is one of the Extenders of the Wrist, arising from the External Knob of the Os humeri, and is inferred in the upper. and external Part of the Os met near pi of the little CUBITiEUS Intemus, is one of the Benders of the Wrist, springs from the inner Extuberance of the - r humeri, and palling along the Vena, ends in the fourth Bone of the Carpus, and the Os metacar - pi o f the little Finger.

CUBE, is a solid Body of fix equal Sides, which are all Squares; ’ tis one of the five regular Bodies, and its Content is found by multiplying any one Side or Face by the Height: See a Table of the different Weight of a Cubick Inch and Foot of fe - veral Bodies under the. Word Weight.

cubitalmuscle.c: CUBITAL Muscle: See Anconaut. CUBO - Cuhe, the sixth Power of any Number or Quantity., r

cuboides.c: CUBOIDES, is the seventh Bone of the T ar [ us of the Foot, it lies in the lame Rank with the Off a Cuneiformia: It is called also Grandinofum and Cubiforme; behind ' tis joined to the Os Cal - as before to the two outer Bones of the Meta - tarsus, and on its inside iris joined to the Os Cunei -

cucullarisandtrapezius.c: CUCULLARIS, and Trapezius, is a Muscle of the Scapula, so named, because this with its Sel - low covering the Back represents a Cowl It anses Flelhv from the OsOccipitis, Tendinous from the Li, amentum Colli, and Apex of the Spine of the last Vertebra of the Neck, and eight fupenor of the Thorax - from which broad Origination becoming Thick and Fleshy, it ’ s so inferred to the CUvicula, and Tendinous to the Spina Scapula. Each Mu - scale is Triangular, and both conjointly compose a Lozenge or Trapezium, whose large Diameter ex - rends from the Occipt to the i th Vertebra; the shorter from near the Extremity of th eSfma Sen - ulre on one Side to that of the other. They con - fain a triple Series of Fibres, the Middle passing dircdly transverse from the sift. Vertebra of the Thorax: Those above descend, and those beneath ascend to their Insertion, whereby the Scapula is variously moved according to their Directions, either obliquely or upward, direCtly back, or obliquely

cucuphaamedicine.c: CUCUPHA a Medicine for the Head, made of Odoriferous and Cephalick Spices beat to Pow - der and stitched between two Pieces of Silk, or else sewed within a Cap and worn upon the Head against Catarrhs and other Diseases of the Head. Blmcha jCXJKBl te; so the Chymifts call a Glass, Earthen or Copper Body of this Shape, because it fomethmg re - semble a Gourd. ThisVelfel, with its Head, is most commonly used m Distillations or Rectifications: They call it usually a Body.

curbtinlumbrici.c: CURB TIN Lumbrici, are broad Worms breed in the Intestines like the Seed of a TirURBlTULA, or Cucurbita, a Cupping - rs is a wide hollow Vessel made of Glass or which is applied to the Body with Scanfi - ’ n or without it, to divert, to drive the Blood the other Part, or to drive it out: If it bear - i without Scarification it is called Cucumta cc - nd Ventofa. Cupptng - Glasses ase appked to the more Fleshy Parts, where the large Vessels and Nerves cannot be hurt. The Drawing, which is performed by these Glasses ? is done thus; After the Skin is scarify ’ d, the Air in the Cupping - Giajfes is rarity ’ d and dilated by the Flame of the Towr that is fired within it, which, after it is cooled and condensed, takes up less Room than before; so that the External Air pressing upon the Flesh with - our, forces the Blood into the Glass. There are two forts of Gupping - Glasses, says Celfus, one of Brass, and the other of Horn; the Former isopea on one Parr, and shut on the other; the Latter is equally open on one Part, on the other has a little Hole: Burning Tow is thrown into the Brazen one, and so its Mouth apply U and forc ’ d upon the Body till it sticks. That of Horn is apply ’ d singly by it self, and by a violent sucking at the little Hole, which must presently be stop ’ d up dole with Wax, it sticks as fall as the other; but if o - ther things fail, then a little Cup or Goblet with a straight Mouth may be very fitly apply ’ d to the fame EffeCt: After it has stuck, if the Skin be scarify ’ d before with a Pen - knife, it draws out the Blood; if it be whole and entire, it draws out the Flatulent Matter; therefore, where the Mat - ter within is hurtful and offenftve, it must be ap - ply ’ d the former Way; where there is an Inflam - motion the Latter. The Egyptians at this Day use those of Horn, as appears from Prosper Alpinus Blanchard. Now in England we commonly use Cupping - Glasses without Fire, which are evacuated by a small Syringe which works like an Air - Pump; and for Scarification they have an Engine that doth it all at once with great Safety and very little Pain and this was the Invention of the Ingenious Mr J Havthjbee in Wine - Office Court in Fleetflreet, who makes thebeft Air - Pumps, and all Pneumatiek En - gines that ever I saw.

cuddy.c: CUDDY, in a first Rate Man of War, is a Place lying between the Quarter - Deck and the Captain Lieutenant ’ s Cabbin under the Poop, vs hich is di - vided into Partitions for the Mailer and the Se - cretary ’ s Officers.

cui.c: CUI ante Divortium, is a Writ that a Woman ' divorced from her Husband hath to recover Lands or Tenements from him, to whom her Husband did alienate them during the Marriage, because he could not gainsay it:

cuiinvita.c: CUI in Vita, is a Writ of Entry that a Widow hath against him to whom her Husband aliened her Lands and Tenements in his Life - time; which must contain in it. That during his Life - time file could not withstand it.

culmiferousplants.c: CULMIFEROUS Plants, ( fee Plants, N.. ) are by the Botanijls accounted such as have a smooth jointed Stalk, and usually hollow; and at each Joint the Stalk is wrap ’ d about with single, narrow, long, sharp pointed Leaves, and their Seeds are contained in chaffy Husks.

CULMIFEROUS Plants, with a greater or larger Seed or Grain, are such as are called Frumentaceous and Cereales, because their Seeds are used for Food; as for Bread, Beer, Broth, &c. These they call the Frumenta, and are S ' pleat. fc, n, l so tempered and baked as to endure the E ?; Fire They are used to melt Metals, to lute MtoS, Oars ’, &c. and are of this Figure; A French Crucible, A German Crucible.

culmieerousplants.c: CULMIEEROUS Plants, are of two kinds, " either having, i. a greater, or,. a ftnaller Grain or Seed.

crudityindiseases.c: CRUDITY, in Diseases, is when the Blood ( as in continued Fevers ) is not yet duly fermented and brought to a right Consistence. Crudity of the Stomach, is when Meat, out of a Defect of Nou - rifhment, or some other Cause, is not rightly fer - mented and turned into Chyle; and it is threefold, Apepfta, Bradypepfia, and Difpepfia, of which m their proper Places. Blanchard..

cruorblood.c: CRU OR Blood: See Sanguis. Helmont makes a Diftindtion betwixt Sanguis and Cruor; the For - mer whereof, he says is the Blood in the Arteries, the Latter, that in the Veins.

crura.c: CRURA, are the two Heads or Beginnings of the Marrowy Substance of the Brain, called Me - dull Oblongata.

cruramedullaoblongata.c: CRURA Medulla Oblongata, the Internal Sub - stance of the ' two Sides of the Cerebrum, gathered together as it were into two Bundles.

cruralartery.c: CRURAL Artery, by some said to be the Ar - tery of the Thigh, among whose Muscles it divi - doth it self: It is a Continuation of the Iliack Ar - tery which pafllng out of the Abdomen, and en - thing into the Thighs, it lies its former Name, and is called Cruralis. Besides: some less remarka - ble Branches, before it come to the Ham, it fends forth the External and Internal Muscle; under the Ham it produces the two Poplitaa ’ s, and some - what lower the Sureties, Afterwards the Trunk it self is divided into the Branches called Anterior and Poflerior and the last of thefeisalfo fubdivi - ded into two smaller Branches which descend to the Foot.

crucalveintheblood.c: CRU CAL Vein the Blood is conveyed from the lower Extremity of the Body by fix Veins cal - led The greater and smaller ifehia, Mufcula, Pop - Htaa, and Saphcena, which joined together, com - pose the Trunk of the Crural Vein, which ascends to the Groin and ends in the Iliaca.

crureusorfmnorevs.c: CRUREUS, or Fmnorevs, is a Muscle of the Leg, so called from its Situation on the Bone of the Thigh, like the Mufcultts Branchieus, on that of the Arm; its Origination is large and fleshy, being continued from between the greater and les - fer Trochanter of the Thigh - Bone forwards to its lower Part; that is, immediately above its Inferior Appendix. Its Fleshy Fibres descend directly, and become perse & ly Tendinous a little below the up - per Part of the Tendon of the ReBus, where it joins with it, and the Tendons of the Vafius Enter - ntt and Internus, which passes over the external Part of the Patella, ( or on each Side of it ) and is inferred to a Prominence at the Superior and Fore - Part of the Tibia it helps to extend the Tibia,

crusormagnuspes.c: CRUS, or Magnus Pes, is all that Part of the Body which reaches from the Buttocks down to the End of the Toes j and it is divided into the Thigh, -, Leg and Foot. Blanchard.

crust.c: CRUST LaBea, is a Species of Achor, Scurf, or crafty Scab, only with this Difference, that an Achor insects only the Head, but this not only the Facej but almost the whole Body of an Infant at the time of its. first sucking. Blanchard Crujla LaBea turns white, but Achors have only one Co - lour.

crustaceousshell.c: CRUSTACEOUS, Shell - Fishes, are fitch as Lobsters, Crabs, Craw - fishes, &c. which are co - vered with Shells consisting of several Pieces, and which usually are softer too than those of the Tejla - ceous Shell - Fishes, which are all entirely of one Piece, and usually much harder, thicker and stronger than the former, as the Oyster, Scollop, Cockle,

crustula.c: CRUSTULA, is the fame as Ecchynoma in the Eye, being a Del cent of Blood from the Arteries into the Tunica ConjunBiva, occasioned by a Wound, Stroak, &c.

crymodes.c: CRYMODES, is a cold shivering Fever, but many times accompanied with an Inflammation of the inner Parts. Blanchard.

crysorchis.c: CRYSORCHIS, is an absconding of the Tefti - cles in the Belly. Blanchard.

crystallinushumoroculi.c: CRYSTALLINUS Humor Oculi, called alio Glacialis, the Chriftalline Humour of the Eye, lies immediately next to the Aqueous, within the open - ing of the Tunica Z ) sea, like a Glass. put over a Hole, collects and refracts the Rays which strike upon it from all Parts: Its Substance is like Glue or the Gum of a Tree, very pellucid, and of a Consistence like melting Wax, which, though it be press ’ d, does not yet easily yield and separate.. In Men it is fliaped like a Lens or Convex Glass, which rises thicker in the Middle than tthe Edges: This Humour is the least of all three, but is much more solid than any of them, arid is cloathed with a small Membrane of its own called Araned, by reason of its Thinness, like to a Spiders Web.

cubatureingeometry.c: CUBATURE, in Geometry, is finding exactly the solid Content of any proposed Body; as the Quadrature of a Surface is finding the Area of that Surface. There is a little Book lately writ - ten by one F ant it a French - man, Entituled, De la Cubature de la Sphere, in which, with great Affu - rance, he pretends to find Geometrically the Solid Content of any Portion of a Sphere; but how lit - tle the Success answers the Boldness of the Title, I leave the Reader to judge;

cubicalartery.c: CUBICAL Artery, by some is said to be a Branch of the Axillary, D d. CUBICK

culminate.c: CULMINATE, is a Word used by Astronomy - cal Writers, to express a Star s or the Sun ’ s being upo n the Meridian, or having the greatest Altitude that: it can have that Day. r ] she Culminating of any Star, or being on the Meridian, may be found by the Globe thus; Ue & is your Globe and Hour Index, and bring the Star to the Brazen Meridian; then the Index will shew the Time of the Star ’ s Culminating.

culmusinbotanicks.c: CULMUS, in Botanicks, is properly the Stalk of. ' Corn or Grass, but of no other Plant, for that Is tailed Caulis.,

culvering.c: CULVERING, a fort of Ordnance, of which there are the Extraordinary, the Ordinary, and the Lift fitted Culver ing.. Culver ing Extraordinary has Inches Bore, r Foot long, weighing Pound Weight its Load above a Pound, carries a Shot - ? Diameter, weighing zo Pound Weight. Culvering Ordinary, is a Size lesser. Culvering of the leaf Sip, is that whose Dia - meter is Inches Bore, iz Foot long, weighing about lb. carries a Shot Inches Diameter, weighing lb. Ounces..

culvertaile.c: CULVERT AILE, the fattening m of a Ship s Carlings into the Beam is so called.

cunorcond.c: CUN, or Cond, a Sea Term, signifying to di - rest or guide: To Cun a Ship is to diredl the Per - fon at Helm how to steer her: See Cond..

cuneiformeos.c: CUNEIFORME Os, is a Bone so called from the Resemblance which it hath to a Wedge; by the Ancients called Multiforme, by reason of the various Processes on the Inside and Outside, which renders it rough and unequal: It is situate in the Midst of the Basis of the Brain, and is placed under it like a Basts, so that it touches upon most of the Bones of the Head and the Upper Jaw. Blanchard.

cuneiformiaoff.c: CUNEIFORMIA Off a, are those Bones of the Tarsus of the Foot which are accounted the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth; and these are so called because they are large above, and narrow below, like Wedges: They link all three at the Side of one a - nother, having their Upper part Convex, and their Lower Concave, by which means the Muscles and Tendons in the Sole of the Foot are not hurt when we go. At one End, each hath a Sinus receiving Os Naviculare, and at the other End they are join - ed to the three inner Bones of the Metatarfm - the inmoftof these Bones isthelargeft, and the mid - dle one the least.

cuneusatriangularprism.c: CUNEUS, a Triangular Prism, hi a Wedge. ’

cuppelorcompel.c: CUPPEL or Compel, an Instrument in Chymi - stry in the Form of a Dish, made of Ashes well wash ’ d ( to cleanse them from all their Salt ) or of Bones throughly calcined: Its Use is to try and purify Gold and Silver which is done by min - going Lead with the Metal, and so exposing it in the Coppel to a violent Fire a great while; the Im - purities of the Metal will then be carried off in Dross, which Brofs is called Litharge of either Gold or Silver: Tis by the Refiners usually cal - led a Test. CUPPING GLASSES: See Cucurbitula.

curatio.c: CURATIO, is a right Way or Method of find - ing out by Symptoms and Indications proper Re - medius for any Disease, in order to the Recovery of Health. Blanchard. CiJRCULIO, the fame with Cion.

curia.c: CURIA avifare vult, is a Deliberation that the Court intends to take upon any Point or Points of a Cause, before Judgment be resolved on.
CURIA C claudenda, is a Writ that lieth against him that should fence and close tip his Ground, if he refuse or defer to do it.

curiassiers.c: CURIASSIERS, are Horfemen that wear Ar - mour.

cursitor.c: CURSITOR, is an Officer or Clerk belonging to the Chancery, that maketh out Original Writs They are called also Clerks of the Course; and there be of these twenty four in number, which have allotted to each of them several Shires, in which they make out such Original Writs, as arse by the Subject required, and are a Corporation of themselves.

curtaininfortification.c: CURTAIN, in Fortification, is the Front of the Wall of a fortified Place between two BajUons j or the longest straight Line that runs about the Rampart, drawn from one Flank to the other ’ and bordered with a Parapet five Foot high, b, e hind which the Souldiers stand to fire Upon the Covert - way and into the Moat. Besiegers seldom carry on their Attacks against the Curtain, be - cause ’ tis the best flank ’ d of any Part.

curtation.c: CURTATION of a Planet, in Astronomy, ac cording to some, is a little part cut off from the Line of his Interval or Distance from the Sun.

courtesyofengland.c: COURTESY of England: See Courtejy of Ends

curvesorcurvilinealfigures.c: CURVES or Curvilineal Figures are in GedP metre, such as are terminated or bounded by Curved or Crooked Lines; as Circles and EUipfes and all Conick Sections, Spherical Triangles, &c e are Curves.

custodeadmittendo.c: CUSTODE Admittendo, and Cufiode amovendo ] are Writs for the admitting or removing of Guar - dians. CU ST ODES L ber tails Angle authoritate Par - liamenti, was the Stile wherein Writs and other Judicial Proceedings did run during the late Times of Trouble, vf. from the Further of King Charles the First, till the Usurpation by Cromwell, men - tioned tionedand declared traiterous by the St at, i Car. i. Cap..

custom.c: CUSTOM, is ( both by Comhioh Lawyers and Civilians, taken to be ) a Law or Right not com - iilitted in Writing, but established by long use, and by the Consent of our Ancestors hath been, and is daily practiced and ’ tis either General of ' Particular: A General Custom, is that which is al - lowed through all England. Particular Cuftorii is that which belongeth to this or that County, or to this or that Lordship, Town, or City.

customsandservices.c: CUSTOMS and Services, or Confuetudlnibus & Servitiis, is a Writ of Right close which lieth against the Tenant that deforceth his Lord of the Rent or Service due to him: Of this fee more at large in the Old Nat. Brev. Sol..

custosbrevium.c: CUSTOS Brevium, a Clerk belonging to the Court of Common - Pleas, whose Office is to receive and keep all the Writs, and put them upon Files, every Return by it self and at the End of every Term, to receive of the Protonotaries all the Re - cords of the Nisi prius, called the P often.

custosplacitorumcorona.c: CUSTOS Placitorum Corona, seems to be the fame with Custos ftotulorum.

custosbptulorum.c: CUSTOS Bptulorum, is he that hath the custom - dy of the Rolls, or Records of the Sessions of Peace; and as some fay, of the Commissions of Peace it self: He is always a Justice of Peace and Quorum in the County where he hath his Office.

custosspiritualium.c: CUSTOS Spiritualium, or Custom of the Spirit - qualities, is he that exercifeth Spiritual or Ecclefi - aftical Jurifdicftion in any Diocese during the Va - fancy of the See, which, by the Canon - Law, be - longs to the Dean and Chapter, but at present with us in England, to the Archbishop of the Pro - since by Prefcriptipn: Howbeit, divers Deans and Chapters do challenge this by ancient Char - ters from the Kings of this Land.

custostemporal.c: CUSTOS Temporal ium, the Person to whose custody a vacant See was committed by the King as Supreme Lord, who as a Steward of the Goods and Profits, was to give account to the Escheator, and he into the Exchequer: His Trust continued till the Vacancy was supplied by a Successor, who obtained f the King ’ s Writ De fteftitutione Tempora - Hum, which was commonly after Consecration yet sometimes before.

cutafeather.c: CUT a Feather; if a Ship hath too broad a Bow, they fay she will not Cut a Feather; that is, she will not pass through the Water so swiftly as to make it foam or froth.

cutaneousdistempers.c: CUTANEOUS Distempers, such as passed the Skin, as the Itch, or Scab, tic.

cutanenusglandsandvessels.c: CUTANENUS Glands and Vessels, are such as are placed or terminated in the r or Skin.

cuticlescarjfskin.c: CUTICLE, Scarjf Skin, is a Cover of the Skin without Sense, extended outwardly over the whole Skin like a Membrane, full of innumerable small Pores, accommodated to the avoiding of In - juries from abroad, to the Hunting up of the Cu - taneous Vessels, and to the more accurate perfect - ing of Tadile Qualities: It is nourished by the Blood, for if it be loft or perifhed, it comes a - gain, though irs Vessels be but little conspicuous. Blanchard. Mr. Luenhoeck found by his Microscope, that the Cuticula consisted of an infinite Quantity of very small Scales, so minute, that a small Grain of Sand would cover near of them; so that he think there are no proper Pores in the Skin, but that the Moisture comes out under or from be - tween the Scales.

cutis.c: CUTIS, is the Skin of a living Man; but Pet - it is that which is fleed off, and it is the outer - most Cover of the whole Body, or a pretty thick Membrane wrought of several Filaments of the Veins and Arteries, Nerves, and Nervous Fibres, complicated and interwoven with one another, full of Glandules and Lymphedu & s, or Vessels that convey away the Vapours and Swear, abounding with a great number of Pores here and there, and sensibly perforated in many places to let in and out, as occasion requires; as at the Mouth, Nostrils, Eyes, Ears, Privities, Fuhdament, &c. it is thick - eft of all upon the Head, moderately hard in the Neck and Back, finer in the Face, Perns, and ou - ter Skin of the Scrotum j thin on the Sides, and thinnest of all on the Lips; in some places, as the Elbow, Forehead, Soles of the Feet, it sticks very close together. Blanchard.

cut.c: CUT - WATER, the Sharpnels of the Head of a Ship below the Be aft, ’ tis so called because it cuts or divides the Water before it comes to the Bow: This is called alio the JKfiee of the Head.

CUT - WRIT, are Words used by the Clerk of the Arraignments, when a Person is indiCted for a Criminal Matter. For after the Indidiment is read in Court ( which is the Crown ’ s Charge ) a - gainst the Prisoner at the Bar, he is put upon his Plea, or asked, Art thou Guilty, or Not Guilty ? If he pleads or answers, Not Guilty there is next a Replication from the Crown, by continuing the Charge - of Guilt upon him, according to the Te - nour of the Indictment; which isexprefs ’ d by pro - enouncing the Words Cul - Writ: Cul being an Ab - breviation of the Latine Word Culpabilis, Guilty. and Prill, or Writ, ( now Pret ) is the old French Ward. for Bpaiy, From these Two Affertions therefore of the Clerk of the Arraignment, That the Prisoner is Culp, or guilty of the Crime char - ged on him; and that the Crown is Writ, or ready to prove it upon him this Word Cul - writ is deri - ved. And that this is the true Explanation of the Terms Cul - writ, is evident from the Form of the Entry of the Record of the Tryal when drawn up I at large which, as to the Replication pronounced by the Clerk, as aforesaid, in the Words Cul and Writ, runs thus: Et PradiBus A. ( the Clerk ) pro Domina Bogina dicit, Quod PrcedicL B. ( the Prifo " ner ) eft Culpabilts, &c. Et hoc paratus eft verificare cc.

cuvetteinfortification.c: CUVETTE, in Fortification, is a deeper Trench about four Fathom broad, which is usually funk in the Middle of the great dry Ditch till you meet with Water, and serves both to prevent the Besiegers Mining, and alio the better to keep off the Enemy.

cycle.c: CYCLE, is a continual Revolution of certain Numbers, which successively go on without any Interruption from the First to the Last, and then return again to the First, and so circulate perpetu - ally. In the Calendar there are three principal Cycles, viz the Solar, the Lunar, and the Cycle of In dipt ion.

CYCLE of the Sun, is a Revolution of Years, in which time the fame Dominical Letter comes about again in the fame Order, and Leap - years expire, and the th Year the Cycle begins again t This Cycle fervesko find the Dominical Letter for any Year past, present, or to come. To find the Cycle of the Sun. I ule. To the Year add, and divide the Sum by, the Remainder is the Cycle of the Sun, Example. To add, the Sum divided by, the Residue is the Cycle of the Sun.

CYCLE of the Moon, is a Revolution of Years, in which time the New Moon's return to the fame Days they were on before, and she be - gins again her Course with the Sum This was invented by Melon the Athenian, and is called the Golden Number. That which occasioned pro - barly the pitching upon this Number, was their Obfervationsthat the Lunar Eclipses happen near - ly again on the fame Day of the Month Years after the former; of which ’ tis easy to give many modern Instances. Enneadecateriaes is with some the Name of this Lunar Cycle. CY CLE of IndiBion, is a Revolution of three Luftrums or fifteen Years, after which those who used it began it again. This is more ancient than the precedent ones, and hath nothing to do with with the Heavenly Motions;, being established by Conftantine, A. D.. Sept.. who substituted them in the room of the Olympiads They were so called according to some Authors, because they denoted the Year that Tribute was to be paid to the Republick. To find this IndiBion, subtract from the Year given, and divide the Remain - der by, and omitting the Quotient, what re - mains is the Year of the Roman IndiBion. Example, A. D. ) ( J IndiBion.

cyclesci.c: CYCLE SCI, are Surgeons Instruments, where - with they scrape away corrupt Flesh, or the like: they are made in the form of an Half - Moon.

That this Eclipse of the Sun is improperly so call'd, and may with much mote justness take the Name which some of our Modern Astronomers have given ir, when they call it an Eclipse of the Earth; for so in reality it is, the Sun by no means being deprived of his Light,. but only some Parts of our Earth loose theirs, by being within the Sha - dow of the Moon ’ s Body, when. it happens to be interposed between them and the Sun. Toiiluftrate this the better, let Us suppose the Earth for a Time deprived of its diurnal do - tation round its Axis, while the Moon freely re - valves round us. And suppose the Moon to be in the very Nodes, and so without any Latitude: Then ’ tis plain that the Centre of the Moon, being in the Plain of. the Ecliptick, directly inter - posed between the Centres of the Sun and Earth, will occasion a Central Eclipse of the Sun, to filch People as inhabit the Earth ’ s Equator; which will be total, if in that Place the Appa - rent Diameter of the Moon exceed that of the Sun; but if it fall sliort of it, as is most usual, then the Eclipse will be annular. , Bu. t if at the ‘ Time of the Eclipse, the Moon be not in the very Node, but a little Di - hance from it: then the Centre of the Moon ’ s ’ a - ' ? Shadow will not defer be the Ecliptick, nor any great Circle on the Earth, but a lesser Cir - cle, or a Chord of a great Circle in the Plane of the Disk. . The Figure of the true Line or Path, which the Centre of the Penumbra and Shadow de - series on the Spherical Surface of the Earth, is not exactly Circular, but, a Portion of a Curve more or less regular, according to the Motion of the Earth and the obliquity of its Incidence., . The Moon ’ s true Parallax, to be eAimated in a Vertical Circle, here, puts on the form of other Parallaxes, and makes a Difference, not only in a Vertical Circle, but even in thole of Longitude and Latitude: So that on this Ac - count, the Apparent Longitude and Latitude of the Moon, do very much vary, and render the exact Calculation of Solar Ecliples very difficult. - - However there hath been a Geometrical Method, found out by Sir Chrijlcpher Wren, Mr.. Flamjled and Mr. Halley, to avoid this te - dious and precarious way of ParallaClick Calcu - lation, and of delineating a Solar Eclipse by Scale and Compass. See Fiamftedes Dolirine of the Sphere, in Sir Jonas Mores Mathematicks, Vol. I; To determine the Moment of theEeginning and Endings and the Duration of a Solar Eclipse. i. jP R O M the Moon ’ s Horizontal Parallax, F & tract the Solar, the Remainder will be the SemicUameter of the Sun ’ s Disk. Then col led ! into one ' Sum, the Horizontal Semidiameters of the ‘ Sun and Moon, which Sum will be equal to the ' Semidianheter of the whole Penumbra of the Moon, from whence a Solar Eclipse arises. - - r. . To the Semidiameter of the Disk, add that of the Penumbra; and if the Most ’ s Latitude ' at the Moment of the true Conjunction in her proper Orbit be left thanthat Sum; there will be, some where on the Earth, an Eclipse of the Sun: But if it be greater, there will be no Eclipse at all. And if the Moon ’ s Latitude be, alone, less than the Semidiasnerer of the Disk, then the Centre of the Shadow will fall Upon the Earth, and for cause somewhere a Central Solar Eclipse, but if it be greater, there will be only a Partial one. . From the jemidiarrseter of the Earth ’ s Disk, take that of the P ’ penumbra, and Note the Re - mainder carefully; for if the Latitude of the Moon, in the Time of the Syzygy in her proper Orbit, be less than such Remainder j then will the whole Penumbra, at the middle Moment of the Eclipse, be confined within the Circumference of the Earth ’ s Disk; but if otherwise, ’ it will not be so. And if by Multiplication, you re - due all these Quantities to Seconds, you will have the Angles of Incidence as they are called; that is, the Distances of the Points where the Penumbra touches the Disk in its Ingress and E - grefs; and also the Point where, in the middle Time between both, the Centre of the Penumbra enters into, and goes out of the Disk, For these Distances being given in Angles, from the Velocity of the Monthly Motion of the Moon from the Sun, there may, by the Rule of Three, be found the Space of Time proper to each Distance; that is, the whole Duration of the Eclipse will be given, and of the absolute Darkness, and also the Time of the More of the Penumbra within the Earth ’ s Disk, as will appear below. . From theTatitude of the Moon at the Time of rhe Conjunction in her own Orbit ( which, as hath been laid above, is the fame with the least Di / lance of the Centres so often mentioned ) you may I o determine the Moment of the beginning and ending of a Solar Eelipfe, may find these Angles of Incidence, of the Im - mersion and Emetfion of the Centre, by these Analogies. As the Sum of the Semidiameters of the Ter - reftrial Disk, and of the Penumbra, is to Radius:: so is the Moon ’ s Latitude, or the least Distance of their Centres, to the Cosine of the Angle of Incidence: And then, As the Semidiameter of the Earth ’ s Disk is to Radius:; so is the Moon ’ s Latitude, to the Co - fine of the Angle of the Immersion of the Centre of the Penumbra And As the Difference between the Semidiameters of the Terrestrial Disk, and of the Penumbra, is to Radius. so is the Moon ’ s Latitude, to the Co - fine of the Angle of the total Immersion. And since in the Egress of the Penumbra, the Angles are equal to those in the Ingress, the fame Numbers will express both. . Having thus gained the Co - fine of these Angles, and consequently, the Angles themselves you mail next Investigate the Motion of the Moon, corresponding to each of the Angles re - spe & ively. By saying. As Radius is to the Sine of the Angle of Inch - dence:: so is the Sum of the Semidiameters of the Penumbra - and the Earth ’ s Disk, to the Mo - tion of half the Duration of the whole Eelipfe; And, - As Radius to the Sine of the Angle of Immer - sion of the Centre:: so is the Semidiameter of the Disk, to the Motion of half the Duration of Central Eclipses. And again, As Radius to the Sine of the Angle of total Immersion:: so is the Difference between the Semidiameters of the Disk and Penumbra, to the Motion of half the More, or continuance of the Penumbra within the Disk. . And when the Motions are thus found, you may gain the corresponding Times by this Ana - logy: As the Horary Motion of the Moon from the Sun, is to one Hour, or Minutes: so is the Motion of half the Duration, ( whether be - longing to the Angle of Incidence, to the Angle of the Immersion of the Centre, or to the Angle of the whole Immersion ) to the Space of Time corresponding to each Motion respectively. - And having thus gained theje Intervals of Time if you add them to, or take them from, the mid - dle Moment of the Eelipfe, you will obtain the Moment of Time, in which is the Beginning and End of the Eelipfe Central or other; the Begin - ning and End of the More of the Centre of the Penumbra universally, for that Place where you are, or for the Meridian of that Place for which your Tables were calculated; which Time, by the Consideration of the Difference of Meridians or Longitudes of Places, may easily be accommo - dated to any other Place. And thus may the General Phenomena of So - lar Eclipses be accounted for and Calculated. Their more particular Affectum s may be obtained from the following Considerations, and Methods of Iriveftigation. But let us premise, . That in that very Place, where the Penumbra first touches and enters the Earth ’ s Disk, the Inha - bitants will see the Beginning of the Eelipfe, in the uppermost Point of the Sun ’ s Vertical Dia - meter, or in the upper extremity of the Limb, ( x. ) In that Place where the Centre of the Pe - umbra enters ' the Earth ’ s Disk, the Spectators will fee a Central Eelipfe bf the Sun, (. ) But I in that Place where the whole Penumbra is first re - ceiled or contained within the Disk, there the End of the Eelipfe will be observed, at the lower End of the Sun ’ s Vertical Diameter. (. ) Where the Path of the Centre of the Penumbra, in the Meridian Circle intense & s the Earth ’ s Axis; and where it intersects the Axis of the Ecliptick in the Nonogefimal Degree, or the Point that is molt elevated above the Horizon, there a Central E - eclipse will be visible. ( J In that Place where the Penumbra begins to emerge out of the Earth ’ s Disk, the Eelipfe will begin in the Weflern Lumi - nary, in the Nadir Point of his Vertical Diahre - ter. (. ) In that Place where the Centre of the Penumbra goes out of the Limb, a total Eelipfe will be visible in the Sun in the Weft. . But where the Centre of the Penumbra goes out of the Disk:, there will be the perfect End of the Eelipfe, which will go off in the Zenith Point of the Sun ’ s Vertical Diameter. These are the General Phenomena of Solar Eclipses; only you may observe, that by Reason the Menstrual Motion is swifter than the Diurnal, they will always begin from the Weft, and so will proceed on from Weft to East, during the whole Time of the Eelipfe. Before I quite leave this Affair, it will be pro - per and ilfeful to acquaint the Reader briefly With Mr. Ftamftedes lare invented Method of iepre - setting Solar Eclipses by a Geometrical Conftru - Cfion, because ’ tis free from all the Embarafs - ment of Farallaxes, and in some Cafes hath the Advantage of Calculation. Suppose then a Plane to touch the Moon ’ s Orbit, and which shall be posited so as that it iliall be at Right Angles, to the Line which corrects the Centres of the Sun and Moon; and that thro ' this Plane, innumerable Ri ht Lines be drawn from the Centre of the Sun, to any Circles upon the Earth ’ s Surface, then will these Lines so drawn, project the Terreflial Sphere, and its Cir - cles on that Plane; so that an Eye placed in the Sun, would observe the Earth and its Annual and Diurnal Motion, as if all were transacted in that Plane: Just as we who Jive on this Earth, observe the Sun and Moon, and rheir various Motions and Changes, as if performed in Circles of the Sphere projected on a Plane. From such a Projection therefore of the Earth ’ s Spherical Surface, there will arise in that Plane a Circle for a Bale, which will be nearly equal to a great Circle on the Earth, and which is called the Earth ' s Disk, and will be every where Nor - mal to the Plane of the Ecliptick. From its Centre, suppose a right Line drawn both ways, representing the Earth ’ s Axis, and which accord - ing to the different Seasons of the Year, will be variously inclined to the Plane of the Ecliptick, which will be represented by one of the Diame - ters of the Disk; for the Parallelism of the Earth ’ s Axis, by reason of its various Position to the aforesaid Plane, will make there unequal Angles. Let there be imagined also in the fame Plane, in - numerable Ellipses to be described by the Diurnal Motion or Rotation of any Point on the Earth ’ s Superficies, these will be the Elliptical Paths of the several V - ei texts, as they are called; by each of these, the Situation of any particular Place is determined, and distinguished from all other its this given Plane. Whence, it will follow, that, CftJ if I beZJfes of the / ifironomical Tables, if in Solar Eclipses, you can ' ( within the Plane of this Disk ) find the Lines and Paths which the Moon her feif. touches or describes, you may find also the very Places on our Earth, which will be then eclipsed by the Interposition of the Moon ’ s Body.
