camberbeam.c: CAMBER Beam, in Architecture, is a Beam or Piece of Timber cut hollow or arching in the Middle: They are us ’ d in Plat - forms, Church Leads, f ' c. and are very proper wherever is oc - casion for long Beams, being much stronger than flat Beams of the lame size; for being laid with the hollow Side downwards, and having good Butments at the Ends, they serve for a Kind of Arch;

canoninmulick.c: CANON in Mulick; Ptolemy rejecting the Ari - ftoxenian Way of measuring the Intervals in Mu - lick by the Magnitude of a Tone ( which they sup - pose to be formed by the Difference between a Diapente and Diateffarcn ) thought that Musical Intervals Ihould be distinguish ’ d according to the Ratio's or Proportions which the Sounds terming - ting those Intervals bare one to another, when con - sider ’ d according to their Degree of being Acute or Grave, which was also before Ariftoxenus, the old Pythagorick. Way. Ptolemy therefore made the Di - apafon to consist in a double Ratio, the Diapente in a Sesquialteral, the Diatessaron in a Sesquitertian, and the Tone it self ( by which the Diapente and Diatessaron differ ) in a SefquioBave j and all the other Intervals according to the Proportion of the Sounds that terminate them. Wherefore taking as Canon ( as ’ tis call ’ d ) a determinate Line of any Length, he shews how this Cation is to be cut ac - cordingly, so that it may represent the refpedrive Intervals and this Method answers exactly to Experiment in the different Lengths of Musical Chord So And from this Canon, Ptolemy and his Followers have been called Canonici, as those of Ariftoxenus were called Muftci. There is a Tradk called SeBio Canonis attributed, but falsely, to Euclid; and which you will find at the End of his Works, in the Oxford Edition. G. L.

cantaliversinarchitecture.c: CANTALIVERS, in Architecture, are a Kind of Modilions, only thole are plain, but these are carved. They are much the lame with Carton and cresset as Modilions are, under the Corona of the Cornish of a Building.

care.c: CARE seems formerly to have been the Word for a certain Quantity of Wool, whereof Thirty made a Sarpler,. H.. c..

capsulateplants.c: CAPSULATE Plants are such as have a Tetra - petalous regularFlower consisting of four diftineft Pet ala in each Flower, and which bear their Seeds in short CapfuUi by which they are distinguish ’ d from the Siliquofte, which bear their Seed in long Cafes or Capsula Seminales, and are the other Branch of this Genus of Plants.

capsquaresingunnery.c: CAPSQUARES, in Gunnery, are those strong Plates of Iron which come over the Trunnions of a Gun, and keep her in the Carriage. They are fattened by Hinges to the Prize Plate, that it may lift up and done j it forms a Part of an Arch in the Middle to receive a third Part of the Thick - ness of the Trunnions, for of them are let into the Carriage, and the other End is fattened by two Iron Wedges, which are called the Fore - locks and Kjys.

cartesiansystem.c: CARTESIAN System of the World. Mr. Des Cartes, in order to account for the Cele - still Appearances, supposes the Matter of the World to have been at first divided by Al - mighty God into innumerable little equal Parts, each endow ’ d with an equ, al Degree of Motion, both about its own Center and separately, so as that this Matter constituted a Fluid. He suppos ’ d also that several Collections of this Matter, were en - dow ’ d with a Motion about different Points, as common Cepters, which Points were placed at equal Distances; so as that the Matter round them compos ’ d different Vortices, as he calls them. He supposes also, that the first Particles of Matter by those intestine Motions were rendred or Ground of a spherical Figure, and so did compose Globules of several Magnitudes: And thele he calls the Matter of his second Element Bu ? O V ' ’ - But the very small Particles which, by the aforesaid Motions, were ground and rub ’ d off from the first Particles of Matter, and driven vi - olently many different Ways, made up a new Mat - ter, which he calls his first Element. And seeing that there wou d be more of this first Element, than was sufficient to fill the Vacuities between the Globules of the second Element, he supposes that the remaining Part would be driven towards the Center by the circular Motion of these Globules, which did for that Reason recede from it and this Matter being there amassed into a Sphere, would in the Center of every Vortex produce a Body like the Sun: Which Sun being thus form'd, and moving about its own Axis with the common Matter of the Vortex, would necessarily throw out some Parts of its Matter, through the Vacub ties of the Globules of the second Element confti - tuning the Vortex; and this especially at luch Places as are farthest from its Poles, receiving at the fame Time in by these Poles as much as it loses in its Equatorial Parts, or about the Equator: And by this Means it would be able to carry round with it those Globules that are nearest, with the greater Velocity, and the remoter, with less. And by this Means those Globules which are nearest the Center of the Sun must be least; because were they greater or equal, they would by Reason of their Velocity have a greater centrifugal Force, and recede from the Center. And if it should happen that any of these Sun - like Bodies in the Centers of the several Vortices, should be so incur - stated and weakened, as to be carried about in the Vortex of the true Sun; if it were of less solidity, or less Motion than the Globules towards the Ex - tremity of the Solar Vortex, then it would descend towards the Sun, till it met with Globules of the fame Solidity and Capable of the fame Degree of Motion with it self and then being fix ’ d there, it would be for ever after carried about by the Motion of the Vortex, without either approaching any nearer to or receding from the Sun, and so be - come a Planet Supposing then all this, we are next to imagine that our System was at first divided into several Vortices, in the Center of each of which was a lucid Spherical Body; and that some of these being gradually incrustate, were swallowed up by others which were larger and more powerful, till at last they were all destroy ’ d and swallow ’ d Up by the biggest Solar Vortex, except some few which were thrown off in right Lines from one Vortex. tq another, and so became Comets. And from henCe it appears, that thole Planets which are nearest the Sun are less solid: That is also Des Cartes ’ s Reason why we fee always the lame Face of the Moon; because the Hemisphere which is opposite to the Sun and the Earth is Ibmewhat more solid than the other: Because also the Mat - ter of th e first Element which makes up the Body of the Sun, moves with greater Velocity the Parts, of the Vortex, and the Bodies Iwjmming in it, than those that are remoter: Therefore those Planets which are nearer to the Sun, must finish their Periods sooner than those which are more remote from him. And the Reason why the Planets revolve round their Axis, is because, according to this Hypothdis, they were lucid, Sun - like, and revolving Bodies before But notwithstanding all this fine Romance, it is ( first, ) certain that a Vortex produced by the Re - volution of a Sphere about its Axis, must be pro - pacated in Infinitum, if nothing hinder it: And Vol. II. ri - t therefore, since there must be as many Vortices as there are fix ’ d Stars, one Vortex would certainly - run into another, and every Particle would be added by a Motion compounded of the Motion of all the central Spheres j which is absurd and con - trary to that Constancy, Limitation and Uniform - ty which is observ ’ d in the P hcenomena oi the Hea - venly Bodies. . Since the Motion and Parts of the Vortices nearest the Center, is fwifeer than that of the more remote, they must press upon the Exterior Parts, and thereby perpetually impart some Part of their Motion to them; and therefore those interior Parts of the Vortex will be continually lessening some Part of their Motion, which never being re - stored, these Parts must still move flower and flow - er by Degrees, till at last all the Motion will be quite destroy ’ d. . According to this Hypothesis, each Planet is of the fame Density with the Parts of the Vortex in which it swims, being govern ’ d by the fame Laws of Motion, and is, as it were, only some concreted Parts of the Vortex. But the Times of the Peri - odical Motion of Bodies carried about by a Vor - tex, are in a duplicate Ratio of their Distances from their Center; as the incomparable Sir Isaac Newton hath demonstrated in Se. IX. of his Princip. Whereas the Squares of the Times of the Periodical Revolutions of the Planets are as the Cubes of their mean Distance from the Center, or from the Sun: Wherefore the Planets cannot be carried about by a Vortex. . If a Vortex run out in Infinitum, then would a Body carried round by it certainly describe a perfect Circle, unless some Thing solid did hin - der it; and therefore the greater Distance there were between those solid Bounds, or the larger the Bason be which contains the Vortex, in refpedfc of the Orbit of the Body Carried about in it, the nearer would this Orbit be to a Circle; that is, the Excentricity of the Planets nearest the Sun, would be less than that of those which are more remote: But the direct contrary to this is true in Fa &, the Excentricity of Mercury being great - ter than that of Saturn . A Body carried about in a Vortex of the fame Density with ir, would necessarily describe a Cir - cle, to - whole Plane the Axis of the central Body producing the Circulation of the Fluid, would be perpendicular: And yet there is not one Planet to the Plane of whose Orbit the Suns Axis is perpen - dicular. . The Comets have their Orbits not only ob - pique to, but some Times at right Angles, with the Plane of the Ecliptick; some Times the Course of these Comets is diametrically opposite to that of the Sfin: They persevere in their Motion without any Change: By Lines drawn from them to the Sun, they describe equal Areas in equal Times; and some Times they enter into the Vor - tex of the Sun. All which is impossible if the Solar Vortex mov ’ d round forcibly enough to carry these vast Bodies of the Planets along with it. Mr. Leibnit hath indeed a little altered and mended this Hypothesis oi Des Cartes; he hath ac - commodated ic better to the Celestial Pheno - mena, and made it more agreeable to the Rules of Geometry. And First he shews, That all Bodies, which in a Fluid describe a Curve - line, are moved by that Fluid: For of themselves they would de -. scribe - very. v KTivrscaBHS scribe right Lines, and nothing ( he faith ) but the Fluid concurrs to turn them out of the Way. Secondly., He endeavours to shew, that every Planet is carried about by a Motion compounded of two other Motions; vi. x he Harmonical Cir - cubation of the different Fluid, and the Paracen - trical Motion of access to, or recess from the Sun. ! The Planets by a Radius from the Sun dekribe Areas proportional to their Times; now the Fluid that carries the Planets;, must of necessity circu - late so as to produce this Effect, which cannot be done otherwise than by supposing innumerable concentrical Orbits of exceeding ' Thinness to make up the Vortex; every one of which, hath its own proper Way of Circulation, vis (. Those Orbs which are nearest the Sun move fafteft, and the Velocities of the Circulations are every where reciprocally proportional to the Distances of the respective Orbs from the Sun, which will necks - warily make the Planet to describe equal Areas in equal Times, let it be in any Part of the Vortex: For these Areas are in a compounded Ratio of their Radii or Distances from the Sun, and in a reciprocal One of the Archs or Lengths of the Circulation, which in this'Cafe will make a pro - portion of Equality: And this Law of Circulati - on of the Vortex, he calls Harmonical. The Paracentric ! Motion is compounded of two others; that is, the Excujfory Impression of the Harmonick Circulation, whereby all Bodies moving in a - Curve endeavour to recede from the Center by the Tangent and the Attra & ion of the Sun, or the. Planets Gravitation towards him. And this, Mr, Leibnit is of Opinion, arises from an Impulse communicatediby the circulating Fluid. Now since the Planets move in EHipfes, in one of whose Foci the Sun is placed, and by Lines drawn from him, do describe equal Areas in equal Times, which no other Law of a circulating Fluid, but the Harmonic A Circulation can account for, we must find out a Law for the Paracentric k Motion that may make the Orbits elliptical. The excuse - sory Impression of the circulating Fluid, would throw off the Planet from the Center by the Tangent, wherefore the Attraction of the Sun, or the Gravitation of the Planets towards it, must be fufftcient to destroy the EffeCts; and besides, to make them move in elliptick Orbits, which cannot be brought about, unless this Attraction or Gravitation be reciprocally as the Squares of the Distances from the Focus: And this is the Sum of Mr. Leibnit s Improvement of this Hypothe - cs. J But this Account must be false for these Rea - sons; First, Because the Comets, as hath been said before, have their Orbits, some of them very ob - pique too; nay, sometimes at right Angles with the Plane of the Ecliptick, and their Courses are some Times quite contrary to those of the Planets. Now these Comets describing about the Sun Areas proportionable to the Times, must also according to their Motion be carried about by an harmony - ly circulating Fluid: But then we fh ’ all have Vortices moving contrary to Vortices, which is very absurd. . In equable Motions, the Times are always iireUly as the Spaces, and reciprocally as the Velo - cities; but in a circular Motion, the Spaces in one Revolution are as the Radii; and in an harm - nica ! Circulation, the Velocities are reciprocally as the tytfiif and therefore the Periodical Times of a Fluid circulating harmonically are in a duplicate Proportion of the Radii: Whereas the Periodical Times of the Planets are in sesquiplicate Proper - tion of their Distances from the Center, or of their radii; and consequently the Planets cannot be carried by an harmonically circulating Fluid, It may, perhaps, be alledged here,, that this harmonical Circulation is not continued from Mer - cury to Saturn, but is interrupted, and reaches on - ly from the Perihelion of Mercury to his Aphelion p. and is there again interrupted, and so on through ' the whole System of the Planets; but this would produce a Deformity, which is very unlike the Am - ple Uniform Measures of Nature every where else And besides the: Comets moving forward in the Zodiack, pass through all thele imaginary Chasms ' and Interfaces, and yet move in the fame Manner as if they were carried by a Fluid circulating har - conically, according ro some uniform Law; new - ther do their Appearances give any Ground to suspect such Interruptions as these. Vid. Dr. Cheyne Phil. Prin. of Natural Religion.

cartilagoscutiformis.c: CARTILAGO Scutiformis, is one of the Car - tilages of the Larynx; ’ tis called in Greek fkfo u - Jv, because of its Figure. It makes that Protube - rance in the fore - part of the Larynx called Pomum Adami. It is about one Inch broad but not so long, being Concave within and Convex without. Its four Angles have each a small Production; the two upper, which are longer, are tied to the Horns of the Os Hyoides; and the two lower to the second Cartilage, which is called Cricoides or Annularis, from its being like a Ring.

cantonsinpainting.c: CANTONS, in Painting, are the most perfect fort of Drawings on Paper, which are subservient to great Works, that must be throughly finished, all Sketches, Drawings, Models, and all other Works being preparatory only, and to be reduced to Cartons. This way was purchased by Michael Angelo and Raphael Vrbin, &c. the Cartons at Hampton Court being the Work of Raphael. They are sometimes made by measuring the Height and Breadth of the Place where the Paint - ing is design ’ d to stand; and then by dividing that Space into Squares, and one afterwards of the fame Dimensions on Paper; they draw on the latter the Subject of their Story or Design, transferring it afterward from the Carton to the Wall, by paint - ing it there in Oil, G ? c. But some Great and Experience ’ d Masters will be able to do all this without the help of the Gratef as they call it; that is, the Division of the Space or Table into Square, tho ’, after all, ’ tis a good fe cure way.

cartouch.c: CAR TOUCH, is a Case of Wood about Inches thick at the Bottom, girt round about with Marlin, and holding about Musket Balls, be - sides or Iron Balls of a Pound Weight. Tis fired out of a Hob t, as they call it, that is, a small Mortar; and is very proper for defending a Pass.

cartouzesinarchitecture.c: CARTOUZES, in Architecture, are much the fame with Modi lions, only these are fet under the Cornifti in Wainicorting, and those under the Cornish at the Eves of a House. Some Workmen call them Dentils or Teeth.

carucatefromcaruca.c: CARUCATE, from Caruca, and French Car - rue, a Plough, was the Ancient Plough Land; and fignificd as much Arable Ground as could be till ’ d with one Plough in a Year. This in Rich.. Reign, was computed at Acres, but Was afterwards varied; and the Measure of a C arm ate was dise - rent according to Time and Place, CASE - C E N C E M

casement.c: CASEMENT, the fame with Cavetto, in Archi - texture, is a hollow Moulding; some fay some of a Circle in Compass.

cassino.c: CASSINO, in the Military Language, is a Farm House where a Number of Soldiers have polled themselves, in order to make a stand against the Approaches of an Enemy.

castellorumoperation.c: CASTELLORUM Operation, was formerly Ser - vice of Work and Labour to be done by inferior Tenants for the Repair or Building of Castles. To this some came in Person, and others contra - buted, and it was one of the three necessary Taxes from which few Persons were exempted. Dr. Kjnnet.

castingofdrapery.c: CASTING of Drapery, is a Term in Painting, hgnifying a free, easy, genteel, negligent way of loathing any Figure j and when the Drapery is so managed, they fay ’ tis well Call.

cavazioninarchitecture.c: CAVAZION, in Architecture, is the digging or hollowing away of the Earth from the Founda - tion of a Building. Palladio faith it ought to be of the whole Height of the whole Building. CaVETTO, in Architecture, is a hollow Moul - ding of about - or of a Circle in Compass.

causinginarchitecture.c: CAUSING, in Architecture, Signifies Dove - tailing across.

caulicoli.c: CAULICOLI are, in Architecture, the little carved Scrolls which are under the Abacus in the Corinthian Capital. !

casualty.c: CASUALTY, is the Tin - miner's Words for the Earth, a Stony Matter which is by washing in the Stamping Mills, c. separated from the Tin Ore, before ’ tis dried and goes to the Crazing Mill.

cementinarchitecture.c: CEMENT, in Architecture, is a strong bind - ing Mortar. Tis used to Cement Bricks together for some kinds of Moulding j to make a Block, f Bricks for the carving of Scrolls, Capitals, Tis of two forts The hot Cement, which is com - mon, is made by putting to a Pound of Rozin and a Quarter of a Pound of Bees Wax, half an Ounce of fine Brick Dull, and as much Powder of Chalk; and boiling all together in a Pipkin, & c. for about - of an Hour, stirring it all the while j then let it stand or Minutes, and " tis fit lor use. The Bricks to be Cemented must be heated in or by the Fire, and rub ’ d one upon another like Boards in glowing. The told Cement is less common, and is thus made. Grate half a Pound of old Chefhire Cheese, well pared, very final !, and to it, in a Pot put half ? Pint of. Milk, and let it stand all Night the next Morning put it into a Tray, &c. With the Cheese and Milk put half a Pound of very fine powdered and lifted quick Lime, and stir all well together with a Trowel, breaking the Knots of the Cheese if any remain; and then add the Whites of z or Eggs, which incorporate well with the Mixture, and then it will be fit for use: If you would have it reddish, colour it with a little very fine Powder of Bricks.

centresofgravity.c: CENTRES of Gravity. ’ Tis plain that the Cen - tre of Gravity of a Circle, and of a Sphere or Globe ( supposing the Matter truly Homogeneous all over them ) will be their Centre of Magnitude; the Centre, of Gravity of all Parallelograms will be in the Point of Intersection of the two Diago - nals j and the Centre of Gravity of all solid Parallelograms or Parallelepipeds will be in the fame Point of the Plane of Gravity, i. e. in the Point found to be the common Interledion of the two Diagonals of that Plane which cuts the Solid into two Triangular Prisms, and consequently is easily found. The Centre of Gravity of all Plane Tri - angles, is in the Point of Intersection of two Right Lines biffeding any two of their Angles ! and of all solid Triangles or Triangular Prisms it will be in the middle Point of the Diameter of Gravity And that Diameter is found by the common Inter - fedion of two Planes, each of which bifteds one Angle of the Top and Base, and consequently of all the Triangles of which the Prism may be con - ceiled to be composed. If the Prism be of a Quadrilateral, or any other more compounded Form, the thing will be more difficult, because the Centre of Gravity will lie at a proportionable Distance from the Centre of Gra - city of all the Triangular Prisms, that the Mul - angular Solid can be divided into. But tho ’ this be a little more troublesome, " tis by no means im - possible, any more than to find the Centres of Gravt C E N Gravity of Cones, Pyramids, &c. for which you have Rules enough in Stcvinus, Lib. z. Elem. Stat. and in many other Authors.

centreofoscillation.c: CENTRE of Oscillation. That Point of any Figure where all the Forces are united is but one, ( supposing the Figure to revolve found a Point or Axis ) and consequently one only simple Pendulum can be made, whole Vibrations ( the Forces in both being equal ) ( hall be Ifochronical to those of the whole Solid and because that Point in the Ff gure wherein all the Forces are so united, deter - mines the Length of the simple Ifochronical Pen - dulum, and is that wherein all the Figure is sup - pefedtobe contracted, with all the Forces, while it vibrated, therefore ’ tis called the Centre of Ofcil - lation and since the Centres of Percussion and Oscillation in every Figure are the fame, the way of Inveffigation of both muff be the fame: See Centre of Percussion.

centreofpercussion.c: CENTRE of Percussion of a Body in motion, is that Point wherein all the Forces of that Body are considered as united in one so that the Force of Percussion in that Point is greater than any where else; so that the Centre of Percussion is the fame with helped to the Forces, as that of Gravity is in helped of the Weights. In calculating the Centres of Gravity, wefuppofe the Figures to be simply suspended to a Point or Axis: But in order to calculate the Centres of Per - cushion, the Figures are supposed to be actually re - solving about a Point or Axis and as there the simple Momenta are considered, here they are confi - dered also with the Velocity super. added. And as the Sum of all the simple Momenta, on each Side the. Centre of Gravity are equal, so here the Sum of all the Forces on every Side the Centre of Percuf - sion muff be equal and therefore, as the Centre of Gravity is found by dividing the Sum of all the Moments by the Sum of all the Weights, so to find the Centre of Percussion you muff divide the Sum of all the Rectangles under all the Momenta, and their relpediveVelocities, by the Sum of all them - ments: See more of this in Hayes ’ Fluxions, P. i

certmoney.c: CERT Money, quasi Certa Money a, was the Head Money or common Fine paid by the Refiants and Tenants of several Mannors to their Lords. In some Ancient Records this is call ’ d Certum Let c.

cerusse.c: CERUSSE. In Phil. Trans. N.. there is this Account of the way of making Geruffe Piggs of clean and soft Lead are cast into thin Plates, a A Yard long and fix Inches broad these are rolled round so as the Surfaces no where meet to touch, for where they do no Cerusse grows. Each of these is put into a Pot just capable of holding one, and upheld by a little Bar from the Bottom, that it come not to touch the Vinegar which is pur into each Pot to effed: the Conversion. Twenty of these a - breast are put into a square Bed of new Horsedung j and each Pot is covered with a Plate of Lead, and then over that with Boards as close - as can well be. This repeated four times makes one Heap as ’ tis called, containing Pots. After three Weeks the Pots are taken up, the Plates unrolled, laid on Boards, and beaten with & Battledore till all the Flakes come off, which, if good, are thick, hard, and weighty. These Flakes are ground with Water between Milftones to al most an impalpable Fineness after which ’ tis mouldred into sey eral Parcels, and exposed to the Sun to dry ’ till it become hard and fit for use. ’ Tis observed that some Pots will yield thick and good Flakes, while others alike ordered and - fet by them, without any possible Diftincftion of Disadvantage, yield few, small, or none at all. Sometimes the Pots are taken up all dry, and fame - times C H A C H A times they prove best; sometime ’ s they are taken up wet. The Plates that cover the Pots yield better and thicker Flakes than do the Rolls within; and the Outside next to the Planks bigger and bet - ter than the Inside next to the Rolls, and to the Spirits which first rife from the Vinegar.

cession.c: CESSION, is one Manner of an Eccjefiaftical Benefice ’ s becoming void. By the Canon Law, if a Clerk have one Living, though under Pound per Annum Value, and takes a Second of what Value soever, the former is void without aDifpen - fation; that is, ' tis void de Jure, fed non defaclo. But by Statute, if a Clerk have one Benefice of Pound per Annum, or upwards, and takes another of any Value whatsoever with Cure of Souls, and without Dispensation, the former Living is pso faElo, void: And this kind of Voidance of a Li - ving is called Cejfton. And what is called CeJJion in other Benefices, is called Creation in relation to a Bifhoprick; for if an incumbent be made a Bi - shop, his Benefice is said to be void by Area - tion.
CESSION, in the Civil Law, is putting ano - her Person, who therefore is called the

cessionary.c: CESSIONARY, into the Place and Right of the true and proper Creditor, in any Case. This is called also Subrogation.

cessorinlaw.c: CESSOR, in Law, is one that cealeth or new - ledleth so long to perform some Duty belonging to him, as that by this his Cejfe or Ceasing he incurs the Danger of the Law, and hath, or may have, the Writ Cessavit ( see Vol. I. J brought against him. And where it is laid in their Terms, the Tenant Cejfeth without any more Words, it is to be under - stood, the Tenant ceafeth to do by his Lands or Tenement.

chafer.c: CHAFER Y, is the Term for one of the Forges in an Iron - work, ( fee Iron. ) The other is called the Finery.

chafe.c: CHAFE - WAX, is an Officer belonging to the Lord High Chancellor who fits the Wax for the Sealing of Writs, and such other Instruments as are his Order made to be lent out.

chalcography.c: CHALCOGRAPHY, is the Art of Engraving, Sculpture, ( c.

chamberlain.c: CHAMBERLAIN, from the French Chambel - lan, i. e. Cubicularim vel PrafeEtus Cubiculi; is used in divers Senses in our Chronicles, and old Books of Laws and Statutes: As the Lord Great Cham - berlin of England, Lord Chamberlain of the King ’ s House, the King ’ s Chamberlain, E.. c.. R.. c.. To whose Office itapper - taiueth to look to the King ’ s Chambers and Ward - robe, and to govern the under Servants and Offi - cers there. There is also a Chamberlain of any of the King ’ s Courts; as Chamberlain of the Ex - chequer, H.. Stat.... it... H... There is a Chamberlain e / North Wales, of Chefter, of the City of London: This Officer is commonly the Receiver of all Rents and Reve - nues belonging to the City whereof he is Cham - berlin. When there is no Prince of Scales and Earl of Chefter, the Chamberlain of Chefter hath the Receipt and Return of all Writs coming thi - ther out of any of the King ’ s Courts. In the Exchequer there be two Officers of this Name, who were wont to keep a Controulment f the Pells of Receipt and Exitw; and kept cer - tain Keys of the Treasury and Records. They kept also the Keys of that Trealury where the Leagues of the Kings Predeceffors, and divers Ancient Books, as Dooms - day Book, and the Black Book of the Exchequer remain.

champion.c: CHAMPION, in the Common Law, isuledno less for him that triet a Combat in his own Cause, than for him that fighrcth in the Quarrel or Place of another: And according to Bra El on and lomeo - thers, it is uled for one that holdeth by Serjeantry, or some such Service, of another. There is also an Officer now called

CHAMPION of the King; who at a Coronati - on, while the King IS thinner, is to ride armed, Cap - a - pee, into FKcftmivfter Ball, and by a Herald make a Challenge, That if any Person shall deny the King ’ s Title to the Crown, he is thereby ready to defend it: Which done, the King drinks to him, and fends him a Guilt Cap with a Cover, full of Wine, which he hath for his Fee.

chancellor.c: CHANCELLOR of the Exchequer; who fits in the Court and Exchequer Chamber, and with the reft of the Court ordereth things to the King ’ s best Benefir. He is always in Commission with the Lord Treafurerfor the letting of Crown Lands, ( c. and hath by the Privy Seal from the King, Power with others, to compound for Forfeitures of Bonds upon Penal Statutes; and his Power extends to the First Fruits Office, ( c.

CHANCELLOR of the Dutchy of Laneafter, is an Officer in that Court principally to judge and determine all Controversies between the King and his Tenants about the Dutchy Land; and otherwise to direct all the King ’ s Affairs belonging to that Court:

chancery.c: CHANCERY, is a Court of Equity and Con - science, moderating the Registers of other Courts, and is ' not tied strictly to the Letter of the Law.. The Officers in it are, The Lord Chancellor, or Keeper of the Great Seal: Twelve Mailers of Chancery, whereof some are always Sitting in; their turn on the Bench, as Afliftanrs. The Sk Clerks, who have under them about Clerks, in the Nature of Attorneys in the Court; two Chief Examiners, who have each of them several Clerks. One Chief Register, who usually hath four or five Deputies. The Clerk of the Crown, The Warden oi the Fleer, the Ufiier, Serjeant lat Arms and Cryer of the Court. The Curfirorfc and their Clerks of the Fetry Bagg. The Clerk, of the Appeals, of the Faculties, Patents, Present - tatior s, Difmiflions. Licences to Allienate, Injun - C H I C H A ctions, Enrollments, Protections, Subpoenas and of the Affidavits, ( c. The Sealer, Chafe - wax, ( c.

chapel.c: CHAPEL, is of two forts; either adjoining to a Church, as a Parcel of the fame, which Men of Worth hold, ut ibidem Familiaria Sepulchra sib conftituant; or else Separate from the Mother Church, where the Pariffi is wide; and is usually called a Chapel of E fe, because Built for the Ease of luch Pariffiioners as dwell too far from the Church. Sometimes this is served by a Curate, provided at the Charge of the ReCtor, and some - times at Theirs that have Benefit by it, according to Custom or Composition. And some of these lat - ter Chapels which have a Maintenance perpetual by some Lands Charitably bestowed on them, or otherwise without the Charge of the ReCtor of the Church j are called Free - Chapels. CHAPTER, Capitulum, in the Canon and Common Law, is either Congregatio Clericorum in Ecclefia Cathedrals, regulars vel Collegiata; or Lo - cus in quo fiunt tommunes traftatus Collegiaibrurn. Covpel. These Chapters arose thus; in Ancient Times the Biffiops had their Clergy residing with them in their Cathedrals, to Assist them in the performance of Sacred Offices and in the Govern - ment and Dilcipline of the Church. And even af - ter Parochial Settlements were made, there were still a Body of Clergy - men, which continued with the Biffiop at his Church and were indeed his Family and Ma stained out of his Income. After the Monastic Life grew into Request an Reputation, many Biffiops chcfe to have Monks rather than Seculars to reside with them and attend them in their Cathedrals. And these Bodies of either Mbnaftickj or Seculars, had the lime Privilege of Chufing the Biffiop and being Els Council, which the whole Clergy of the Dio - cele had before. But by degrees their Dependance upon the Biffiop and Relation to him grew less and less and then they had distend Parcels of the Bi - ffiop ’ s Estate Assigned for their Maintenance; at last the Biffiop had little more left than the Power of Visiting them. And on the other hand, thele Capital Bodies did by degrees also lose their Privi - leges; particularly that of causing the Biffiop, for Which the Kings of England had a long struggle with the Pope, but at last Men. got this Power veiled in the Crown, and now the Dean and Chapter have only the Shadow of it. The fame Prince did also rejeCt the Monks out bf these Cathedrals and placed Secular Canons in their Room. And those whom he thus Regulated are called Deans and Chapters of the Nevo Founda - tion: As are Canterbury, Winch eft er, Worcefter, Ely, Carlifte, Durham, Rpchefter and Norwich; and of such fort are the Chapters of the five New Sees, of Peterburgh, Oxford, Glaueefter and Bristol, to which may be added Westminster; though this last Biffioprick is now funk, and the Monastery i turned into a Collegiate Church by Queen Eli a - j both.

chaptrellsinarchitecture.c: CHAPTRELLS, in Architecture, are the fame with Impofts; and signify those Parts on which the i Feet of Arches stand. Their height of thickness: ought to be equal to the breadth of the lower part of the Key Stone.

chargedcylinder.c: CHARGED CYLINDER is that Part of the Chace, of a great Gun where the Powder and Ball s are placed.

chargeoflead.c: CHARGE of Lead is Pigs, and each Pig: contains Stone wanting Pound i. e. every: Stone ( here ) is Pound,

charterinlaw.c: CHARTER, in Law, is a written Evidence of any Thing done between Man and Man: And some Times Charters are called Charters of the Kjng, as when the King passeth any Grant to any Person, Body, Politick, ( c. to excuse a Man from being empanelled on a Jury Charters of Par - don, whereby Men are forgiven Fellonies, ( c.

charts.c: CHARTS uled at Sea, are either the or Mercators Charts, as his usually called, though it ffiould indeed be rather ' called Wrights Chart, See the Word Plain Chart and Mercator in Vol. I.

chattelscatada.c: CHATTELS, Catada, is a Word Which came to us from the Normans, who called all movable Goods by this Name, the contrary was called Fief, or as we now call it Fee: But now in our Law, Chattels are all Sorts of Goods movable and immovable except such as are in the Nature of Free - hold or Parcel thereof. They Reckon Chattels also to be either personal or real. The Former are such as either do belong immediately to the Person of a Man, as his Horse, Sword, ( c. or such Things as being injuriously withheld from him, a Man hath no way to recover but by personal ACtion. But Chattels real do not appertain to the Person, but to some other Thing by way of De - tendance, as a Box with Charters of Land, Ap - ples upon a Tree, ( c. Such Things also as ne - ceflfarily issue out of some immovable Thing to a Person, as a Lease or Rent for Years, they call a Chattel real. Alio to hold at will, is a Chattel real.

chantry.c: CHANTRY is a Church or Chapel endow - ed with Lands or other yearly Revenue, for the Maintenace ( formerly, ) of one or more Priests day -, ly Saying or Singing Mass for the Souls of the Donors, and such others as they shall appoint. CHEMISE, the Art of Calling Figures in Me tals.

chest.c: CHEST - ROPE, in a Ship, is the fame with the Guest or Gift - Rope, and is added to the Boat - Rope when the Boat is towed at the Stern of the. Ship, to keep her from Shearing j i. e. from swing - ing to and fro;

chissels.c: CHISSELS used in Joynery and Carpentry are of several Kinds j as. The Former, which is used first of all before the Paring Chiffel, and just after the Work is scribe ’ d, and a. little without the scribed Stroaks, and with its Basil outwards. . The Paring Chiffel hath a very fine and smooth Edge, and ’ tis used to pare off, or smooth the Irregularities which the Former makes. This is not struck with the Mallet as the Former is, but prdfed with the Shoulder of she Work - man, who hold C H Y e h o holds the Chijjel between the Fore and little Fin - gers of his right Hand, and with the two middle Fingers clutched upon it. . The Skew Former, Which is a Chijjel used for cleansing Acute Angles by the Point or Corner of its narrow Edge, and where the Angles of other Cbijfels cannot come. . The Mortefs CbiJJeH is narrow, but very thick and strong to endure hard Blows with the Mallet, and tis ground to a very broad Basil; its Use is to cut deep square Holes in the " Wood, Which are called Mortejfes: These are of several Sites, according as the Breadth of the Mortejfes require. ’..,, . The Gouge is a Chijjel with a round Edge, one Size of which serves to prepare the Way for an Augre; and others to cut such Wood as is to be rounded or hollowed, &c. . Socket Chtjfels are such as are chiefly used by Carpenters, and have their Shank made with a hollow Socket at the Top, to receive a strong wooden Sprig made to fit into that Socket, with a square Shoulder above it; which makes them very strong to bear the heavy Blows of the Mallet. They diftingiulh these Socket Cbijfels according to the Breadth of the Blade, and call them half Inch, three quarter Inch Cbijfels, Inch and half, Two Inch, and three Inch Chilfels. . The Ejpping Chijjel is a Socket Chijjel about an Inch broad, and having a blunt Edge with no Basil to it; its Use is to rip or tear two Pieces of Wood fattened together from one another, by forcing in the blunt Edge between the two Pieces.

chrism.c: CHRISM was anciently ( in Times of Popery ) a Confection of Oil and sweet Balsam, which was consecrated by the Bishop, and used in Baptism, Confirmation, Extreme Undion, ( Jc.

chrisomchrijmale.c: CHRISOM, Chrijmale, was the Face - cloth r Piece of Linen laid over the Child ’ s Head when it was baptized: Whence in our Weekly Bills of Mortality, such Children as die in the Month are called Chrijbms.

clampnails.c: CLAMP NAILS, are such Nails as are used to fallen on Clamps in building and repairing of Ships.

clamp.c: CLAMP ’ D. When a Piece of Board is fitted with the Grain to the End of another Piece of Board across the Grain, the former Board is said to be clamp ’ d. And thus are the Ends of Tables usually clamfd, to keep them from warping or calling.

clark.c: CLARK - OBSCURE, is a Term in Painting; and signifies the Art of distributing Lights and Shadows advantageously, as well on particular Objedls as on a Picture in general. On particular Objedls ' tis necessary to give them an agreeable Roundnels and a convenient Relieve; and in the Pidlure in general, to expose the Objects with Pleasure to the View of the Spectators, by giving the Eye an Occasion to reft; which is belt done by an happy Distribution of great Lights and Sha - dows, which by their Opposition fet off one a - nother.

clasp.c: CLASP - NAILS, are such whose Heads are brought into a little Compass, so that they will sink into the Wood, and when drove home, let a Smoothing Plane go over them.

clench.c: CLENCH - NAILS, are such as will drive with - out splitting the Boards, and draw without break - ing. They are used by Boat and Barge Builders and are proper for any Building with Boards that mull be taken down again: For fine Work they are made with Clasp - heads.

clepsydra.c: CLEPSYDRA. In the Memoirs of the French Royal Academy for Apr.. there is an Ac - count, by Mr. Varignon, of a General and Geo. metrick Method to make Clepfydrcc or Water - Clocks with any kind of given Vessels; and with any gi - ven Orifices for the Water to issue out at, and ac - cording to any given Velocity of the Waters De - stent.

clouts.c: CLOUTS, are thin Plates of Iron nailed on that Part of the Axle Tree of a Gun - Carriage which comes through the Nave, through which the Lins - pin goes.

clout.c: CLOUT - NAILS, are such as are commonly used for nailing on of Clouts ( or Plates of Iron ) to the Aide Trees of Carriages, and are proper to fallen any Iron to Wood.

cocket.c: COCKET, is a Seal appertaining to the'Queen s Custom - Houle: And also a Scroll of Parchment sealed and delivered by the Officers of the Cu - flom - House to Merchants, as a Warrant that, their Merchandize be Customed; This Word is used also in the Statutes of Bread and Ale, made. where there is mentioned Cocket Bread, among several other kinds: And it seems to have been hard Sea - Bisket, which perhaps had then some Cocket Marmot Seal; or else was so called from its being designed for the Use of the Ccckfwains or Sea - men. !

cocks.c: COCKS, aboard a Ship, are little square Pieces ofBrafswith Holes in them, and put into Wooden Shivers, to keep them from splitting and galling by the Pins of the Blocks in which they move.

codicil.c: CODICIL, is a Schedule or Supplement to a Will or other Writing. ’ Tis used as an Addition to a Testament, when any thing is omitted Which the Testator would add, Explain, Alter; or Re - trad; and is of the fame Nature with a Tefta - ment, but that it is without an Executor i So that a Codicil is a less Solemn Will of one that Dies either Testate or Intestate, without the Ap - ointment of an Heir. Testate, when he that made his Codicil, hath either before dr afterwards made his Testament, on which that Codicil depends, as to which it refers. Intestate, when one leaves be - hind him only a Codicil without ' a Testament, wherein he gives Legacies duly to ' be paid by the Vol. IL C o H Heir at Law, and not by any Heir Instituted by a Will or Testament. ' Codicils first came in use in the Time of Auguftus. A Codicil as well as a Will may be either written or nuncupative Infli - tute of Imp, or Civil Law.

coffer.c: COFFER is a long square Box of the firmeft Timber, about Fobt long, and. Foot broad, wherein Tin Ore is broken to Pieces in a stamp - ing Mill. See T in.

cofferer.c: COFFERER of the King or Queen ’ s House - hold, is a principal Officer in the Court, next un - der the Controller; that in the Counting - house and elsewhere at other Times hath a special Charge and oversight of other Officers of the House for their good Demeanour and Carriage in their Of - fices, to all which he pays their Wages. Vid..

cohesion.c: COHESION of the Parts of Matter. Sir If a Newton at the end of the Latin Edition of his Ad - mirable Opticks, concludes from the Coherence of the Parts of hard and solid Bodies, that their Par - titles do Attract one another by a certain Force - which adts most intensely when the Particles touch one another: at foffie little distance it produces thole Chemical Ejfe & s or Operations, Which you will find an Account ot under the Word AttraBion, and which doth not extend to Remoter Distances, as far at least as Sense can determine j and indeed ’ tis hardly possible to Account for the firmness and so - lidity of many Bodies, which have either a vast number of Pores, o iMeatus in them, and consequent - ly Whose Particles cannot touch one another with their whole Surfaces, Without supposing that thole Particles be either strongly Comprest together, of do strongly Attract the another. But it doth not seem reasonable to attribute this Cohaffion of the Partsfof Matter to any Pressure bf t ) xe / Ether, z. s some have imagined, because there is no certain Experiment of the Existence of any such thing as their / Ether; nor if there were, would it be effectual to Solve this Phenomenon, any more than if is for many others, which they Account for only by this means. But this mutual Attraction of the Parti - cles of Matter within such very narrow, Bounds and Limits, which feerns tb be as much the Law of Nature, as Gravity, &c, will fairly Account: for this hitherto inexplicable Phenomenon. Dr Cheyne takes into Consideration the Plainhefs of the Surfaces bf the Cohering Parts of Matter, in or - der to Account for this Property which indeed seems a necessary requisite. He thinks we may suppose some of the Primary Atoms of Matter of which Bodies are Constituted, td be terminated with plain Surfaces on all Sides: And Such pro - due Bodies bf the ftfidfceft and firmeft Cohesion, others may be terminated partly with Curve as well as partly with plain Surfaces, and these Com - bined may produce Bodies of A Middle Degree of Cohesion, and such as hive Surfaces entirely Curve may produce Fluids; But this will not do a - lone, for though it will bring Bodies to immediate Contadt, it will not keep them there, nor hinder them from being separated by any Force, how small soever: And the Fluids which surround our Globe, as the Particles of Light and Air, will get in between the Surfaces of Bodies when they are at any Distance greater than the Diameters of the Conftitueht Particles of those Fluids, and so by their lateral Pressure Will destroy the Efficacy of that Attractive Force by which Bodies Cohere; For since Light and Bodies At mutually one upon another and that the Panicles of Air endeavour ' G to to recede one groin another ( fee Air and Light ) they will render that part of Attraction whereby Bodies Cohere, altogether insensible at any Dist - ance greater than the length of the Diameters of the Particles of these Fluids: So that the Force by which Bodies Cohere, cannot A t but at very lmallDiftances, and certainly is much greater in im - mediate Contadt, than at any Distance how small soever.

colaptice.c: COLAPTICE, is the Art of Carving or Cut - ting the Refembiances and Figures of Natural Things in Stone. The Term for the Artist here is Lithoxos.

coldshireiron.c: COLDSHIRE Iron, is such as is Brittle when it is Cold. See Iron.

collationeheremitagii.c: COLLATIONE Heremitagii, is a Writ where - by the Queen Confers the keeping of a Hermitage upon a Clerk.

collegiatechurches.c: COLLEGIATE Churches, are Churches Built and Endowed for a Body, Corporate of a Dean or Other President and Secular Pnefts; as Canons or Prebendaries in the said Church. Such as are with us, Wedminfter, PVindfor, Pippon, Woolverhamp - ton, Southwell, Manchejler, &c. None of these Collegiate Churches are Epifeopal Sees or Ca - thedrals. compositionofquantities.c: COMPOSITION of Quantities, with respect to the DoCtrine of Combinations, in the joyning in any Number of Given Quantities, Letters or Figures, one Row with another Row of the fame, or with two or three, or more other Rows. See Combination.

composetioninpainting.c: COMPOSE TION in Painting, comprehends two Parts, Invention and Disposition j one of which finds out ( by the means of History ) proper ObjeCts for a PiCture j and the other places them a - right: the just mixture of which Two Things, according to a true Oecpnomy, is properly Composition.

conatuscentrifugus.c: CONATUS Centrifugus: This is lbmetimes called the Conatm Excujforius, and is always express - fed by the versed Sine of the Angle of Circulation, and these Conatus Centrifugi of Bodies revolving in equal Circles, with an equable Motion, are in a duplicate Ratio, or as the Squares of their Veloci - ties. But if the Bodies revolve in unequal Circles, their Conatus Centrifugi will be in a Ratio, com - pounded of the Ratio of the Squares of the Veloci - ties direBly, and the Simple Ratio of the Radii of those Circles Inverfley. If the Body describe equal Areas, in equal Times ( as is the Case of the Planets which revolve in Ellipses round the Sun ) then the Conatus Centrifugi will be reciprocally as the Cubes of the Radii.

congeneresmujculi.c: CONGENERES Mujculi; are such Muscles in an Animal Body, as serve together to produce the fame Motion; and they are so called, becaufethey. assist one another in their Aftion.

contrate.c: CONTRATE, is a French Term used in Pain - ting and Sculpture, and signifies the due placing of the Different Objects and Parts of the Figures; and produces that Variety which is so pleasing in j the Attitudes, as if in a Grouppe of three Figures, one stand out forward, the other backward, and the third appear to the middle between them / they fay, e o p. ay ’ tis well Contrasted: So they lay also, that to render the ' Attitudes of Figures agreeable and just,, they must be natural and a & ive, varied in their A & ions, and Contrasted in their Members: So that for Figures to be well Contrasted, is for them to be lively, and to fxprcfs the Motion proper to the Design of the whole piece, or of any particular Grouppe.

converginghyperbola.c: CONVERGING Hyperbola, is one. whose Con - cave Legs bend in towards one another, and run both the fame way. See Curves. Converging Series, is a Method of Approxima - tion still nearer and nearer towards the true Root of any Number or Equation, even tho ’ it be im - possible to find any such True Roots in Numbers. See Approximation and Square stoots in VoL I.

copperas.c: COPPERAS. The way of making Copperas is aS follows Copperas Stones, which some call Gold Stones, are found oh the Sea - shore in EJfex, Hamp - shire, and so Weft - ward. There are great Quantities " in the Clifts, but not so Good as those on the Shore, where the Tides Ebb and Flow over them. The best of them are of a bright shining Silver Colour the next, such as are of a Rusty d ep Yellow the worst are such as have Gravel and Dirt in them, of a ladder Umber Colour. In the midst of tiiefe Stones are sometimes found the Shells of Cockles, and other fniall Shell - Fishes small pieces of the planks of Ships, and pieces of Sea - coal ”. In order to the making of Copperas, they make Beds according as the ground will permit those at Deptford are about ioo Foot long, and Foot broad at the Top, and Foot deep, shelving all the way to the Bottom. They Ram the Bed very well, first with strong Clay, and then with the Rubbifii of Chalk, where - by the Liquor which drains out of the Dissolution of the Stones, is convey ’ d into a Wooden Shallow - Trough, laid in the middle of the Bed, and cove - red with a Board being also boarded on all sides, and laid lofi / er at one End than. the other, whereby the Liquor is Convey ’ d into a Cistern under the Boiiing - House. When the Beds are indifferently well dryed, they lay on the Stones about two Foot Thick. These Stones will be five or fix Years before they yield any considerable Quantity of Liquor and before that, the Liquor which they yield is but Weak., They Ripen by the Sun and Rain; yet Experience proves, tha Watering the Stones, although with Water prepared by Lying in the Sun, and poured thro ’ very small Holes of d Watering - Pot, doth Retard the Work. In Time these Stones turn into a kind of Vitri - lick Earth, which would Swell and Ferment like Leavened Dough. When the Bed is come to PerfebHon, then price In four Years they Refresh it, by laying New Stone on the Top. When they make a New Bed, they take a good quantity of the Old Fermented Earth, and mingle St - with New Stones, whereby the Work is fastned. ‘ Thus the Old Earth never becomes Useless. The Cistern before - mentioned is made of strong Oaken ' Boards, well Joined and Calked: That at Deptford will contain Tun of Liquor. Great Care is taken, that the Liquor doth not Drain thro " the Beds, or out of the Cistern. The best way to prevent the fame, is to divide the Cistern in the middle, by Oaken Boards Calked as ber fore whereby one of them may be mended in case of a Defecft. The more Rain falls, the more but the Weaker will be the Liquor: The Goodness whereof is tryed by Weights prepared for that purpose. Four - teen - penny Weight is Rich; or an Egg being put into the Liquor, the higher it swims above the Li - quor, the stronger it is. Sometimes the Egg will Swim near half above the Liquor. Within one Minute after an Egg is put in, the ambient Liquor will Boil and Froth and in three Minutes the Shell will be quite worn off. A Drop of this Liquor falling on the Manufac - tures of Hemp, Flax or Cotton Wool !, will pre - gently burn a hole thro ’ it. As also in W pollen and Leather. Out of the aforesaid Cistern, the Liquor is pump - ed into a Boiler of Lead, about Foot Square, containing about iz Tuns, which is thus ordered. First, they lay long pieces of Cast Iron, z Inches Square, as long as the Breadth of the Boiler, a - bout z Inches one from another, and Inches above the Surface of the Fire. Then Cross - wife they lay ordinary flat Iron Bars as close as they can lye, the Sides being made up with Brick - work: In the middle of the Bottom of this Boiler is laid a Trough of Lead, wherein they put at first pound Weight of Old Iron. The Fewel for Boiling is New - cast le Coals. By degrees, in the Boiling, they put in more Iron, a - mountingin all to pound Weight in a Boiling. As the Liquor waftes in Boiling, they Pump in in frefli Liquor into the Boiler: Whereby, and by aDefedtin ordering the Fire, they were wont to be above Days before it was enough when that is, they Try, by taking tip a small Quantity of Li quor into a shallow Earthen Pan, and observing how soon it will gather and crust about the Sides thereof. But now of late, by the Ingenious Con - trivance of Sir Nicholas Criftp, the Work is much Facilitated.. For at his Work at Deptford, they Boil off three Boilers of ordinary Liquor in one Week which is done, first by ordering the Fur - name so, as that the Heat is convey ’ d to ail Parts of the Bottom and Sides of the Furnace. Then, whereas they were wont to pump Cold Liquor into the Boiler to supply the waste in Boil - ing, whereby the Boiler was checked sometimes so hours, Sir Nicholas hath now a Vessel of Lead, which he calls a Heater, placed at the end of the Boiler, and a little higher, supported by Bars of Iron as before, and fill ’ d with Liquor, which, by a Conveyance of Heat from the Furnace, is kept near Boiling Hot and so continually supplies the Waste of the Boiler without hindring the Boiling. Thirdly, by putting due Proportions of Iron from time to time, in the Boiler as soon as they per - weive the Liquor to Boil slowly, they put in more Iron, which will soon Quicken it. Besides, if they do not continually supply the Boiling Liquor with Iron, the Copperas will gather to the bottom of the Boiler and Melt it and so it will do if the Liquor be hot presently drawn off from the Boiler into a Cooler, so soon as it, is enough. The Cooler is oblong, Foot Long, Foot o ver at the Top, Foot Deep, Taper ’ d towards tfie Bottom, made of Tarras. Into this they let the Liquor run so soon as it is Boil ’ d enough. The, Copperas herein will be Gathering or Shooting, ' or Days, and gathers. as much on the sides, M as ' ! as in. the Bottom fc. above Inches thick. Some put Bufhes into the Cooler, about which the Cop - peras will gather: But at Deptford they make no use. of any. That which sticks to the sides and to the Bufhes, is of a bright Green, that in the Bottom of a foul and dirty - Colour. In the end of Days, they convey the Liquor into another Cooler, and Reserve it to be Boil ’ d again with new Liquor. The Copperas they ftiovel on a Flour adjoin - ing: So that the Liquor may Drain from it into a Cooler. The Steam,, which comes from the Boiling,;. is of an Acrimonious Smell. - Copperas may be Boiled without Iron, but with Difficulty; without it the Boiler will be in danger of Melting. Sometimes in flirting the Earth upon the Beds, they find pieces of Copperas produc ’ d by lying in the Sun.

corbettinarchitecture.c: CORBETT, in Architecture, is a short piece of Timber placed in a Wall with its end sticking out or Inches as occasion serves. The underpart of the end thus sticking out is sometimes cut into the Form of a Boultin, sometimes of an O G - - -, and sometimes of a Face, Sec. according to the Workman ’ s Fancy, the upper side being plain and flat. These Corbets are usually placed for flrengths fake, immediately under the Semigirders of a Platt - form, and sometimes under the Ends of Camber Beams; si which latter Case they are com - monly placed a Foot or two below the Beam, and have a piece of Timber Standing upright close to the W all, from the Corbett to the Beam. Corbetts, also is a Term used by some Architects, for the hallow Nicks in Walls which are left for Images or Figures, or Statues to Hand in;

cornage.c: CORNAGE, in our Law signifies a kind of Grand Sergeanty; the Service of which Tenure is to blow a Horn, when an Invasion of a Northern Enemy is perceived: And by thistmany hold Land in the Northern parts about the Wall, i. e. the Old Picis Wall.

corsned.c: CORSNED, in the Saxon is Ordeal Bread, Panw Conjuratus: For the Saxons had a Superstitious way of Purging themselves of an Accusation, by taking a piece of Bread and eating it with Solemn Oaths and Execrations, that it might prove their Poison,, &c. if they were guilty, which way of speaking is retain ’ d in some places to this day, especially in Sent.

corvus.c: CORVUS, was a Machine invented by the Romans, in the Time of their Conquefts of Sicily y when they first engage ’ d the Carthaginean Fleer, and was framed ( as Polybius describes it Lib. r. ) ' after this manner, On the Prove of their Ships they ereCted a round piece of Timber about i Foot in Diameter, and; Feet in Length, on the Top of which was a Block or Pulley; round this piece of Timber was; a Plat - form of Boards Feet in Length, and is a - bout Foot Long, well framed and fastned with Iron; the Entrance was long ways, and it was; moveable round the aforesaid upright piece of Timber, and could also be hoisted up andfdown, within Foot of the Top, about this Frame was a fort of Parapet Knee high, which was defended ! with upright Bars of Iron, sharp at the Ends, and towards the Top there was a Ring, by the help of which and a Pulley or Tackle it was hoisted and I lowered at pleasure, with this moveable Gallery they Boarded the Enemies Ships ( when they did S not lie Side by Side ) sometimes on their Bow, and ! sometimes in the After - part of the Ship; the Sol - diers keeping the Bofs of their Bucklers Level with the Top of the Parapet, and by the means of i this new Engine got the day of the Carthagineam, in their first Sea Fight with them, tho ’ the Enemy were long before well skill ’ d in Naval Affairs, and ! the Romans perfectly raw and unspilt ’ d.

crownsofcolour.c: CROWNS of Colour i, are certain Coloured Rings which like Halos appear, but of the Colours ol the Rainbow, and at a less Distance than the common Halo ’ s, about the Body of the Sun or Moon. T hese Sir Isaac Newton, in his Opt. Book.. f ag.. slews to be made by the Sun ’ s shining in a fair Day, or the Moon in a clear Night, through a thin, Cloud of Globules of Water or Hail, all of the fame Bigness: And according as the Globules are bigger or lesser, the Diameters of these Crowns, or Rings, will be larger or Smaller; and the more equal these Globules are to one another, the more Crowns of Colours will appear, and the Colours will be the more lively

The Wedge, One of the Five Mechanical Powers, is in the Form of a Prism v whose Top ' and Sides are Parallelograms, but its Ends Isosceles Triangles j whose Altitude is called ! the Altitude of the Wedge, as the Base of each laid Triangle is the Thickness of the Wedge. The right Line connecting the Vertices of the Two Triangles, I is called the Edge; as the Parallelogram which joins their Bases, is called its Dorsum, or Back. The Power of this Engine is easily estimated. and is ( when direCtly applied to the Top or Dorsum of the Wedge ) to the Resistence to be overcome, as the Thickness of the Wedge is to its Altitude ! In the Figure j BA is the Way of the Power, and C D the Way of the Impediment or Resistance s So that while the Wedge is driven down into the Wood, &c. by its whole Altitude, the Wood is di - vided by the entire Thickness of the Wedge, and this every where proportion ably, as follows from the Nature of a Triangular Figure. Wherefore a Wedge, whose Thickness is to its Altitude or Length in a little greater Proportion, than as the Power applied is to the Resistance or Tenacity of the Wood, will cleave or divide it. cupuloinarchitecture.c: CUPULO, in Architecture is an Arched Room or Turrent standing on the very Top of a Dome or great Building; in Form either Circular or Po - lygonal; Lome call it a Lanthorn.

curator.c: CURATOR, in the Civil Law is a Person Re - gularly appointed to take care of another, as sup - pose of a Minor, by his Confcent from Years of Age to; on the Determination of a Trial at Law, where the Magistrate may appoint a Cu - razor ( ot the Minor. The Magistrate also might appoint a Curator for a Mad - man, a Prodigal Deaf or Dumb Person, as also for the Estates of Debtors, and of Persons dying without Heirs.

currents.c: CURRENTS, are certain Progressive Motions of the Water of the Sea in several Places, either quite down to the Bottom, or to a certain determin - name Depth; by which a Ship may happen to be carried forward more swiftly, or retarded in her Course, according to the Direction or Setting of j the Current in, with, or against the Course or Way of the Ship.. The first thing therefore to be known, is which j Way the Current lets; and if its Motion be fwif t, j great and strong this will be - best discovered by I keeping an exaCt Account of the Ships Way both Outward and homeward, according to the belt Me - tho of what the Seamen call their Dead Heckr king, being very curious indbferving the way the Ship makes by the Log - line; for us not the Cor - rest Account, but the Dead Reckoning, that must here assist you. Therefore you must be very care - ful to observe how the Ship goes by it, when you fail near the Meridian; how she is drawn from her Course; as also, when Hie is steered direCtly East and Weft; take good Notice Whether she alter her Latitude. As for those Guejfes, by th z Rjpplings of the Wa - ter, and by the driving of Froth, &c. along Shore, when you are in fight of it, they will be of little wfe. But the most usual and most useful way of observing the setting of a Current is thus ' When there is a smooth Sea, and not much Wind, heave out the Boat, with three or four Hands in her, together with a Compass, a Log - line, and Half - minute Glass, with also a Line or Small War ? of about an Hundred Fathoms long; Eo the End of which Line fasten a Triangular Piece of Board, as a b c, and to one of the Angles fallen a good heavy Piece of Lead to sink it. Some use instead of this Board a Kettle tied by the Bail, ( which may do tollera - bly well ). When you are off from the Ship, cast over your Board or Kettle, letting it sink at least. Fathom; and if you have Line enough, let it down ioo or io Fathom: Then belaying the Line fast about her Stem, it will bring her up, and make her ride as if file were at an Anchor. Then cast ' over your Log, turn up the Glass, and as you veer out the Log - line, fet the Drift of the Log with your Compass: So shall you know whether there be any Current or no; and if any, how it lets; as also the Rate of its driving. Only remem - ber to add always to the Drift, if the Line she ride by be of Fathom, Part; if of Fathom,; if of ioo Fathom, the f Part, &c. of the Drift more, for the Drift of the Boat; for though the Boat may seem to ride r lie still, yet she is found by Experience to drive at the fame Time. N. B. Whether these Allowances be the very j Truth or not, I cannot fay: They are said to agree with Experience, and therefore may be us ’ d till f better Observations of these things may be made Only this is certain, That the bigger the Board and Weight is that the Boat is to ride by, the less will be her Drift. As if a Ship fail N. N. E. Miles, in a Cur - rent setting the fame way, and in the fame Time Miles, her true Course will be N. N. E, Miles in the fame Time. But if the Current fet direCtly against the Ships Course, it will abate of her Motion forward in Proportion to the Velocity ot the Drift. As if a Ship fail N. E. Miles in a Current setting S. cursory.c: CURSORY, is a Piece or little Ruler or Label of Brass being divided like a Line of Sines, and Sliding in a Groove or Notch along the middle of another Label or Ruler, representing the Horizon, and always at Right Angles to it: ’ Tis used in the Analemma, which lee. CURVATUREo / a Line, is the peculiar man - ner of its bending or Flexure, whereby it, becomes a Curve of such peculiar Properties. Thus the Curvature of the Circle is such, that all Points of the Periphery are equally Distant from one Point within call ’ d the Center. The Curvatures of dis - ferent Circles are to one another Reciprocally as their Radii.

The incomparable Sir Isaac Newton gives this following Enumeration of Geometry - cal Lines of the Third orQubickJOrder; in which you have an admirable account of many Species of Curves which exceed the Conick - Se & ions, for they go no higher than the Quadratic or Se - Second Order. " f The Orders of Geometric Lines. . cothickmannerofbuilding.c: COTHICK Manner of Building, Was uncap - pily brought into Use, after the Irruption of those barbarous Nations, the Goths and Vandals s &c. from the North, and the Moors and Arabs, from the South and Eafi, into the Civiliz ’ d World.. These rude People demol idl ’ d what they could of the Ancient Greek and Roman Ar - chitecture, and instead of those Admirable arid Regular Orders and Mariner of Building, intro - due ’ d a licentious and fantaftical Manner, which, tho ’ sometimes adorned with Expensive Carvings / and Costly, tho ’ Lamentable, Imagery, is without any of that August Beauty, and just Symmetry, - which the Fabricks of the Ancients entertain us with.

catching.c: CATCHING, is a Term us ’ d in the Art of Drawing or Designing in Black and White; and by it is understood a manner of Shadowing by a continual Series, or Succession of many Lines shorter, or longer; closer or more separate; ob - pique, or direct, according as the Work re - quires, to render it more or less enlighten ’ d.

char.c: CHAR - Pewwy, Scharn - penny, and sometimes Schorn - penny. It appears from our old Books, that formerly some Customary Tenants were obliged to pen up their Cattle at Night in the Pound or Yard of their Lord, for the benefit of their Dung, or Scearn, as is the Saxon Word '. And if they did not do this, they were obliged to pay a fmallCom - sensation which therefore was called by this name of Scbarn - penny, that is, Muclypenny, or Dung - penny.
